aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription:
Welcome to Dr Nimra | Health After 60 🩺

I'm Dr Nimra, this channel exists for one reason: to explain, in plain and simple language, what your 15-minute doctor's visit doesn't have time to explain.

Every week I break down what really happens inside your body after 60, and what you can do about it:
💊 Medicines: what your pills really do, side effects, and dangerous combinations
🥗 Food & diet: what to eat, what to limit, and why
🚶 Exercise & mobility: simple movement that keeps you strong and independent
😴 Sleep, bathroom and daily habits: the small things that add up
❤️ Heart, blood pressure, blood sugar, kidneys, bones, brain and eyes

⚠️ Disclaimer
The content on this channel is for general education and information only. It is not personal medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Never start, stop or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have a medical emergency, call your local emergency number.

records.text:
Is 150 Normal After 65? The REAL Blood Pressure Target (Doctor Explains)

Is 150 "normal" for your age? Is "100 plus your age" true? After 65, there is a lot of confusion about blood pressure targets. In this video, Dr Nimra explains what the biggest studies in older people really found, what today's guidelines recommend, and the three things that decide what YOUR number should be.

In this video, Dr Nimra explains:
✅ Why "100 plus your age" is a myth
✅ What the HYVET, SPRINT and STEP trials found in people over 60, 75 and 80
✅ The warning signs that your blood pressure is too low
✅ How to measure your blood pressure at home the right way
✅ 5 questions to ask your doctor

🔔 Subscribe for new videos every Tuesday and Saturday: https://www.youtube.com/@DrNimraHealth?sub_confirmation=1
💬 Tell me in the comments: did you grow up hearing "100 plus your age"?
📤 Share this with someone over 65 who checks their blood pressure.

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 Is 150 normal after 65?
2:36 The "100 plus your age" myth
4:25 What the big studies found
7:31 The blood pressure targets today
8:56 3 things that decide your number
11:13 When blood pressure is too low
12:42 How to measure at home the right way
14:40 5 questions for your doctor
15:27 Recap

#seniorhealth  #healthafter60  #bloodpressure  #hypertension  #hearthealth 

⚠️ Disclaimer: This video is for general education and information only and is not personal medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Do not start, stop or change any medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist.

subtitles.plaintext:
Picture this.
You're sitting at your kitchen table.
You wrap the cuff around your arm, press
the button, and wait.
The numbers come up, 150 over 85.
Now, what do you think?
Is that fine for your age?
Or is it a problem?
If you ask three people, you might get
three different answers.
Your neighbor says, "That's normal at
our age."
Somebody on the internet says, "After
65, you should never push it lower. It's
dangerous."
And your doctor wants to add another
tablet.
So, who is right?
Here's the truth.
There is a lot of confusion about blood
pressure after 65, and a lot of it comes
from one old idea that has been passed
around for 50 years.
It sounds sensible.
It's easy to remember.
And it's wrong.
Today, I'm going to clear this up
properly with the actual numbers from
the biggest studies ever done in people
your age.
I'll show you what the latest guidelines
really say about the target after 65 and
after 80.
I'll explain the three things that
decide what your number should be,
because it isn't the same for everyone.
I'll tell you the warning signs that
your blood pressure has gone too low,
which matters just as much.
And I'll show you how to measure it at
home the right way, because most people
make at least one mistake that adds 10
points or more to the reading.
And stay with me until the part about
the studies, because one of the results
surprised even many doctors.
Before we start, tell me in the
comments, what was your last blood
pressure reading?
Just the top number is enough.
I read these, and it helps me see what
people are really dealing with.
If we haven't met, I'm Dr. Nimra.
On this channel, I explain, in plain
language, the things a short appointment
doesn't have time for. What your
medicines really do, what to eat, how to
move, and the habits that protect you
after 60.
One important thing before we begin.
This video is education, not personal
medical advice.
Please don't stop or change any blood
pressure medicine because of something
you hear today.
Everything I mention is something to
discuss with your own doctor. And at the
end, I'll give you the exact questions
to ask.
Let's start with that old idea.
Many people grew up hearing that a
normal top number is 100 plus your age.
So, at 70, a reading of 170 would be
fine.
That rule is not true, and it hasn't
been for a very long time.
No guideline anywhere in the world uses
it.
A reading of 170 is high blood pressure
at any age.
But I understand why it feels true,
because the top number really does tend
to rise as we get older.
Let me explain why.
Think of your main arteries as garden
hoses.
When you were 30, they were soft and
springy rubber.
Each time your heart pushed blood out,
the wall stretched a little and absorbed
the force.
Over the decades, those walls slowly
stiffen, like a hose left out in the sun
for years.
A stiffer pipe can't absorb the push, so
the pressure at the top of each
heartbeat climbs.
That's the top number, the systolic.
So, yes, rising blood pressure is common
with age.
But common is not the same as harmless.
Those stiff arteries are exactly where
strokes, heart attacks, kidney damage,
and heart failure begin.
After 60, the top number is the one that
matters most, and that's why doctors pay
so much attention to it.
So, the real question isn't, is it
normal to be higher?
The real question is, does bringing it
down actually help people over 65?
Or does it cause more harm than good?
That's exactly what the big studies set
out to answer.
For years, many doctors were cautious
about lowering blood pressure in older
people.
The worry was simple. Older bodies might
not cope, and lower pressure might cause
dizziness, falls, and confusion.
It was a reasonable worry.
So, researchers tested it.
Study one, people over 80.
In 2008,
a trial called HYVET treated almost
4,000 people aged 80 and over.
Their average age was 83.
Half got blood pressure tablets, aiming
for 150/80.
Half got a dummy pill.
The trial was stopped early because the
results were too clear to continue.
In the treated group, deaths from any
cause were 21% lower, deaths from stroke
were 39% lower, and heart failure was
64% lower.
So, the first lesson is, blood pressure
treatment helps even in your 80s.
Study two, people over 75, including
frail people.
Then came a large American trial called
SPRINT.
One part of it looked only at people
aged 75 and older, more than 2,600 of
them.
It compared a stricter target, a number
below 120
with the usual target of below 140.
Here is the result that surprised many
doctors.
The stricter group had about a third
fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart
failure, and about a third fewer deaths.
That's one serious heart event prevented
for roughly every 27 people treated over
3 years.
And the researchers checked the frail
participants, too. The people who walked
more slowly and had more health
problems.
They benefited as well, and the stricter
target did not significantly increase
serious falls.
Study three, people 60 to 80.
In 2021,
a Chinese trial called STEP followed
more than 8,000 people aged 60 to 80.
One group aimed for a top number between
110
and 130.
The other aimed for 130 to 150.
The lower group had 26% fewer heart
problems overall and a third fewer
strokes.
Now, I promised you honesty, so here is
the other side.
In these trials, the stricter groups had
more episodes of blood pressure going
too low and more side effects like
dizziness and changes in blood tests.
That's real, and it's why the way your
doctor lowers your pressure matters as
much as the target itself.
So, when someone online tells you,
"After 65, don't let them lower your
blood pressure." The biggest trials in
people your age simply don't support
that.
What they support is lowering it
carefully.
So, what are doctors told to aim for
now?
Here is the simple version.
In the United States, the 2025 guideline
from the American Heart Association and
the American College of Cardiology
recommends a target below 130 over 80
for most adults, including most people
over 65 who live independently.
It even encourages going a little lower
on the top number if you tolerate it
well.
In Europe, the 2024 guideline recommends
a top number between 120 and treatment.
And both say something very important
about frail people and the very old.
For them, the European guideline says
aim for pressure that is as low as
reasonably achievable, meaning as low as
is safe and comfortable for that person.
Doctors judge frailty, not just age.
So, back to our reading at the kitchen
table, 150 over 85.
For most people over 65, that is above
the target, and it's worth a
conversation with your doctor.
It's not an emergency.
But it isn't just your age, either.
Which brings us to the most important
part of this video.
How does your doctor decide which of
those rows is you?
Thing one, your overall health, not your
birthday.
A 78-year-old who walks every day, lives
independently, and does her own shopping
is a very different person from a
78-year-old who has had several falls,
lives in a care home, and has memory
problems.
They are the same age, but they might
get different targets.
For the first person, the evidence says
a stricter target protects her.
For the second, the goal is gentler,
prevents strokes, but above all avoid
dizziness and falls.
If you're not sure which group your
doctor puts you in, ask.
It's a perfectly fair question.
Thing two, how you feel when you stand
up.
When you stand, gravity pulls blood down
into your legs.
A young body tightens the blood vessels
in a second to push it back up.
After 65, that reflex is slower.
And some blood pressure tablets slow it
further.
If your pressure drops too much when you
stand, you feel light-headed, your
vision goes gray for a moment, or you
feel unsteady.
Doctors call this orthostatic
hypotension, a fall of 20 or more in the
top number, or 10 or more in the bottom
number, within 3 minutes of standing up.
This is one of the main reasons your
target might be set a little higher.
And it's easy to test at home, which
I'll show you in a moment.
Thing three, your real numbers, not one
reading at the clinic.
A single reading in a doctor's office
can mislead in both directions.
Some people's pressure jumps up in the
clinic from nerves.
That's called white-coat hypertension,
and it can lead to more tablets than
they need.
For other people, it's the reverse. The
reading looks fine at the clinic, but
runs high at home, especially in the
morning.
That's called masked hypertension, and
it can go unnoticed for years.
The only way to know your real pattern
is to measure at home correctly for
about a week.
That log is often more useful to your
doctor than any single office reading.
Now, the other side of the coin.
Blood pressure can also go too low, and
after 65, this happens more easily than
people realize.
Here are the warning signs to tell your
doctor about. Feeling dizzy or
light-headed when you stand up, a fall,
or a near fall, especially at night or
first thing in the morning, fainting or
feeling like you might faint, new
confusion, unusual tiredness or
weakness,
and home readings with a top number that
keeps coming in well below your target,
especially below about 110 when you also
feel unwell.
And there are moments when it can drop
suddenly.
A hot summer day,
a bout of vomiting or diarrhea,
not drinking enough,
a new medicine added, even one for the
bladder or prostate or for sleep.
If you're unwell and not eating or
drinking, call your doctor or pharmacist
and ask which of your tablets you should
pause until you recover.
Many people have never been told this,
and it can prevent a hospital visit.
But please hear this part clearly.
If you feel dizzy, don't simply stop
your tablets on your own.
Stopping some blood pressure medicines
suddenly can make your pressure bounce
up quickly, and a few, like some beta
blockers, can be risky to stop at once.
The answer is to tell your doctor, so
the dose or the timing can be adjusted
safely.
Here's how to get a reading you can
trust.
These steps come from the American Heart
Association.
One,
use a validated upper arm monitor, not a
wrist one.
Wrist monitors are more easily thrown
off by the position of your hand.
Ask your pharmacist for a validated
model, and make sure the cuff is the
right size for your arm.
Two,
for 30 minutes before, no coffee, no
exercise, and no smoking.
Empty your bladder first.
Three,
sit in a chair with your back supported,
feet flat on the floor, legs uncrossed.
Four,
put the cuff on your bare arm, never
over a sleeve.
A reading over clothing can be off by a
surprising amount.
Rest your arm on a table at the level of
your heart.
Five.
Sit quietly for 5 minutes first.
No talking, no television news, no
phone.
Six.
Take two readings, 1 minute apart, and
write both down.
Seven.
Do this in the morning, before your
tablets and before breakfast, and again
in the evening.
Keep it up for a week before your next
appointment.
And once a week, do the standing test.
Take a reading after sitting for 5
minutes.
Then stand up and take another reading
after 1 minute, and again after 3
minutes.
If the top number drops by 20 or more,
or you feel dizzy, write that down and
show your doctor.
One more thing, home readings run a
little lower than clinic readings, and
the usual home target is also below 130
over 80.
So bring the whole notebook, not just
one number you remember.
Here are five questions to take to your
next appointment.
Write them down.
One.
What is my blood pressure target, and
why that number for me?
Two.
Do you see me as fit or as frail for my
target?
Three.
Could any of my dizziness be from my
blood pressure tablets?
Four.
Can you check my blood pressure lying or
sitting, and then standing?
Five.
If I get sick and can't eat or drink,
which tablets should I pause?
A good doctor will be glad you asked.
These questions don't challenge your
doctor.
They help them treat you rather than an
average patient.
Let's recap.
100 plus your age is a myth.
Your pressure tends to rise with age,
but that doesn't make it harmless.
The big trials in older people found
real benefit even after 75, even after
80, and even in frail people.
For most people over 65, the target is
below 130.
For the frail and very old, it's as low
as is safe for you.
Too low matters, too.
Dizziness when you stand, falls, and
fainting are signs to tell your doctor,
not reasons to stop tablets on your own.
Measure at home the right way and bring
the notebook.
Blood pressure isn't about chasing the
lowest number, and it isn't about
accepting a high one because of your
age.
It's about finding the number that
protects your brain, your heart, and
your kidneys while still letting you get
up from your chair steadily and live
your life.
Now, the comment I'd love to read, did
you grow up hearing 100 plus your age?
Just type yes or no.
And think of one person over 65 who
checks their blood pressure, a parent, a
partner, a friend.
Send them this video.
It might start a better conversation at
their next appointment.
If this was useful, subscribe.
In the next video, I'll explain why
heart attacks and strokes happen most
often in the morning and the simple
habits that make the first hour of your
day safer.
I'm Dr. Nimra.
Look after yourself and I'll see you in
the next one.

5 Morning Habits That Raise Heart Attack Risk After 60

Heart attacks and strokes really do happen more often in the morning. But how much more, and why? And what can you actually do about it? In this video, Dr Nimra explains what happens in your body in the first hours after you wake up, and the 5 morning habits the evidence really supports after 60.

In this video, Dr Nimra explains:
✅ The real numbers behind the "morning heart attack" peak
✅ What happens to your blood pressure, hormones and blood when you wake
✅ How to get out of bed safely and avoid falls
✅ Why there is no "wrong time" for your blood pressure pill
✅ Toilet straining, cold mornings and snow shovelling
✅ The warning signs you should never wait out

🔔 Subscribe for new videos every Tuesday and Saturday: https://www.youtube.com/@DrNimraHealth?sub_confirmation=1
💬 Tell me in the comments: which of the 5 habits will you start tomorrow?
📤 Share this with someone over 60 who jumps straight out of bed.

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 Do heart attacks really peak in the morning?
2:24 How big is the morning risk?
3:50 What happens in your body when you wake
5:21 Habit 1: Get up in stages
6:55 Habit 2: No "wrong time" for your BP pill
8:54 Habit 3: Don't strain on the toilet
10:19 Habit 4: Cold and heavy effort
12:14 Habit 5: Never wait out warning signs
13:17 Water, smoking and coffee
14:28 Recap

📚 Research & sources
1. Muller JE et al. Circadian variation in the frequency of onset of acute myocardial infarction. N Engl J Med 1985;313:1315–1322.
2. Cohen MC et al. Meta-analysis of the morning excess of acute myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac death. Am J Cardiol 1997;79:1512–1516.
3. Elliott WJ. Circadian variation in the timing of stroke onset: a meta-analysis. Stroke 1998;29:992–996.
4. Tofler GH et al. Concurrent morning increase in platelet aggregability and the risk of myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac death. N Engl J Med 1987;316:1514–1518.
5. Kario K et al. Morning surge in blood pressure as a predictor of silent and clinical cerebrovascular disease in elderly hypertensives. Circulation 2003;107:1401–1406.
6. Mackenzie IS et al. Cardiovascular outcomes in adults with hypertension with evening versus morning dosing of usual antihypertensives in the UK (TIME). Lancet 2022;400:1417–1425.
7. Garrison SR et al. BedMed and BedMed-Frail trials of bedtime vs morning antihypertensive dosing, 2025.
8. Auger N et al. Association between quantity and duration of snowfall and risk of myocardial infarction. CMAJ 2017;189:E235–E242.

subtitles.plaintext:
Heart attacks don't strike at random. If
you plotted every heart attack across a
whole day, you'd see the line climb in
the morning. It rises soon after people
wake up and peaks a few hours later,
somewhere around 9:00.
Strokes follow the same pattern.
So does sudden cardiac arrest.
That part is true. Doctors have known it

records.title: After 70, Winter Is Not Just Cold. 7 Things to Do Before It Starts (Doctor Explains)
records.channelDescription:
Welcome to Dr Nimra | Health After 60 🩺

I'm Dr Nimra, this channel exists for one reason: to explain, in plain and simple language, what your 15-minute doctor's visit doesn't have time to explain.

Every week I break down what really happens inside your body after 60, and what you can do about it:
💊 Medicines: what your pills really do, side effects, and dangerous combinations
🥗 Food & diet: what to eat, what to limit, and why
🚶 Exercise & mobility: simple movement that keeps you strong and independent
😴 Sleep, bathroom and daily habits: the small things that add up
❤️ Heart, blood pressure, blood sugar, kidneys, bones, brain and eyes

⚠️ Disclaimer
The content on this channel is for general education and information only. It is not personal medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Never start, stop or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have a medical emergency, call your local emergency number.

records.text:
Over 70? Before winter really starts, do these 7 simple things. Cold weather quietly raises blood pressure, thickens the blood, and makes falls and chest infections more likely, which is why far more older people fall ill in winter than in summer. In this video, Dr Nimra explains the one big winter mistake most older people make (trusting how cold you feel), how warm your home should be (at least 18°C / 64°F), how to protect your heart in the cold, why blood pressure goes up in winter, eating and drinking in winter (including winter constipation), winter vaccines and vitamin D, making your home safe now the clocks have changed, and how to stay active, in the light and in touch. Plus the warning signs of hypothermia and when to get help the same day.

💬 Tell me in the comments: which of the 7 things will you do first? Just write the number, 1 to 7.

👍 Please share this with a parent, grandparent or neighbour who lives alone, and subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

CHAPTERS
0:00 A cold winter morning after 70
1:11 1. Keep your home warm (the big mistake)
3:22 Staying warm without heating the whole house
5:15 2. Protect your heart from the cold
8:16 3. Check your blood pressure at home
9:47 4. Eat warm and drink even when not thirsty
12:11 5. Winter vaccines and vitamin D
15:00 6. Make your home safe for the dark
18:24 7. Keep moving, in the light and in touch
20:29 Hypothermia: the warning signs
22:14 For family and carers
23:02 The 7 things: recap

Sources:
NHS. Keep warm, keep well (heat the rooms you use to at least 18°C)
UK Health Security Agency. Cold weather and health: guidance and advice
Stergiou GS et al. Seasonal variation in blood pressure: evidence, consensus and recommendations for clinical practice. J Hypertens 2020
CDC. Older adult fall prevention: facts and statistics
CDC. RSV vaccine guidance for older adults
NHS. Vitamin D: advice for autumn and winter

Important: this video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. Please never stop, start or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. Chest pain, sudden breathlessness, signs of a stroke, or someone who is cold, confused and sleepy: call for help straight away.

#healthafter60 #seniorhealth #winterhealth #over70 #coldweather

records.text:
Constipated in winter after 60? You are not imagining it. Cold weather makes us drink less, move less and eat less fibre, and the cold bathroom makes many older people hold it in, which slowly makes constipation worse. In this video, Dr Nimra explains why winter slows the bowel, the one winter mistake most older people make, and the simple warm morning drink that helps the bowel wake up and move. You will also learn which popular morning drinks really help (prune juice, coffee, tea) and which are just stories (lemon, honey, apple cider vinegar, detox teas), the best warm winter breakfast for the bowel, a gentle morning toilet routine, which winter medicines can cause constipation, and a simple 7-day winter plan you can start tomorrow.

💬 Will you try the warm morning drink tomorrow? Write "warm" in the comments, and tell us your own morning drink if one works for you.

👍 Please share this with a parent, grandparent or friend who struggles with this in winter, and subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Why winter constipation happens
1:21 Why winter is hard on the bowel after 60
4:35 The big winter mistake
6:29 1. The warm morning drink
9:38 2. A gentle boost: prune juice, coffee, tea
12:12 Lemon, honey, vinegar, detox tea: what really helps
14:00 3. A warm breakfast that keeps you going
16:29 4. Your morning toilet routine
18:16 5. Keep drinking and moving through the cold day
21:26 6. Winter medicines that slow the bowel
23:47 When it is not just winter constipation
24:56 For family and carers
26:34 Your 7-day winter plan

Sources:
Brown SR, Cann PA, Read NW. Effect of coffee on distal colon function. Gut 1990
Rao SSC et al. Is coffee a colonic stimulant? Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 1998
Chey SW et al. Exploratory comparative effectiveness trial of green kiwifruit, psyllium, or prunes in US patients with chronic constipation. Am J Gastroenterol 2021
British Dietetic Association. Dietary management of chronic constipation in adults, 2025 guideline
IARC Monographs volume 116. Very hot beverages (above 65°C)
NHS. Constipation: causes and treatment

Important: this video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. Please never stop, start or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. Severe tummy pain, vomiting, a swollen tummy, blood in the stool, or not passing wind: get medical help straight away.

subtitles.plaintext:
It is a cold winter morning. You wake up, and the
bedroom is chilly. The bathroom is even colder.
You know you should go, but the thought of that
cold seat makes you wait.
Later, you sit down, and nothing happens. Again.
And you think, it is always like this in winter.
If this sounds familiar,
you are not imagining it.
Many doctors and nurses notice the same thing
every year. When the weather turns cold,
older people become more constipated. There are
clear reasons for it, and
once you understand them,
the fix is surprisingly simple. Today I will show
you one warm drink, taken
at the right time in the
morning, that helps the bowel wake up and move. I
will tell you why winter slows the bowel down,
the one winter mistake that makes it much worse,
and which popular morning drinks really help,
and which ones are just stories. And at the end,
I will give you a simple
seven-day winter plan you
can start tomorrow morning. Quick note, this is
general education, not personal medical advice.
Let me start with why winter is so hard on the
bowel after 60. Your large bowel moves stool
along with slow waves of muscle, a little like
squeezing toothpaste along a tube. As the stool
travels, the bowel takes water back out of it.
When the waves are slow,
the stool sits for longer,
more water is taken out, and soft stool becomes
hard, dry, and difficult to pass.
After 60, those waves are already a little slower
and weaker. And then winter comes along,
and adds five more things on top. The first is
less water. In cold weather we feel even less
thirsty than in summer. We do not sweat, the air
is cold, and a drink of cold water is the last
thing we want. Many older people also drink less
on purpose in winter because getting up at night
to a cold bathroom is miserable. So the bowel
gets less water, and the stool gets harder.
The second is less movement. When it is cold,
dark and icy outside, we
stay in. We sit by the fire
or the heater for hours. And walking is one of
the best natural bowel movers there is.
Every step gently massages the bowel from the
outside. When the walking stops, the bowel slows
down too. The third is the heating. Central
heating and heaters make the air very dry.
You lose more water through your skin and your
breath without even noticing it.
So you need more to drink in winter, not less,
even though you feel less thirsty.
The fourth is winter food. In summer, we eat
salads, fresh fruit, juicy vegetables.
In winter, we eat more bread, more pies, more
biscuits with our tea, more white rice and pasta.
All comforting and all low in fiber and water.
Fresh fruit is also more expensive and harder
to get to the shops for. And the fifth is the
cold bathroom. This one surprises people,
and it is the mistake I promised to tell you
about. I will come back to it in a moment.
Before we go on, I would love to know something.
Do you find you get more constipated in winter?
You can simply write "yes" in the comments and
your age if you like. You are not alone,
and your comment helps other people find this
video when they need it.
And if we have not met before, I am Dr. Nimra. On
this channel I talk about health after 60 in
plain, calm language, the kind of conversation a
short appointment does not always have time for.
If that sounds useful, you are
very welcome to subscribe and stay.
Now, the mistake. In winter, many older people
start holding it in. The bathroom is cold.
The toilet seat is freezing. You are warm and
comfortable in your chair, and you think,
"I will go later." Or you wake up early in the
morning, feel the urge, and stay in your warm
bed instead. It seems harmless. But here is what
happens. Your bowel gives you a signal when it is
ready. That signal is strongest in the morning,
and it does not last long. If you ignore it,
the stool goes back up a little and sits there.
The bowel keeps taking water out of it. By the
time you do go, it is harder and drier, and you
have to strain. And if you
keep ignoring the signal,
day after day, the signal itself gets weaker.
Your body slowly stops asking.
That is how a few weeks of winter habits can turn
into months of constipation.
So the first fix costs almost nothing. Warm the
bathroom. If you can, put the heating on in the
bathroom for a little while in the morning. A
small, safe heater placed well away from water
or simply leaving the bathroom door open to a
warm hallway can help. A
soft, padded toilet seat cover
makes a cold seat much kinder. Keep a warm
dressing gown and slippers by
the bed. Anything that makes
it easy to say yes when your body says it is
time. Now let me tell you
about the warm morning drink,
because this is the heart of today's video. Step
number one, a large mug of warm water
as soon as you get up. Not cold water. Not a
little sip. A large mug, about a cup and a half,
of warm water. Drink it slowly, over five or ten
minutes, while you sit on the edge of the bed
or in the kitchen. Why warm and why in the
morning? Let me explain. When you wake up,
your bowel wakes up too. Studies that measured
the muscle activity of the bowel found that it is
quiet during the night and then becomes much more
active soon after waking. And when you put food
or drink into your stomach, the stomach sends a
message down to the bowel that says, "Make room,
something is coming." Doctors call this the
gastrocolic reflex. It is strongest in the
morning. So a warm drink first thing in the
morning does three things at once.
It gives the bowel water after a long, dry night.
It fills the stomach and switches on that reflex.
And it does this at the very time of day when the
bowel is most ready to move.
What about the warmth itself? Here I want to be
honest with you. Most of the studies on warm
water are small, and many were done in people
recovering from operations whose bowels had
stopped working for a while. In some of those
studies, people who drank warm water passed wind
and opened their bowels sooner than people who
did not. That is
encouraging, but it is not strong
proof. What I can say is this. Warm water is
easier to drink in winter. Most people drink
much more of it than cold water when it is cold
outside. And it feels soothing to the tummy.
In winter, that alone makes it worth it. Now, a
very important safety point.
I said warm, not hot. Please never drink very hot
drinks straight from the kettle.
Drinks that are very hot, hotter than about 65
degrees Celsius, can burn the food pipe,
and over many years, drinking them very hot has
been linked to cancer of the food pipe.
So boil the kettle, pour the water into your mug,
and let it stand for a few minutes.
Or mix it half and half with cold water. It
should feel comfortably warm on your lips,
like a warm bath, not like a scald. And if your
doctor has told you to limit how much you drink,
for example, because of heart failure or kidney
disease, please follow their advice.
Ask them how much you can have, and make the
morning drink part of that amount.
Step number two, give your drink a gentle boost.
Plain warm water is a good start,
but you can make it work even better. Here are
the boosts that have real reasons behind them.
The first boost is prune juice. Prunes and prune
juice contain a natural sugar called sorbitol.
Your body does not absorb sorbitol well, so it
stays in the bowel and
draws water into the stool,
making it softer. Prunes also contain fiber and
natural plant substances
that help the bowel move.
So here is my favorite winter drink. Put a small
amount of prune juice in a mug,
about a quarter of a cup, and top it up with warm
water. It tastes a little like a warm fruit tea.
Start small because too much sorbitol can cause
wind and cramps. And if you have diabetes,
keep the prune juice to a small amount because it
does contain natural sugar.
The second boost is your morning
coffee if you already drink coffee.
This one surprises people. Scientists in Britain
studied coffee and the bowel,
and they found that in about three people out of
ten, a cup of coffee brought on the urge to open
the bowels, sometimes within a few minutes.
Another study measured the muscle activity of
the bowel directly. Coffee woke the bowel up
about as strongly as a
full meal and much more than
plain warm water. Even decaffeinated coffee had
some effect, though less. So if coffee suits you,
a warm cup about 20 minutes after your warm water
can help. But please do not start drinking
strong coffee if it makes your heart race, upsets
your stomach, or keeps you awake.
And one cup is enough. It is the warmth and the
timing that matter, not the strength.
The third boost is tea. A cup of ordinary tea
counts towards your water.
It is warm, it fills the stomach, and it switches
on that same reflex. Some
people find strong black
tea a little binding, so if you drink a lot of
very strong tea, try making it a bit weaker.
Now, let me be honest about some other popular
morning drinks you may have heard of.
Warm water with lemon. Lovely, refreshing, and it
may help you drink more, which is good.
But the lemon itself does not have special bowel
powers. It is the warm water that does the work.
And lemon is acidic, so
if you drink it every day,
rinse your mouth with plain water
afterwards to protect your teeth.
Honey in warm water. A small spoon makes it taste
nicer, and that is fine.
But honey is sugar, so if you
have diabetes, please leave it out.
Apple cider vinegar. There is no good evidence
that it helps constipation.
It can upset the stomach and harm the teeth. I
would not bother. And the one drink I would
warn you about is the strong herbal laxative tea.
These are often sold as detox or slimming teas,
and many contain senna. Used every now and then,
senna can help. But drinking a strong laxative
tea every day can cause cramps, diarrhea, and a
loss of salts from the body, which is especially
risky after 70. If you need a laxative regularly,
please talk to your doctor or pharmacist about
the right one. So the warm morning drink is
simple. A large mug of
warm water when you wake up.
With a little prune juice if you like. Then, if
coffee suits you, a warm cup of coffee or tea
with breakfast. Step number three. A warm
breakfast that keeps the wave
going. Your warm drink switches
the bowel on. A good breakfast keeps it going. In
winter, the best breakfast for the bowel is warm
porridge. Oats contain a soft, gentle kind of
fiber that holds water, so
it makes the stool soft and
bulky, not hard. Make it with milk or water and
add some fruit. Here is a lovely winter trick.
Before bed, put five or six prunes in a small
bowl with a little water
and leave them overnight.
In the morning, they are soft and plump. Chop
them into your porridge and pour in the soaking
water too, because some of the goodness goes into
the water. If you prefer,
stewed fruit is wonderful in winter.
Warm stewed apples or pears, cooked with the skin
on, with a little
cinnamon. Warm, sweet and full of
fiber. You can also stir one tablespoon of ground
flaxseed into your
porridge. Flaxseed adds a gentle,
soft fiber. It must be ground, not whole, because
whole seeds can pass straight through.
And always have a drink with it. And remember the
green kiwi. Two green
kiwis a day have been tested
in real studies of constipation, and people found
them gentle and easy. In
winter, kiwis are usually
easy to find in the shops and they keep well.
Have one with breakfast and one in the afternoon.
One important rule with all of these. Add fiber
slowly. If you suddenly eat a lot of fiber,
you will get wind and bloating, and you will give
up. Start with a little and add a bit more every
few days, over two or three weeks. And always
drink more when you eat
more fiber. Fiber without water
is like a sponge without water. It stays hard and
dry. With water, it swells and becomes soft.
That is why the warm drink and
the fiber work so well together.
Step number four, your morning toilet routine.
You have had your warm drink. You have had your
breakfast. Now, about 15 to 30 minutes after
breakfast, the bowel is at its most active of
the whole day. This is your best chance. So use
it. Go to your warm bathroom, even if you do not
feel a strong urge. Sit on the toilet and put a
small footstool under your feet, so your knees
are higher than your hips. Lean forward a little
and rest your elbows on your knees.
This position straightens the natural bend at the
end of the bowel and opens the way.
If you do not have a footstool, a small pile of
thick books or an upturned plastic box works just
as well. Then relax your tummy and breathe
slowly, low down into your
belly. Do not hold your breath
and do not push hard. Straining raises your blood
pressure and when you let
go, it can drop suddenly
and make you dizzy. In winter, when the body is
already under strain from the cold, that matters
even more. Give it five to 10 minutes. If nothing
happens, that is fine. Get up, carry on with your morning,
and try again later or tomorrow. Over a week or
two, many people find that the body learns the
rhythm again. Same drink, same breakfast, same
time, same place. The bowel loves a routine.
Step number five, keep drinking and keep moving
through the cold day. The morning drink is a
wonderful start. But the bowel needs water all day long. As
we get older, the thirst signal becomes weaker
and in winter, it becomes even weaker. So please
do not wait until you feel thirsty.
Drink on a schedule instead. A warm drink when
you wake up. Another mid-morning. One with lunch.
One mid-afternoon. And one with your evening
meal. Warm water, tea, milky drinks, and soup
all count. A bowl of vegetable soup is one of the
best winter foods for the bowel because it gives
you water and fiber together. What about the
nighttime bathroom trips? This is why so many
people drink less in winter. Here is the answer.
Drink well during the day and then have your last
big drink about two hours before bed. That way,
you get the water your bowel needs and you are
less likely to be up in the night. Cutting down
your drinks for the whole day does not solve the
problem. It just swaps a nighttime trip for a
hard, painful stool. Now, movement.
I know walking outside in winter can be difficult
and on icy days, it is not safe.
So bring the walking indoors. Every hour, get up
and walk around your home for a few minutes.
Walk to the kitchen and back. March on the spot
while holding the back of a sturdy chair.
Do some simple leg lifts while sitting. All of
these gently wake the bowel up.
And here is a lovely, warming
winter habit. A gentle tummy massage.
Lie on your back in bed in the morning with your
knees bent. Rub your
hands together until they are
warm. With a flat hand, make slow, gentle circles
on your tummy. Start low on the right side,
just inside your hip bone. Go up towards your
ribs. Across under the ribs to the left side.
And down the left side towards your left hip.
This follows the path of the large bowel.
Five to 10 minutes before you get up. Some small
studies suggest it can help,
and most people find it very calming. You can
also place a warm hot water bottle in a cover
on your tummy while you rest. The warmth can ease
cramps and help you relax.
Please use warm water, never boiling, and always
use a cover, especially if you have diabetes or
numb skin. Step number six, check your winter
medicines. This is the step most people miss.
Winter brings new medicines, and some of them
slow the bowel down.
Calcium tablets. Many older people
start calcium, or calcium with vitamin D, in the
autumn and winter. Calcium can cause constipation
in some people. If you notice your bowel slowing down
after starting calcium, please
tell your doctor or pharmacist.
Sometimes a different type, or a different dose,
helps. Vitamin D on its
own does not usually cause
constipation. Iron tablets. These are a common
cause of hard, dark
stools. Cough and cold medicines.
Some cough medicines contain codeine, which is a
strong cause of constipation.
And some older type allergy and cold remedies,
the kind that make you
drowsy, can slow the bowel and
also cause confusion and difficulty passing urine
in older people. Always ask the pharmacist before
you get a cold remedy. Painkillers. In winter,
joints often ache more, and
many people take more painkillers.
Codeine, tramadol, and other strong painkillers
often cause constipation.
And there are many others.
Some blood pressure tablets, like amlodipine and
verapamil. Some bladder medicines.
Some medicines for depression or nausea. And some
antacids for the stomach.
If you take several of these, the effect adds up.
So please ask your doctor
or pharmacist to look at
your whole list of medicines this winter, and ask
one simple question,
"Could any of these be making
me constipated?" Often, a small change makes a big
difference. But please never stop a medicine on
your own. Now, I want to make sure you are safe,
so let me tell you when this is not just winter
constipation. Please see your doctor if your
bowel habit changes and
stays changed for more than a few
weeks. Especially if you see blood in the stool,
if you are losing weight
without trying, or if you
feel unusually tired. Most of the time it is
something simple. But after 50, a lasting change
in the bowel should always be checked, because
finding a problem early makes it much easier to
treat. And please get help the same day if you
have severe or worsening tummy pain, a swollen,
hard tummy, vomiting, or if you cannot pass any
wind at all. Those can be signs of a blockage.
Also, if you have not opened your bowels for
several days and then watery stool starts leaking
out, please do not take a diarrhea medicine. That
can be stool leaking around a hard, stuck plug,
and diarrhea medicine can make it much worse.
Speak to a doctor or pharmacist first.
Now, a few words for anyone caring for an older
parent or partner. In winter, check the bathroom.
Is it warm enough to use comfortably? Is there a
footstool? Check how much they are drinking.
Many older people will say they drink plenty, but
when you count, it is two cups of tea a day.
Make them a warm drink every time you visit. Look
at what is in the fridge and the fruit bowl.
And if they are frail or have memory problems,
keep a simple calendar with a tick on the days they open their bowels.
If three days pass without a tick, start the
gentle steps early and call the doctor or
nurse if there is no result. Quiet signs to watch
for are going off their food, being restless or
more confused than usual, or holding their tummy.
So let me bring it all together. One,
a large mug of warm water as soon as you get up.
Two, a gentle boost like a little prune juice
or coffee or tea with breakfast.
Three, a warm, high-fiber breakfast.
Four, a morning toilet routine in a warm
bathroom. Five, keep
drinking and moving through the cold day.
Six, check your winter medicines. And above all,
do not hold it in because the bathroom is cold.
Now, here is the simple seven-day winter plan I
promised. Tonight, before bed, put five or six
prunes in a little water to soak. Put a footstool
in the bathroom and leave your dressing gown and slippers by the bed.
Day one. When you wake up, drink a large mug of
warm water slowly, then
eat your porridge with the
soaked prunes. Twenty minutes later, go to the
warm bathroom and sit for five to ten minutes,
feet on the footstool, breathing slowly. No
pushing. Whatever happens, it is fine.
You are teaching your body a new routine. Day
two, do the same. And
today, add the drink schedule.
Set five times for a warm drink through the day
and write them on a piece of paper on the fridge.
Day three, add movement. Every hour, get up and
walk around your home for a few minutes.
Day four, try the warm tummy
massage before you get up. Day five,
add a little prune juice to your morning warm
water or have a green kiwi in the afternoon.
Day six, look at your list of medicines and make
a note to ask your
pharmacist about any that might
slow your bowel. Day seven, look back at your
week. Are your stools a little softer? Is it a
little easier to go? For most people, the change
is gentle and steady, not sudden. Keep going for
three or four weeks. It takes time for the bowel
to learn a new rhythm and
the longer you keep it up,
the better it usually gets. Let me finish with
this. Winter constipation is not something you
just have to put up with until spring. It is not
a sign of weakness and it is nothing to be
embarrassed about. Every doctor has helped many
people with exactly this. Most of the time,
it comes down to a few small winter habits, a
warm drink at the right time, a warm breakfast,
a warm bathroom and a body that is not rushed.
Small, gentle changes done every morning can make
this winter much more comfortable. One last
reminder, this video is for general education
and is not personal medical advice. Please never
stop, start or change any
medicine without speaking
to your own doctor or pharmacist. And if you have
severe tummy pain, vomiting, a swollen tummy,
blood in your stool or you cannot pass wind,
please get medical help straight away.
Now, before you go, I would love to hear from
you. Will you try the
warm morning drink tomorrow?
Just write "warm" in the comments. And if you
already have a morning drink that works for you,
please tell us what it is. I will be reading and
your answer may help someone else this winter.
And please share this video with one person who
struggles with this in the cold months.
A parent, a grandparent, a friend. Many people
suffer quietly with this
and a simple warm drink could make their mornings
easier. And if you have ever felt that stool was
stuck and would not come out, even with all of
this, my video on exactly
what to do is right here
on your screen. Thank you for watching. Stay warm
and take good care of yourself.

records.channelDescription:
Welcome to Dr Nimra | Health After 60 🩺

I'm Dr Nimra, this channel exists for one reason: to explain, in plain and simple language, what your 15-minute doctor's visit doesn't have time to explain.

Every week I break down what really happens inside your body after 60, and what you can do about it:
💊 Medicines: what your pills really do, side effects, and dangerous combinations
🥗 Food & diet: what to eat, what to limit, and why
🚶 Exercise & mobility: simple movement that keeps you strong and independent
😴 Sleep, bathroom and daily habits: the small things that add up
❤️ Heart, blood pressure, blood sugar, kidneys, bones, brain and eyes

⚠️ Disclaimer
The content on this channel is for general education and information only. It is not personal medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Never start, stop or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have a medical emergency, call your local emergency number.

records.text:
Which laxative is safe after 60? In this video, Dr Nimra ranks 10 common laxatives from the safest to the ones to be careful with, using the 2023 guideline from the American Gastroenterological Association and the American College of Gastroenterology, plus FDA safety warnings.

You will learn which laxative got the strongest recommendation, why magnesium needs care if your kidneys are weak, why phosphate enemas carry an FDA warning for people over 55, the one mistake that makes people take far too much, and the truth about the "lazy bowel" myth.

💬 Tell me in the comments: which laxative do you use most often?

👍 If this helped, please share it with someone who keeps a cupboard full of laxatives. Subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.


CHAPTERS
0:00 Choosing a laxative after 60
1:11 1. Polyethylene glycol (the strongest recommendation)
2:31 Which laxative do you use?
3:08 How laxatives work: 4 types
3:39 2. Psyllium (isabgol) and its 3 rules
4:45 3. Senna
5:21 4. Bisacodyl and sodium picosulfate
6:24 The mistake: stacking doses
7:33 3 myths, including the "lazy bowel"
9:28 5. Magnesium and your kidneys
11:19 6. Lactulose
11:49 Heart failure, diabetes, kidney disease
12:45 7. Docusate (does it work?)
13:40 8. Phosphate enemas: the FDA warning
15:10 9. Mineral oil by mouth
15:44 10. Castor oil and detox teas
16:20 Potassium, water tablets and opioids
17:23 When NOT to use a laxative
18:35 For carers
19:16 3 questions I am often asked
20:27 Your step-by-step ladder
22:23 Recap
23:05 An honest note

This video is general education, not personal medical advice. Always read the label, never take more than the stated dose, and check with your doctor or pharmacist before using a laxative with your regular medicines, especially if you have kidney or heart disease.

Sources:
AGA-ACG Clinical Practice Guideline: Pharmacological Management of Chronic Idiopathic Constipation (Chang et al., 2023)
FDA Drug Safety Communication on over-the-counter sodium phosphate laxatives (January 2014)
Müller-Lissner et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2005: Myths and misconceptions about chronic constipation
McRorie et al., Aliment Pharmacol Ther 1998: psyllium vs docusate
Tarumi et al., J Pain Symptom Manage 2013: docusate in hospice patients
Wakai et al., J Pharm Health Care Sci 2019: hypermagnesemia with magnesium oxide
American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria (mineral oil by mouth)

subtitles.plaintext:
It has been 3 days. Your tummy feels
full and heavy and you reach for the box
at the back of the bathroom cabinet.
Maybe it is the one your neighbor swears
by. Maybe it is the one your mother
used. Or maybe it is the enema you
bought years ago just in case. After 60,
choosing a laxative is not as simple as
it looks on the pharmacy shelf. Some are
gentle and well tested and doctors are
happy for you to use them even for a
long time. Some barely work at all and a
few can be genuinely dangerous for older
people, especially if your kidneys are
not as strong as they were. Today, I
will sort them for you from the safest
to the ones to be careful with using the
newest guidelines from American Gut
Specialists.
I will also tell you about the one
mistake that makes people take far too
much. A common myth about the lazy bowel
and at the end a simple step-by-step
ladder you can follow. Quick note, this
is general education, not personal
medical advice.
Let me start with the one many doctors
reach for first.
Number one on the safe list, a powder
called polyethylene glycol. You may know
it as myax in America or Muvikol or
Laxido in Britain. In Pakistan and
India, you may see other brand names.
So, always look for the words
polyethylene glycol or macro on the box.
It is a powder with almost no taste that
you stir into a glass of water, juice,
or tea. It works in a very simple way.
It holds onto water inside the bowel, so
the stool stays softer and moves more
easily. It does not squeeze the bowel,
so it rarely causes cramps.
In 20123,
the American Gastroenterological
Association and the American College of
Gastroenterology wrote a joint guideline
on long-term constipation.
They gave polyethylene glycol a strong
recommendation.
That is the highest level they give and
very few laxatives received it. There is
one thing you must know about this
powder. It is not fast. It usually takes
1 to 3 days to work. Please remember
that because it is the key to the
mistake I will tell you about in a few
minutes. Before we go on, I would love
to know something. Which laxative do you
use most often, if any? You can simply
write the name in the comments or write
none if you do not use them. Your answer
helps other people find this video when
they need it. And if we have not met
before, I am Dr. Nimra. On this channel,
I talk about health after 60 in plain
calm language. The kind of conversation
a short appointment does not always have
time for. If that sounds useful, you are
very welcome to subscribe and stay.
Now, here is a very short guide to how
laxatives work because it explains the
rest of the list. There are four main
types.
Some hold water in the bowel so the
stool stays soft. Some add bulk like
fiber.
Some gently stimulate the bowel muscles
to push and some work from below as
suppositories or enemas.
Each type works at a different speed and
each has its own risks. after 60. Number
two on the safe list, fiber supplements,
and the best tested one is psyllium
husk. Many of you know it as isol.
Psyllium soaks up water and makes the
stool bigger and softer. The joint
guideline suggests fiber supplements as
a first step, especially if you do not
eat much fiber from food. And when
researchers looked at different fibers,
psyllium was the one that clearly
worked.
But psyllium has three rules after 60.
First, always take it with a full glass
of water and keep drinking through the
day. Without enough water, it can make
things worse. And in rare cases, the
swollen husk can cause choking or a
blockage.
Second, take your other medicines at
least 2 hours before or after it because
it can stop some of them being absorbed.
And third, it is not the right choice if
you are bed bound, cannot drink much, or
have stool that is already badly stuck.
In those cases, more bulk can make the
jam worse.
Number three, Senna. This is one of the
oldest laxatives in the world made from
a plant. It is a stimulant laxative,
which means it gently wakes up the
muscles of the bowel so they push. Senna
usually works in 6 to 12 hours, which is
why many people take it at bedtime and
go in the morning. The guideline
suggests Senna 2 with one practical tip.
Start with a low dose and only go up if
you need to. The most common side effect
is tummy cramps and a lower dose often
avoids them. Number four, two stronger
stimulant laxatives called bicycodel and
sodium pyosulfate.
You may know bicycodel as dulax.
The guideline gave these a strong
recommendation as well for short-term
use of up to four weeks or as a rescue
when nothing else has worked for a few
days. It also said that longer use is
probably fine, but there is less
research on that. So, it is best done
with your doctor's advice.
Viscodel comes as tablets which work
overnight and as suppositories which go
into the back passage and usually work
within about 15 minutes to an hour. That
makes the suppository useful when stool
is low down and you need help today. One
small tip about the tablets.
They have a special coating. So do not
take them within an hour of milk or
antacid tablets. Those can dissolve the
coating too early and upset your
stomach. Now I promise to tell you about
the mistake that makes people take far
too much. Here is how it happens.
You take a laxative in the morning. By
the afternoon, nothing has happened. So
you take another dose. By the evening,
still nothing. So you add something
else. Maybe a different product from the
cabinet.
And the next morning everything works at
once. You have cramps, loose stools, you
rush to the toilet. And for older
people, that is how falls, dehydration,
and accidents happen. The mistake is
stacking doses because you expect a
laxative to work faster than it is
designed to. Polyethylene glycol takes 1
to 3 days.
Fiber takes a day or more.
Senna and bicycodal tablets take 6 to 12
hours.
So before you take more, ask yourself
one question. Have I waited long enough
for this one to work? And please never
mix several laxatives on the same day
unless your doctor has told you to. Now
let me bust three very common myths.
Many people are afraid of stimulant
laxatives like senna and biccodle.
They have been told these will make the
bowel lazy, that the bowel will forget
how to work, or that they are addictive.
In 2005, a group of gut experts looked
carefully at all the evidence for these
fears. They concluded that it is
unlikely that stimulant laxatives at
recommended doses harm the colon. They
found no good evidence that they cause
addiction and no evidence that people
get rebound constipation when they stop.
The old pictures of a damaged lazy bowel
mostly came from people who took huge
doses of older harsher laxatives for
years. So if your doctor has suggested
senna or bicodle at a normal dose, you
do not need to feel guilty or afraid.
What does matter is taking the right
dose, drinking enough, and telling your
doctor if you need them every day. Myth
number two, if I do not go every day,
toxins build up and poison my body. The
same experts found no evidence for this.
Still sitting in the bowel for an extra
day does not poison you. It may feel
uncomfortable, but it is not a reason to
panic or to reach for a strong laxative
or a cleanse. Myth number three, if I
just drink lots more water, my
constipation will be cured.
Water matters and many older people do
drink too little. But the experts found
that drinking extra water mainly helps
if you are actually dehydrated.
If you already drink enough, pouring in
more will mostly send you to the toilet
to pass urine. So drink enough to keep
your urine pale yellow. And then look at
fiber movement and the right laxative.
Now we move to the laxatives that need
more care after 60. Number five,
magnesium.
This includes milk of magnesia, which is
magnesium hydroxide and magnesium oxide
tablets.
Magnesium pulls water into the bowel and
works quite reliably, sometimes within a
few hours. The guideline does suggest
magnesium oxide,
but it adds an important warning. Avoid
it if your kidneys are not working well.
Healthy kidneys get rid of extra
magnesium.
Weak kidneys cannot and the magnesium
can build up in the blood. How common is
that? In a Japanese study of 320
hospital patients taking magnesium
oxide, almost one in four had a high
magnesium level in the blood. The risk
was highest in people with weaker
kidneys, people on higher doses, and
people who had taken it for more than
about 5 weeks.
When all of these were present, the risk
was very high. A very high magnesium
level can cause drowsiness, weakness, a
slow heartbeat, and rarely collapse.
Japan's health ministry now advises
regular blood tests for older people on
long-term magnesium.
And many people over 60 have some loss
of kidney function without knowing it.
So, if you use magnesium regularly,
please ask your doctor to check your
kidney blood test first.
Magnesium also stops some medicines
being absorbed, including thyroid
tablets, some antibiotics, and some bone
strengthening tablets.
So, space them apart by a few hours and
ask your pharmacist for the exact
timing. Number six, lactulose.
This is a sweet syrup that pulls water
into the bowel. It works, but it is
slow, often taking a day or two, and it
commonly causes wind, bloating, and
tummy rumbling. The guideline suggests
it for people who have tried the common
shopboard options without success. It is
safe for most older people, but many
find the gas uncomfortable, and you need
to keep drinking well while you use it.
Now, three quick notes for special
situations because many of you live with
more than one condition. If you have
heart failure or your doctor has told
you to limit salt or fluids, check with
them before using the polyethylene
glycol sachets sold as muvacol or
laxido.
Those versions contain added salts
including sodium and potassium.
The plain powder sold as myax does not.
If you have diabetes, many flavored
fiber drinks contain added sugar, so
look for a sugar-free version. Laculose
is a sugar syrup, but very little of it
is absorbed. So, it is usually fine.
Still, mention it to your doctor if your
sugar readings change. And if you have
kidney disease, the two to be most
careful with are magnesium and phosphate
products. Your doctor or pharmacist can
help you choose something safer.
Number seven, the stool softener called
Docusate. Often sold as coll.
This one surprises people because it is
one of the most widely used. But when
doctors tested it, the results were
disappointing.
In one study of 170 adults, Docusate did
not make the stool any wetter or bigger,
while psyllium did. In another study of
74 people in hospice care, adding
Docusate to Senna was no better than
adding a dummy pill. The joint guideline
did not even make a recommendation on
docusate because the evidence was too
poor. Docusate is not dangerous.
But if it is the only thing you are
taking and nothing is changing, it may
simply not be doing much.
Ask your doctor whether polyethylene
glycol or another option would suit you
better. Now the ones I would ask you to
be most careful with after 60. Number
eight, phosphate enemas and phosphate
laxatives you drink. You may know the
enemas by the name Fleet. In 2014, the
US Food and Drug Administration issued a
warning. Using more than one dose of
these sodium phosphate products in 24
hours or more than the dose on the label
can cause severe dehydration, dangerous
changes in the salts in your blood,
kidney damage, heart problems, and in
rare cases, death. And the people at
higher risk were adults over 55 and
people with kidney disease, dehydration,
or a blockage or inflammation in the
bowel. The FDA also named some medicines
that raise this risk. Water tablets
called diuretics,
blood pressure tablets in the groups
called ACCE inhibitors and ARBs like
ramipril, leinipril or loartin
and anti-inflammatory painkillers like
ibuprofen.
Many people over 60 take at least one of
these. So my advice is simple. Do not
use a phosphate enema or drink phosphate
laxatives without asking your doctor
first and never use more than one dose
in a day. If you need a quick option
from below, ask about a glycerin or
bicycodal suppository instead.
Number nine, mineral oil also called
liquid paraffin. Taken by mouth, it
coats the stool so it slides out. But in
older people, especially those who are
frail, bed bound, or have trouble
swallowing, a little oil can slip into
the lungs that causes a type of
pneumonia that can be serious.
Mineral oil can also reduce the
vitamins's A, D, E, and K you absorb
from food. Medication safety lists for
older adults advise avoiding mineral oil
by mouth. Number 10, castor oil and
detox or slimming teas. Castor oil is a
very strong stimulant.
It can cause painful cramps, sudden
diarrhea and dehydration. And there are
gentler, better tested options today.
And many herbal cleansing or detox teas
contain senna or similar plants,
sometimes in high and unknown amounts.
If you drink them every day on top of
another laxative, you may be taking far
more than you realize.
Always read the label. Now, a word about
salts in your blood. Any laxative that
causes a lot of diarrhea can wash out
water and potassium.
That matters most if you take water
tablets or a heart medicine called
dejoxin because low potassium can upset
the heart rhythm. If laxatives are
giving you loose watery stools, the dose
is too high. Cut back and tell your
doctor. And if you take strong
painkillers called opioids like codine,
tramodol or morphine, constipation is
very common. Fiber alone often does not
help and can even make things worse.
Polyethylene glycol or Senna are usually
better choices and there are also
prescription medicines made specially
for opioid constipation.
Ask your doctor about them. Many other
everyday medicines can also cause
constipation.
I am making a separate video on exactly
that. So, subscribe if you would like to
see it. Now, the most important part.
When is constipation not something to
treat at home with a laxative?
Please see a doctor the same day or go
to hospital if you have severe tummy
pain, a swollen, hard tummy, vomiting or
you cannot pass any wind at all. These
can be signs of a blockage and laxatives
can make a blockage worse. There is also
one confusing situation I see often in
older people. Sometimes a large hard
stool gets stuck and watery stool leaks
around it. It looks like diarrhea. So
people take antid-diarrhea tablets.
That makes things much worse. If someone
has been constipated and then suddenly
has small amounts of watery leakage,
think of this and ask for help and see
your doctor soon. Not just for more
laxatives. If constipation is new for
you, if your bowel habit has changed for
more than a few weeks, if you see blood
in your stool, if you are losing weight
without trying, or if you need a
laxative every single day to go, these
things need to be checked, not just
treated.
Now, a word for carers, sons, daughters,
and anyone looking after an older
person. Please keep a simple list of
every laxative your loved one takes,
including the ones bought without a
prescription and any herbal teas. Many
families find three or four different
products in the cupboard, all being used
at once. Bring that list to the doctor
or pharmacist.
Watch for loose, watery stools,
weakness, confusion, or dizziness, which
can mean too much laxative or
dehydration.
And if your loved one has trouble
swallowing, ask before giving any
oil-based laxative or a thick fiber
drink. Now, three questions I am often
asked.
Question one, is it safe to take a
laxative every day? For many people,
yes, if it is the right one at the right
dose. Polyethylene glycol is well
studied for regular use. But if you need
a laxative everyday, your doctor should
know. Check your medicines and make sure
nothing else is going on. Question two,
should I have a bowel movement every
day? No. A normal range is anywhere from
three times a day to three times a week.
If you go every second day and it is
soft and easy, you do not need a
laxative just to go daily. Taking
laxatives to chase a daily bowel
movement is one of the most common
reasons for overuse.
Question three, are natural laxatives
safer? Not always.
Senna is natural and so is castor oil.
Natural does not mean gentle. The safest
choice is the one that is well tested at
the right dose for your body and your
medicines.
Now, as promised, here is a simple
ladder. Start at the bottom and only
climb one step at a time, giving each
step enough time to work. Step one,
every day, drink enough so your urine is
pale yellow. Eat fiber from food like
oats, fruit with the skin, vegetables,
and lentils.
Take a short walk after meals and sit on
the toilet at the same time each day,
ideally after breakfast, with your feet
on a small stool. Step two, if that is
not enough, add a fiber supplement like
psyllium with a full glass of water.
Give it a week or two. Step three, if
you are still struggling, ask your
doctor or pharmacist about polyethylene
glycol. Give it one to three days to
work before deciding it has failed.
Step four, for a rescue. If you have not
been for a few days and feel
uncomfortable, Senna or biccodal tablets
at bedtime or a glycerin or biccodal
suppository if the stool is low down.
One more gentle option worth knowing
about is the glycerin suppository.
It is one of the mildest things you can
use from below. It softens and
lubricates the stool right at the exit
and gently encourages the bowel to
empty, usually within about 15 minutes
to an hour. Many doctors prefer it to a
phosphate enema for older people who
feel the stool is stuck low down. If you
have never used a suppository, your
pharmacist can explain how, and it is
nothing to be embarrassed about. And
step five, if you are using laxatives
most days and still struggling, see your
doctor. There are prescription medicines
that work in different ways. And your
doctor can also look for a cause. So let
me recap. The safest choices after 60,
polyethylene glycol, which got the
strongest recommendation, fiber like
psyllium with plenty of water and senna
or bicodal at normal doses.
Use more care with magnesium if your
kidneys are weak. And remember that
lactulose can cause gas and docusate may
not do much. Be very careful with
phosphate enemas. Never more than one a
day and only with your doctor's advice
and avoid mineral oil by mouth, castor
oil, and detox teas. And the mistake, do
not stack doses.
Give each laxative the time it needs to
work. An honest note before I go. Most
of the laxative studies were done over
weeks or a few months, not years, and
many included younger adults.
The guideline itself says more research
is needed on long-term use in older
people. That is one more reason to keep
your doctor in the loop, especially if
you take several medicines.
Please remember this video is general
education.
It is not a diagnosis and not a
treatment plan for you. If you have
pain, bleeding, weight loss, or a change
in your bowels, please see your own
doctor. And always check with a
pharmacist before mixing a laxative with
your regular medicines.
If this was helpful, please share it
with someone who keeps a cupboard full
of laxatives.
It might save them from a fall or a
hospital visit. And if you want to try a
food first approach before any laxative,
watch my video on kiwi and prunes.
You will find it on the screen now. I am
Dr. Nimra.
Thank you for watching and look after
yourself.

5 Common Pills That Quietly Strain Your Heart After 60 (Doctor Explains)

If you are over 60, some of the most ordinary medicines in your cabinet (painkillers, cold tablets, "PM" sleep aids and fizzy tablets) can raise your blood pressure or make your heart work harder. And one common heart medicine is dangerous to stop on your own.

In this video, Dr Nimra explains what each medicine does inside an older body, who needs to be most careful, and safer alternatives to ask your pharmacist about. At the end, you'll get a simple 5-minute plan to check your own medicine cabinet.

In this video, Dr Nimra explains:
✅ Why everyday painkillers like ibuprofen and naproxen carry an FDA heart warning
✅ Why cold and flu tablets can raise your blood pressure
✅ The one heart medicine you should never stop without your doctor

🔔 Subscribe for new videos every Tuesday and Saturday: https://www.youtube.com/@DrNimraHealth?sub_confirmation=1

💬 Tell me in the comments: which number surprised you most?
📤 Share this with someone over 60 who takes medicine every day.
