subtitles.plaintext:
Tonight, before bed, millions of people
over 60 will take something from the
bathroom cabinet. A pill for the knee
that's been aching since the afternoon,
a cold tablet because the nose is
blocked again, something with PM on the
box because sleep hasn't been easy
lately. None of it prescribed, none of
it written down anywhere, and almost
nobody will mention it at their next
doctor's appointment because it doesn't
feel like real medicine. It's just what
you buy at the pharmacy. But, here's
what I want you to understand. After 60,
your heart, your blood vessels, and your
kidneys handle medicines differently
than they did at 40. Some of the most
ordinary pills in that cabinet can raise
your blood pressure, make your heart
work harder, or increase your risk of a
heart attack or stroke. And these aren't
rumors. They are official warnings on
the labels from the drug regulators
themselves that most people have never
read.
>> [clears throat]
>> Today, I'm going to walk you through
five everyday medicines that can quietly
strain your heart after 60. For each
one, I'll explain what it does inside
your body in plain words, who needs to
be most careful, and what you can use
instead. And I'm going to tell you
something most videos on this topic
leave out. One of these five is a
medicine where the biggest danger is not
taking it. It's stopping it on your own.
So, please don't throw anything away
until you've heard number one. At the
end, I'll give you a simple 5-minute
plan to check your own medicine cabinet
and the exact questions to take to your
pharmacist. One important thing before
we begin, this video is education, not
personal medical advice. Please don't
stop or change any medicine because of
something you hear here. Everything I
mention today is something to discuss
with your own doctor or pharmacist. And
at the end, I'll show you exactly how to
do that. Let's begin with number five.
Number five surprises almost everyone
because the medicine itself isn't the
problem. It's what's added to it. Many
effervescent fizzy or soluble tablets,
the ones you drop into a glass of water,
use sodium to make them fizz. That's the
same sodium that's in salt. Some soluble
painkillers and vitamin tablets contain
several hundred milligrams of sodium in
a single tablet. If you take two tablets
up to four times a day, you can swallow
more sodium from your medicine than most
doctors would want you to eat in a whole
day. Why does that matter? Because
sodium holds water in your blood
vessels. More water in the system means
higher pressure. And for someone with
heart failure, it can mean swollen
ankles and breathlessness. In 2013, a
large British study in the BMJ looked at
over a million patients and found that
people using sodium-containing soluble
medicines had higher rates of high blood
pressure, stroke, and death than people
taking the same drugs as ordinary
tablets. Now, I want to be honest with
you, because that's the whole point of
this channel. A later study in 2023 in
the European Heart Journal looked at
about 475,000
people aged 60 to 90 taking soluble
paracetamol and did not find a clear
increase in heart disease overall. So
this isn't a reason to panic. Here's
where it really matters. If you have
heart failure, kidney disease, or your
doctor has told you to limit salt, fizzy
tablets can quietly undo that advice.
What to do instead? Look at the label
for sodium per tablet. If you've been
told to cut salt, ask your pharmacist
for the ordinary swallow whole version
of the same medicine. Same drug, none of
the salt. That was the gentle one.
Number four is something many people
take every single night. If you've ever
bought a painkiller with PM or night on
the box, or an allergy tablet to help
you sleep, there's a good chance it
contains an old antihistamine called
diphenhydramine. In some countries, a
similar one called doxylamine is used.
These drugs make you drowsy by blocking
a chemical messenger in the brain called
acetylcholine. But, acetylcholine
doesn't only work in the brain. It helps
control your heart rate, your bladder,
your bowels, and your memory. So, after
60, when your body clears these drugs
more slowly, they can make your
heartbeat faster, cause confusion or
grogginess the next morning, make it
harder to empty your bladder, and make
you unsteady on your feet at night. That
last one worries me most. The Centers
for Disease Control and Prevention
reports that falls are the leading cause
of injury and injury deaths in adults
over 65. A drowsy, unsteady trip to the
bathroom at 3:00 a.m. is exactly how
many of those falls happen. This is why
the American Geriatrics Society, in its
Beers Criteria, the list doctors use for
medicines that are risky in older
adults, recommends that people over 65
generally avoid these antihistamines.
And research published in JAMA Internal
Medicine in 2015 found that heavy
long-term use of this type of medicine
was linked to a higher risk of dementia.
What to do instead? If you need
something for sleep more than a few
nights, that's a conversation for your
doctor because poor sleep after 60 often
has a cause worth finding. Pain, a full
bladder at night, sleep apnea, or a
medicine taken at the wrong time. The
treatment the American College of
Physicians recommends first for
long-term insomnia isn't a pill at all.
It's a short program called CBT-I,
cognitive behavioral therapy for
insomnia, which is now available in many
places online. And if you take it for
allergies, ask your pharmacist about
newer antihistamines that don't cause
drowsiness. Number three is the one I
see people reach for every winter,
especially people who already take blood
pressure medicine. When your nose is
blocked, a decongestant works by
squeezing the small blood vessels in
your nose, so the swelling goes down.
The problem is, the tablet doesn't only
go to your nose. It travels through your
whole body and tightens blood vessels
everywhere. Tighter blood vessels mean
higher blood pressure and a faster heart
rate.
The [clears throat] two common ones are
pseudoephedrine, usually kept behind the
pharmacy counter, and phenylephrine,
which is in many cold and flu tablets on
the open shelf. The American Heart
Association advises people with high
blood pressure to be careful with
decongestants and to read the labels of
cold medicines because they can raise
blood pressure and interfere with blood
pressure medication. And here's
something that surprises people. In
November 2024, the US Food and Drug
Administration proposed removing oral
phenylephrine from cold medicines
altogether. Not because of the heart,
but because their review concluded that
as a tablet, it doesn't actually work as
a decongestant. So many people over 60
have been taking something that may not
unblock their nose in the same box as
other ingredients they didn't need.
That's the other hidden danger with cold
and flu products. They're combinations.
One box can contain a decongestant, a
pain killer, and a sleep antihistamine
all at once. If you then take your usual
pain killer as well, you can double up
without knowing it. What to do instead?
For a blocked nose, simple salt water
nasal spray or rinses are safe for most
people. A steroid nasal spray is another
option to ask your pharmacist about. And
if you have high blood pressure, tell
the pharmacist before you buy any cold
product. Many pharmacies stock products
made for people with high blood
pressure. Now, number two. This is the
one I most want you to hear because it's
in almost every home. These medicines
belong to a group called NSAIDs,
nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
Ibuprofen, naproxen, and diclofenac are
the most common. They're sold
everywhere, they work well for pain, and
because they're so easy to buy, most
people think they're harmless. But in
2015, the US Food and Drug
Administration strengthened the warning
on these medicines. The warning says the
risk of heart attack and stroke can
increase even with short-term use, and
may begin within the first few weeks of
taking them. It says the risk is higher
with higher doses taken for longer, and
that it's greatest for people who
already have heart disease, but that
people without heart disease can be at
risk, too. Why does a painkiller affect
the heart? Three reasons in plain words.
One, these drugs make your kidneys hold
on to salt and water. More fluid means
higher blood pressure and more work for
the heart. Two, they can make blood
pressure medicines work less well. So,
someone whose pressure was well
controlled can see it creep up without
knowing why. Three, in people with a
weak heart, that extra fluid can tip
them into heart failure. Swollen legs,
breathlessness, waking up needing to sit
up to breathe. After 60, your kidneys
are usually less able to cope with this,
which is why these drugs are also a
common cause of kidney problems in older
adults, especially when combined with
certain blood pressure pills and water
tablets. And one more risk I have to
mention, stomach bleeding, especially in
people who also take aspirin or blood
thinners. What to do instead? For
everyday aches, paracetamol, called
acetaminophen in the US, is usually the
safer first choice for the heart, as
long as you stay within the dose on the
label, unless if you drink alcohol
regularly or have liver problems. For a
sore knee or hand, a painkiller gel
rubbed on the skin puts much less of the
drug into your bloodstream than a
tablet. Ask your pharmacist. Warmth,
gentle movement, and strengthening
exercises help arthritis pain more than
most people expect and I'll make a full
video on that. And if you need an
anti-inflammatory for more than a few
days, speak to your doctor first,
especially if you have high blood
pressure, heart disease, kidney
problems, or you've ever had a stomach
ulcer. Now, number one. And this is
where I need you to listen very
carefully because this one works the
opposite way. Low-dose aspirin is one of
the most common daily medicines in
people over 60 and the advice about it
has changed, which has left a lot of
people confused.
>> [cough]
>> Here's [clears throat] the change. For
years, many healthy people took a daily
aspirin just in case to prevent a first
heart attack. But in 2022, the US
Preventive Services Task Force, the
panel that set screening and prevention
guidance, recommended that adults 60 and
older should not start taking aspirin to
prevent a first heart attack or stroke.
The reason? For many older people, the
risk of bleeding in the stomach or the
brain outweighs the benefit. So, you
might think, then I should stop mine.
And this is exactly the mistake. If you
take aspirin because you've already had
a heart attack, a stent, a bypass, or a
stroke, aspirin is doing a very
important job and stopping it suddenly
can be dangerous. In 2017, researchers
in Sweden studied more than 600,000
people taking low-dose aspirin,
published in the journal Circulation.
People who stopped taking it had a 37%
higher risk of heart attack, stroke, or
cardiovascular death than people who
kept taking it. The risk rose soon after
stopping and didn't fade with time.
Among people who took aspirin because
they'd already had a heart attack or
stroke, about one in every 36 who
stopped had an extra cardiovascular
event within a year. Why? Aspirin makes
the tiny cells in your blood called
platelets less sticky, so they're less
likely to form a clot inside a narrowed
artery. When you stop, that protection
disappears. What to do instead? Don't
start aspirin on your own. Don't stop it
on your own, either. At your next
appointment, ask one simple question.
Why am I taking aspirin? To prevent a
first problem or because I've already
had one? If it's the first, your doctor
may decide, with you, to stop it safely.
If it's the second, you'll probably be
told to keep taking it. Either way, it's
a decision you make together, not alone.
The same is true of many heart
medicines, including beta-blockers and
blood thinners. Some of them should
never be stopped suddenly. That's why
the plan I'm about to give you starts
with a conversation, not a rubbish bin.
Here's what I'd like you to do this
week.
Step [clears throat] one, the bag. Put
every medicine you take into one bag.
Prescriptions, painkillers, cold
tablets, sleep aids, vitamins, herbal
supplements, creams, and eye drops.
Everything. Step two, take the bag to
your pharmacist or doctor. This is
sometimes called a brown bag review or a
medication review, and in many places,
it's free. Pharmacists are experts in
exactly this, spotting duplicates,
interactions, and medicines that are no
longer needed. Step [clears throat]
three, ask these four questions. Write
them down. Do I still need each of
these? Do any of them raise my blood
pressure or affect my heart? Are any of
them the same drug under two names?
Which ones must I never stop suddenly?
Step four, know your number. If you're
over 60, a home blood pressure monitor
is one of the most useful things you can
own. Check it a few mornings a week,
before coffee and medicines, sitting
quietly for 5 minutes first. If your
pressure climbs after starting a new
medicine, even an over-the-counter one,
that's something to tell your doctor.
Step five, one list. Keep a written list
of everything you take with doses in
your wallet or on your phone. If you
ever end up in an emergency room, that
list can save precious time.
>> [clears throat]
>> Let's recap the five.
Number five, fizzy tablets with hidden
salt that matters most if you've been
told to limit salt.
>> [clears throat]
>> Number four, PM Sleep and nighttime
allergy pills, which bring a fast heart,
confusion, and falls.
>> [clears throat]
>> Number three, cold and flu
decongestants, which raise blood
pressure, and one of them may not even
work.
>> [clears throat]
>> Number two, everyday anti-inflammatory
painkillers, where the risk can start
within weeks. Number one, low-dose
aspirin, where the decision to stop
belongs with your doctor, never alone.
None of this is about being afraid of
your medicine cabinet. Medicines are
some of the best tools we have. It's
about knowing what you're taking and
why, because after 60, the small daily
choices add up. Now, the comment I'd
love to read. Which of these five
surprised you most? Just type the
number, 1 2 3 4 or 5. And please do one
kind thing today. Think of one person
over 60 who takes something every day, a
parent, a neighbor, a friend. Send them
this video. One question at their next
appointment could make a real
difference. If this was useful,
subscribe. In the next video, I'll talk
about the blood pressure number after 60
that most people misunderstand. I'm Dr.
Nimra. Look after yourself, and I'll see
you in the next one.

Were you told to avoid nuts, seeds and popcorn because of diverticulitis? Or that every attack needs antibiotics, and two attacks mean an operation? In this video, Dr Nimra explains the 5 old rules that doctors no longer follow, based on the latest guidelines and real trials, and what to do instead after 60.

The 5 changes:
1. Nuts, seeds and popcorn are allowed again
2. Antibiotics are no longer automatic (and who still needs them)
3. Most mild attacks are treated at home
4. After an attack, fibre is your friend (the mistake many people make)
5. Surgery is no longer decided by counting attacks

Plus: the common painkillers that raise your risk, 5 myths, warning signs that mean hospital straight away, tips for carers, and a simple 7-day plan for the week after a flare.

💬 Tell me in the comments: were you ever told to avoid seeds or nuts?

👍 If this helped, please share it with someone who still picks the seeds out of their bread. Subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: Over 60 and Hard to Go? 2 Kiwis a Day or Prunes: Which Works Better

CHAPTERS
0:00 The old diverticulitis rules
1:04 1. Nuts, seeds and popcorn are allowed
2:33 Were you told to avoid seeds?
3:09 What diverticula really are
4:42 What an attack feels like

This video is general education, not personal medical advice. If you have tummy pain, fever, bleeding or a change in your bowels, see your own doctor. Never stop a prescribed medicine, especially aspirin or a blood thinner, without talking to your doctor.

a sharp pain low on the left side of
your tummy. A doctor says the word
deticulitis
and then very often someone hands you a
list. No nuts, no seeds,
no popcorn,
no strawberries, no tomatoes with pips,
antibiotics straight away. And if it
happens twice, an operation.
If you were told any of that, you were
told what doctors believed 20 or 30
years ago. A lot has changed since then,
and much of it in your favor. Today, I
will walk you through five things
doctors now do differently with
dieticulitis.
Some of them will surprise you. I will
also tell you about the one mistake many
people make after an attack. The common
pills that raise your risk, five myths,
and at the end, a simple 7-day plan for
the week after a flare. Quick note, this
is general education, not personal
medical advice.
Change number one, nuts, seeds, and
popcorn are allowed again. For decades,
people with diabetic were told to avoid
anything small and hard. The idea
sounded logical. A seed or a bit of
popcorn might get stuck in one of the
little pockets in the bowel wall and
start an infection.
So, people picked the seeds out of their
bread and gave up strawberries for life.
But nobody had actually tested it. Then
in 2008, researchers at Harvard followed
47,000 men for 18 years. They recorded
what these men ate and who developed
diverticulitis.
81 men had a first attack over those
years. And the result was the opposite
of the old advice.
Men who ate nuts at least twice a week
had about 20% less diverticulitis than
men who almost never ate them. The men
who ate the most popcorn had about a
quarter less. Corn made no difference at
all. Seeds did not cause attacks.
Today, the American Gastroenterological
Association says there is no need to
avoid nuts, seeds, or popcorn to prevent
diverticulitis.
If one particular food always upsets
you, of course, you can leave that one
out. But you do not need a forbidden
list. Before we go on, I would love to
know something. Were you ever told to
avoid seeds or nuts? You can simply
write yes or no in the comments.
Your answer helps other people find this
video when they need it. And if we have
not met before, I am Dr. Nimra. On this
channel, I talk about health after 60 in
plain calm language. The kind of
conversation a short appointment does
not always have time for. If that sounds
useful, you are very welcome to
subscribe and stay now. So the rest of
this makes sense, let me explain in one
minute what diverticulara are. Your
large bowel is a long muscular tube.
Over the years, the wall can develop
small weak spots. Under pressure, the
inner lining pushes out through these
weak spots and forms little pockets like
small balloons on the outside of the
tube. Each pocket is called a deticulum.
Many of them together are diverticula.
Having these pockets is called
deticulosis.
It is very common. In colonoscopies done
in the United States, almost half of the
adults examined had them. And the older
we get, the more common they are. Most
people with these pockets never know
they have them. They cause no pain at
all.
Diabeticulitis is different. That is
when one or more pockets become
inflamed.
That is the painful attack. And here is
some good news. In a large study of more
than 2,000 veterans with an average age
of 67, only about four in a 100 people
with these pockets went on to have
diverticulitis,
even after many years.
And the older people were when the
pockets were first found, the lower
their risk. So if a scan or a
colonoscopy has told you that you have
diverticulara, please do not panic. For
most people, they stay quiet for life.
Now, what does an attack feel like? Most
often, a steady pain low on the left
side of the tummy. It usually does not
come and go in seconds like wind.
It stays sometimes for days. There may
be a fever, feeling sick, loss of
appetite, and a change in your bowels,
either constipation or loose stools. The
area can be tender when you press on it.
One thing I want to mention for viewers
of Asian background.
In Western countries, the pain is almost
always on the left. But in many Asian
countries, somewhere between about four
and seven in 10 cases are on the right
side. On the right, it can look just
like appendicitis.
So the side of the pain does not rule it
out. Change number two, antibiotics are
no longer automatic.
This is the one that surprises people
the most. For a long time,
diverticulitis was treated like a simple
infection.
pain on the left, a cause of antibiotics
every time. Then doctors started asking
a question. Is it really an infection in
every case or is it mainly inflammation?
And they tested it properly. In Sweden,
a trial called Avod gave 623 people with
a mild uncomplicated attack either
antibiotics or no antibiotics.
recovery, complications, and repeat
attacks were about the same in both
groups. In the Netherlands, a trial
called Diablo did the same in 528
people. Half had antibiotics, half had
careful observation.
The people who had antibiotics recovered
in about 12 days on average. The people
without antibiotics recovered in about
14 days.
That difference was small and not
significant.
But here is the interesting part. The
group without antibiotics actually spent
less time in hospital, 2 days instead of
three. And side effects from the
antibiotics themselves, like stomach
upset or rash, happened in about 8 in
100 people who took them and almost
nobody in the other group. Because of
studies like these, the American
Gastroenterological Association now says
antibiotics should be used selectively,
not routinely, for mild, uncomplicated
diabeticulitis.
The American College of Physicians says
something similar.
Now, please listen carefully because
this is important.
Selectively does not mean never and it
does not mean you should decide this
yourself at home. Antibiotics are still
needed for many people. Your doctor will
usually give them if you are frail, if
you have other serious illnesses, or if
your immune system is weak. That
includes people on steroid tablets,
chemotherapy, or medicines after a
transplant.
They are also needed if you are vomiting
and cannot keep fluids down. If the pain
is severe or not improving, if your
blood tests show a lot of inflammation,
or if a skin shows an abscess, which is
a pocket of pus. And many people over 60
have at least one of those things.
So, the honest message is this.
Antibiotics are no longer automatic. And
if your doctor does not give them, that
is not neglect.
It may be the modern correct approach,
but if your doctor does give them, take
the full course exactly as prescribed.
Change number three, most attacks are
now treated at home. Not long ago, many
people with diverticulitis were admitted
to hospital. Today, the American College
of Physicians suggests that most people
with a mild attack who are otherwise
well and have support at home can be
treated as outpatients.
There was no evidence that a hospital
bed made a mild attack heal faster. A
scan is also used more wisely. Now, if
it is your first attack or the doctor is
not sure, a CT scan of the tummy
confirms what is going on and checks for
complications.
If you have had confirmed attacks before
and this one feels the same and is mild,
your doctor may not need to scan you
every time. So, what do you eat during
the attack itself?
For a mild flare, many doctors suggest
keeping food light for a few days. Clear
soups, water, weak tea, broth, then
soft, simple foods as the pain settles,
white rice, eggs, yogurt, a banana, soft
cooked vegetables without skins, toast.
There is not strong evidence that a long
liquid diet helps. So most people can
move back towards normal food as soon as
they feel able. Your doctor will guide
you. Please drink enough during an
attack. A fever and poor appetite can
dry you out quickly after 60 and that
can make you dizzy and confused.
A pale yellow urine is a simple sign you
are drinking enough. And for pain, many
doctors suggest paracetamol, also called
acetaminophen,
not ibuprofen.
In a moment, I will explain why. Change
number four. After the attack, fiber is
your friend, not your enemy. And this is
where many people make the one mistake I
promised to tell you about. During the
attack, you eat soft, low- fiber food.
That is fine for a few days.
The mistake is staying on that soft,
low- fiber food for weeks, months, or
for the rest of your life out of fear.
White bread, white rice, no fruit skins,
no beans, no vegetables with any
texture.
People do this because they think rough
food will trigger another attack. But
the evidence points the other way. In a
large British study called Epic Oxford,
more than 47,000 adults were followed
for over 11 years. People who ate around
25 g of fiber a day had about 40% less
serious diverticular disease than people
who ate less than 14 g.
And vegetarians who usually eat more
fiber had about a third less. Fiber
keeps the stool soft and bulky, so the
bowel does not have to squeeze as hard.
Less squeezing means less pressure on
those weak spots in the wall. Fiber also
feeds the friendly bacteria in your gut.
So once the attack has settled and your
doctor is happy, slowly bring fiber
back. Not all at once. If you jump from
almost none to a big bowl of beans, you
will have gas, cramps, and bloating, and
you will think fiber is the problem.
Start with one extra portion a day. Oats
or porridge in the morning, a piece of
fruit with the skin, like an apple or a
pear, soft cooked vegetables at lunch.
Over two to four weeks, build up to
whole grain bread, brown rice, lentils,
beans, and chickpeas. If food alone is
hard, a spoon of psyllium husk in water,
which many of you know as isol, is a
gentle way to add soluble fiber. Start
with a small amount and always take it
with a full glass of water. As fiber
goes up, water must go up, too. Fiber
without water can make stools harder,
not softer. Change number five, surgery
is no longer decided by counting
attacks.
For many years, there was a simple rule.
Two attacks and you were sent for an
operation to remove the affected part of
the bowel. The thinking was that each
attack makes the next one more
dangerous.
Doctors now know that is not true for
most people. The first attack is usually
the most serious one, and most people
never have another. A review of 27
studies found that only about one in
eight people had a repeat attack of mild
diverticulitis.
So about seven out of eight did not.
Today guidelines say the decision about
surgery should depend on how severe the
disease is and how much it affects your
life, not on the number of attacks.
Surgery is still very important for some
people. For example, if there is a hole
in the bowel, a large abscess, a
blockage, or an abnormal connection
called a fistula, often to the bladder.
And some people with frequent attacks
that ruin their quality of life choose
surgery and are glad they did. But it is
a personal decision made with a surgeon,
weighing the risks and the benefits,
not an automatic rule. There is one more
thing doctors now do after an attack and
it is important.
A colonoscopy.
A bowel cancer can sometimes look like
diverticulitis on a scan. So after an
attack with complications or after a
first attack if you have not had a good
colonoscopy in the last year, guidelines
suggest one. It is usually done about 6
to 8 weeks later when the inflammation
has calmed down. If you have warning
signs like blood in the stool, weight
loss, or anemia, it may be done sooner.
Please do not skip this test. In most
people, it is clear. But if something is
found early, it can save your life. Now,
I promise to tell you about some common
pills that raise your risk. The first
group is the anti-inflammatory
painkillers.
ibuprofen, neproxen, dicopenac, and
similar tablets.
In the same Harvard group of 47,000 men,
those who took these regularly, at least
twice a week, had about 70% more
diverticulitis.
Regular aspirin was linked to about 25%
more. Both were also linked to more
bleeding from the pockets.
Now, many of you take a small dose of
aspirin every day for your heart after a
heart attack or a stent. Please do not
stop that aspirin because of this video.
For many people, protecting the heart
matters far more. Talk to your doctor
who can weigh up your heart and your
bowel together. But if you take
ibuprofen or similar tablets for aching
joints, often bought without a
prescription, that is worth discussing.
Paracetamol is usually gentler on the
bowel, though it has its own safe daily
limit.
Strong painkillers called opioids like
codine, tramodol, and morphine slow the
bowel down and cause constipation.
They have also been linked to more
serious complications of deticulitis.
Steroid tablets like predniscolone can
hide the signs of a serious attack. If
you take any of these, make sure your
doctor knows you have diverticulara.
And a few everyday things matter, too.
In another Harvard study, the men who
ate the most red meat had about 60% more
diverticulitis than those who ate the
least. Swapping one daily portion of red
meat for chicken or fish was linked to
about a fifth less. Being very
overweight and smoking both raise the
risk of attacks and complications.
And being active, especially brisk
walking or other exercise that gets you
a little out of breath, has been linked
to less diverticulitis.
Now, let me bust five common myths about
diverticulitis.
Myth number one, if I have diverticula,
I will get diverticulitis.
Not true. Most people with these pockets
never have a single attack. As we saw in
the veteran study, it was about four in
a 100. Myth number two, seeds and nuts
get stuck in the pockets.
There is no good evidence for this. The
large study we talked about found that
people who ate more nuts and popcorn had
fewer attacks, not more. Myth number
three, every attack needs antibiotics.
For mild, uncomplicated attacks in
healthy people, the trials showed
similar recovery without them. But for
many people, especially frail people or
those with other illnesses, they are
still needed. Your doctor decides.
Myth number four, after an attack, I
should eat a low- fiber diet forever.
This is the mistake we talked about. Low
fiber is only for the few days of the
flare. After that, slowly building up
fiber is what most guidelines recommend.
Myth number five, probiotics or a
special tablet will stop it coming back.
Many people are offered a medicine
called misalamine to prevent new
attacks.
Large trials found it did not work and
the American College of Physicians now
recommends against it. And for
probiotics, there is not yet good
evidence that they prevent attacks
either. The most reliable prevention is
still the simple things. Fiber, water,
movement, a healthy weight, not smoking,
and avoiding regular anti-inflammatory
painkillers where you can. Now, the most
important part, when should you go to
hospital straight away?
Please go to the emergency department or
call an ambulance if you have any of
these. Severe tummy pain that is getting
worse. A tummy that is hard, swollen or
very painful to touch. A high fever with
shivering. Vomiting so that you cannot
keep fluids down. Feeling faint,
confused or very unwell. Or you cannot
pass any wind or stool at all. And there
is one more which surprises many people.
Deticular can bleed. This bleeding is
usually painless.
You may suddenly pass a lot of red or
maroon blood or clots from the back
passage. It often stops by itself, but
sometimes it is heavy. If that happens,
especially if you feel dizzy or weak or
if you take blood thinners, go to
hospital straight away. Do not wait to
see if it stops. Also, see your doctor
soon within days, not weeks. If you
notice a change in your bowel habit that
lasts more than a few weeks, blood in
your stool, weight loss without trying,
or feeling unusually tired and pale,
these are not always deticular and they
need to be checked. Now, a word for
carers, sons, daughters, and anyone
looking after an older person. In older
people, diverticulitis can be quiet.
Some do not get a fever. Some do not
complain of much pain. Instead, they may
simply go off their food, seem confused,
become very tired, or have a fall. Older
people on steroids may have hardly any
signs at all, even with a serious
problem. So, if someone you care for has
known diicular and suddenly seems not
themselves, gently press low on their
tummy and ask if it hurts. Check if they
have opened their bowels and do not be
afraid to call the doctor. You know them
best.
Now, three questions I am often asked.
Question one, can I eat strawberries,
tomatoes, kiwi, and grapes?
Yes. These were all on the old forbidden
list because of their tiny seeds. There
is no evidence they cause attacks.
They are good sources of fiber.
If one particular food always gives you
pain, leave that one out. Otherwise,
enjoy them. Question two, my doctor did
not give me antibiotics.
Should I be worried? Not necessarily
for a mild attack in someone who is
otherwise well. This follows the new
guidelines,
but your doctor should tell you what to
watch for. If the pain gets worse, you
develop a fever or you start vomiting,
go back to your doctor or to hospital
the same day. Question three, will it
come back? For most people, no. Most
people who have one attack never have
another. Keeping your bowels soft and
regular, staying active, and avoiding
regular anti-inflammatory painkillers
all help your chances.
Now, as promised, here is a simple 7-day
plan for the week after an attack. Once
your doctor says you are on the mend,
day one and day two, keep food soft and
simple. Rice, eggs, yogurt, a banana,
clear soup, soft cooked carrots, or
corette without the skin. Drink steadily
through the day. Take paracetamol for
pain if needed, not ibuprofen, and
finish any antibiotics you were given.
Day three, add oats or porridge for
breakfast.
Keep everything else soft. Take a short,
gentle walk around the house or garden
if you feel able. Day four, add one
piece of soft fruit, like a ripe pear or
a kiwi. Have one more glass of water
than usual.
Day five,
swap white bread for one slice of whole
grain bread. Add a portion of soft
cooked vegetables with lunch. Walk a
little further. Day six. Try a small
portion of lentils or dal or a few
spoons of beans well cooked. If you get
some wind, that is normal. Keep the
portion small and try again in a day or
two. Day seven.
Look back at your week. If the pain is
gone and your bowels are moving
comfortably, keep building fiber slowly
over the next two to four weeks.
Book or ask about your colonoscopy if
your doctor recommended one and put a
handful of nuts back into your life if
you enjoy them. If at any point the pain
comes back strongly or you get a fever,
stop the plan and contact your doctor.
So, let me recap the five things doctors
now do differently.
One, nuts, seeds, and popcorn are
allowed.
People who ate more of them had fewer
attacks.
Two, antibiotics are no longer automatic
for mild, uncomplicated attacks.
But many people, especially frail people
or those with other illnesses, still
need them, and your doctor decides.
Three, most mild attacks are treated at
home with light food for a few days and
plenty to drink. Four, after the attack,
fiber is your friend. Build it back up
slowly with water. Staying on a low-
fiber diet forever is the mistake. Five,
surgery is no longer decided by counting
attacks.
It depends on how severe your disease is
and how it affects your life. And a
colonoscopy after an attack is often
recommended.
Plus, be careful with regular ibuprofen
type painkillers and know the warning
signs that mean hospital straight away.
An honest note before I go. Most of the
big diet studies I mentioned were done
in men, mostly in America and Britain.
They show strong links, but they cannot
prove cause and effect on their own. The
antibiotic trials were done in carefully
chosen people with mild attacks
confirmed on a scan in hospitals that
could watch them closely. That is why
this video is not a reason to refuse
treatment your doctor offers. It is a
reason to understand it and to ask good
questions.
Please remember this video is general
education.
It is not a diagnosis and not a
treatment plan for you. If you have
tummy pain, a fever, bleeding, or any
change in your bowels, please see your
own doctor. And never stop a prescribed
medicine, especially aspirin or a blood
thinner, without talking to them first.
If this was helpful, please share it
with someone who still picks the seeds
out of their bread. It might give them
back a few foods they love. And if your
problem is more about hard stools and
straining, I made a video on exactly
that, about two fruits that really help.
You will find it on the screen now. I am
Dr. Nimra.
Thank you for watching and look after
yourself.

Welcome to Dr Nimra | Health After 60 🩺

I'm Dr Nimra, this channel exists for one reason: to explain, in plain and simple language, what your 15-minute doctor's visit doesn't have time to explain.

Every week I break down what really happens inside your body after 60, and what you can do about it:
💊 Medicines: what your pills really do, side effects, and dangerous combinations
🥗 Food & diet: what to eat, what to limit, and why
🚶 Exercise & mobility: simple movement that keeps you strong and independent
😴 Sleep, bathroom and daily habits: the small things that add up
❤️ Heart, blood pressure, blood sugar, kidneys, bones, brain and eyes

⚠️ Disclaimer
The content on this channel is for general education and information only. It is not personal medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Never start, stop or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have a medical emergency, call your local emergency number.

records.text:
Has your bowel pattern changed since you turned 60? Most bowel changes are harmless, but some are your body asking for a proper check. In this video, Dr Nimra explains 10 bowel changes after 60 that mean you should see a doctor, including the one people miss most often, when blood is not "just piles", black stools, night-time diarrhoea, pale greasy stools and more.

You will also learn the hidden warning sign that has nothing to do with the toilet, 3 myths that stop people getting checked, when to go the same day, and the 4 things to tell your doctor so you are taken seriously.

💬 Tell me in the comments: has your bowel pattern changed since you turned 60? Yes or no.

👍 If this helped, please share it with someone over 60 who might be keeping quiet about a change. Subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: 10 Common Medicines That Cause Constipation After 60

CHAPTERS
0:00 "I suppose that is just age"
1:09 1. A change that does not go back to normal
2:20 Has your pattern changed?
2:54 2. Blood in the stool (not always piles)
3:50 3. Black, tarry stools
4:50 4. Weight loss you cannot explain
5:54 5. Diarrhoea for weeks, at night, or after antibiotics
7:22 6. Pale, greasy, floating stools
8:46 7. Sudden pain, then bloody diarrhoea
10:09 3 myths that stop people getting checked
11:27 The hidden warning sign
12:48 8. Not emptying, thin stools or a lump
13:38 9. New leakage or urgency
14:23 10. Constipation with watery leaking
15:19 Same day or within days?
16:09 What will the doctor do?
17:22 4 things to tell your doctor
18:27 For families and carers
19:27 Bowel screening
20:15 Recap
21:12 An honest note

This video is general education, not personal medical advice. If you have any of these changes, please speak to your doctor. If you have heavy bleeding, severe sudden tummy pain, or black stools with dizziness, get help the same day.

Sources:
NICE guideline NG12: Suspected cancer, recognition and referral (updated 2023)
American Cancer Society: Colorectal cancer survival rates (people diagnosed 2014 to 2020)
US Preventive Services Task Force: Colorectal cancer screening recommendation (2021)
Chari et al., Gastroenterology 2005: new-onset diabetes and pancreatic cancer risk
American Academy of Family Physicians 2020: Clostridioides difficile infection
Mayo Clinic: Ischemic colitis; Microscopic colitis

subtitles.plaintext:
A lady in her late 60s came to see me
about her knee. As she picked up her
bag, she said, "Oh, one more thing,
doctor. My bowels have been a bit
different for a couple of months. But I
suppose that is just age." I asked her
to sit down again. I suppose that is
just age is a sentence I hear every
week. And sometimes it hides something
that should have been checked months
earlier. Most bowel changes after 60 are
not cancer. But some are your body
asking for a proper look and the earlier
that look happens, the better the
result. Today I will walk you through 10
bowel changes after 60 that mean you
should see a doctor. Number one is the
one people miss most often. I will also
tell you about a hidden warning sign
that has nothing to do with the toilet
at all. Three myths that stop people
from getting checked. And at the end,
the four things to tell your doctor so
you are taken seriously.
Quick note before we start, this is
general education, not personal medical
advice.
Number one, a change in your normal
pattern that does not go back to normal.
Every person has their own normal. For
one person, it is once a day after
breakfast.
For another, it is every second day.
That is fine. What matters is change. If
your stools have become looser or harder
or you are going much more often or much
less often and it has lasted more than
about 3 or 4 weeks that needs a doctor.
Why is it missed so often? Because it is
slow and quiet.
There is no pain, no drama.
People think it is my diet, it is my
age, it will settle. In the UK,
guidelines say that anyone over 60 with
a lasting change in bowel habit should
be checked promptly, and this often
starts with a simple stool test. Notice
that the guideline does not say wait and
see. It says check. So, if your pattern
has changed and stayed changed, do not
wait for something worse. A change alone
is enough reason to go. Before we go on,
I would love to know something. Has your
own bowel pattern changed since you
turned 60? Just write yes or no in the
comments.
There is no shame in this. I promise
you. Talking about it openly is how we
help each other. And if we have not met
before, I am Dr. Nimra. On this channel,
I talk about health after 60 in plain
calm language.
If that is useful to you, you are very
welcome to subscribe.
Number two, blood in your stool or blood
on the toilet paper. Bright red blood is
very often from piles which doctors call
hemorrhoids or from a small tear near
the back passage.
Those are common and usually harmless.
But here is the problem. Many people
over 60 have had piles for years. So
when they see blood, they say, "Oh, that
is just my piles again." And they never
get it checked. Bleeding from piles and
bleeding from something higher up in the
bowel can look exactly the same. You
cannot tell the difference by looking.
Neither can I without an examination.
So any new bleeding after the age of 50
without a clear reason should be seen by
a doctor. Darker blood or blood mixed
into the stool rather than sitting on
the surface is even more important to
report.
Number three, black sticky stools that
look like tar. This is different from
blood that you can see as red. Black
terry stools often with a strong smell
can mean bleeding high up in the stomach
or the first part of the gut. Blood that
travels a long way through the gut turns
black. Common causes include stomach
ulcers which can be triggered by
painkillers like ibuprofen, neproxen or
even aspirin.
Now there is one important exception.
Iron tablets can make your stools dark
green or black. So can bismouth
medicines and black licorice.
If you have just started iron, dark
stools are expected. But true black tar,
sticky and shiny, especially if you also
feel dizzy, weak or short of breath,
needs to be seen the same day. If you
are not sure, it is always fine to ask.
Number four, weight loss you cannot
explain. If you are losing weight
without trying, without changing your
diet or doing more exercise, that is
something your doctor must know about,
especially if it comes with a change in
your bowels or with pain in your tummy.
A good rule is this. If you lose about
5% of your body weight over 6 to 12
months without trying, tell your doctor.
For someone who weighs 70 kilos, that is
only about 3 and 12 kilos.
Weigh yourself once a month on the same
scales at the same time of day and write
it down. Then you will know for sure.
Many people notice it first through
their clothes.
Trousers feel loose. A belt needs a new
hole. A ring slips off. Weight loss on
its own has many causes including
thyroid problems, low mood, diabetes,
and poor appetite.
But together with a bowel change, it
moves higher up the list. Number five,
new watery diarrhea that goes on for
weeks, especially if it wakes you up at
night. A short tummy bug that lasts two
or 3 days is common and usually settles.
But diarrhea that lasts for weeks is
different. And diarrhea that wakes you
from sleep is a sign that something real
is happening because ordinary irritable
bowel symptoms usually rest when you
rest. One cause that many people have
never heard of is called microscopic
colitis.
It is inflammation in the lining of the
bowel that you cannot see with the naked
eye. Even during a camera test, the
bowel can look completely normal. The
doctor has to take tiny samples called
biopsies and look at them under a
microscope.
Microscopic colitis is common in older
people in people over 65 with
long-lasting diarrhea. It is one of the
most common causes found. And the good
news is it is usually very treatable.
There is another kind of diarrhea to
watch for. If you develop three or more
loose stools a day during or within a
few weeks after a course of antibiotics,
especially with fever or tummy cramps,
call your doctor. That can be an
infection called C difference.
It is more common after 70 and it needs
proper treatment.
Number six, pale, greasy, floating
stools that are hard to flush. If your
stools have become pale, clay colored or
oily, if they float and leave a greasy
ring in the toilet, and they smell much
worse than usual, that can mean your
body is not digesting fat properly. One
common reason is that the pancreas, the
gland behind your stomach that makes
digestive juices, is not working well.
Sometimes this comes with yellow skin or
yellow eyes, dark urine, and itching.
Yellow skin or eyes always need a doctor
quickly.
Now, here is something very few people
know. In people over 50, new diabetes
that appears suddenly, especially with
weight loss, can occasionally be an
early sign of a problem in the pancreas.
A study from the Mayo Clinic found that
people over 50 with brand new diabetes
had about eight times the usual risk of
pancreatic cancer in the next 3 years.
That sounds frightening. So, let me put
it in real numbers. That was still only
about one in every hundred people. 99
out of 100 did not have it. But if you
have new diabetes, unexplained weight
loss, and pale greasy stools altogether,
please mention all three to your doctor
at the same visit. Number seven, sudden
tummy pain followed by bloody diarrhea.
Here is a pattern I want every person
over 60 to know. A sudden cramping pain,
often on the left side of the tummy, and
then usually within a day, loose stools
with red or maroon blood. This can be a
condition called eskeemic colitis.
It means part of the bowel is not
getting enough blood for a while, a bit
like a small stroke, but in the bowel.
It is more common after 55 and in people
with heart disease, narrowed arteries or
blood pressure that drops too low, for
example, after dehydration or with some
medicines.
Many mild cases get better with rest and
fluids in hospital, but some are
serious.
So, severe sudden tummy pain with blood
is not something to sleep on. Call for
help the same day. Let me pause here for
a moment because I know some of this can
feel worrying. If you are watching this
and recognizing yourself, please take a
breath. Recognizing a sign is not the
same as having a disease.
It simply means it is time for a
conversation with your doctor. That is
all. Most of those conversations end
with reassurance or with a simple
treatment.
Now, before the last three, let me deal
with three myths that stop people from
getting checked. Myth one, if it was
serious, it would hurt. This is not
true. Early bowel cancer is often
completely painless.
That is exactly why changes in your
pattern and hidden bleeding matter so
much. Pain often comes late. Do not wait
for pain.
Myth two, I had a clear camera test a
few years ago, so I am fine. A clear
test is very good news and it does lower
your risk, but it is not a lifetime
guarantee.
And more importantly, if you have new
symptoms now, the old result does not
cover them. New symptoms need a new
look. Myth three, my screening test was
normal, so I can ignore this.
Screening tests are designed for people
who have no symptoms at all. They look
for hidden problems in healthy people.
If you have symptoms, you are no longer
in the screening group. You are in the
see a doctor group. Please tell your
doctor about your symptoms. Even if your
last screening kit came back normal. And
now the hidden warning sign I promised
you. It has nothing to do with the
toilet. It is tiredness,
specifically tiredness and
breathlessness caused by low iron. Here
is how it works. A growth in the bowel
can bleed very slowly, a tiny amount
every day, so little that you never see
it. Over months, your body loses iron,
and you become anemic.
You feel tired, you get breathless on
the stairs, you look pale, you may feel
cold, or your heart may race.
Many people blame this on age. Then a
blood test shows iron deficiency anemia.
In a man of any age or a woman after
menopause, iron deficiency without a
clear reason must be investigated,
usually with a look inside the bowel and
the stomach. In the UK, anyone over 60
with iron deficiency anemia should be
referred quickly.
So, here is my advice. If a blood test
ever shows that you are low in iron, do
not just take iron tablets and stop
there. Ask your doctor, why am I low in
iron? That one question has saved many
lives.
Let me go on with the last three
changes.
Number eight, the feeling that you have
not emptied properly or stools that have
become much thinner. Some people
describe it as always needing to go
again even though they have just been.
Doctors call that tenezmus.
Others notice their stools have become
narrow like a pencil every time for
weeks.
Now the shape of stool changes from day
to day and a thin stool once in a while
means nothing. But a feeling of not
emptying that will not go away or a lump
you can feel near the back passage or a
lump in your tummy should always be
checked. A doctor can often feel
something during a simple quick
examination.
I know it is uncomfortable to think
about. It takes a minute and it can tell
us a lot. Number nine, new leakage or
sudden urgency. If you have started
leaking stool or you suddenly cannot
hold on long enough to reach the toilet,
please do not hide it. Many older people
are so embarrassed that they stop going
out, stop visiting family and wear pads
in secret for years. That is very sad
because there is often a cause and often
a treatment.
New leakage can come from weak muscles
after child birth or surgery, from
diarrhea, from nerve problems, from some
medicines, or from a problem inside the
back passage.
Your doctor has heard it all before. I
promise you, it is far more common than
people think. Number 10, constipation
with watery leaking. This one confuses a
lot of families.
An older person seems to have diarrhea.
Their underwear is soiled with loose,
watery stool, so they take
antid-diarrhea tablets.
But the real problem is the opposite. A
large hard lump of stool is stuck low
down in the bowel and watery stool from
higher up is leaking around it. Doctors
call this overflow.
If you give antidiarrhea tablets, you
make the blockage worse. Signs to look
for include days without a proper bowel
movement, a swollen tummy, loss of
appetite, and in some older people, new
confusion.
This needs a doctor, not the pharmacy
shelf. I made a whole video on what to
do when stool is stuck, and I will put a
link on the screen. So, how quickly
should you go? Let me make this very
simple. Go the same day or call
emergency services if you have a lot of
blood, black tarlike stools with
dizziness or fainting, severe sudden
tummy pain, a tummy that is swollen and
hard with vomiting, or if you cannot
pass stool or wind at all. Also go the
same day for yellow skin or eyes.
Book to see your doctor within a few
days if you have any new bleeding, a
change in pattern lasting more than
three or four weeks, weight loss without
trying, diarrhea for weeks or at night,
pale greasy stools, new leakage, or a
blood test that shows low iron. And if
you are not sure which group you are in,
ring your doctor's surgery and ask. That
is what they are there for. Let me
answer a question I am asked a lot. What
will the doctor actually do? Usually the
first step is a chat and some simple
questions.
Then often a quick examination of your
tummy and sometimes of the back passage
with a gloved finger. It takes about a
minute. You may have a blood test to
check iron, blood count, and thyroid.
Very often there is a simple stool test
called fit which you do at home. You
collect a tiny sample with a little
stick, put it in a tube, and send it
back. It looks for tiny traces of blood
that you cannot see, and if needed, the
doctor will arrange a camera test called
a colonoscopy, where a thin flexible
tube looks at the lining of the bowel.
During a colonoscopy, the doctor can
also remove small growths called polyps
before they ever have a chance to turn
into cancer. Many people are frightened
of colonoscopy.
The bowel preparation the day before is
the hardest part. The test itself is
usually done with sedation and many
people remember very little of it. Now
the four things to tell your doctor so
you are taken seriously.
Write these down. First say what changed
and when. Not my bowels are funny, but
since about August, I go three times a
day instead of once and it is loose.
Second, say whether you have seen any
blood and what color it was. Third,
mention anything else even if it seems
unrelated.
Weight loss, tiredness, being
breathless, new diabetes, a change in
appetite.
Fourth, mention any family history. A
parent, brother, sister, or child with
bowel cancer, especially if they were
young when it was found. It also helps
to bring a list of all your medicines
because some medicines change the
bowels, too. I made a whole video on
medicines that cause constipation if you
want to check yours. Doctors are busy.
When you give clear facts like these,
you make it easy for them to act.
A few words for families and carers.
Older people often do not mention bowel
problems out of embarrassment or because
they do not want to be a burden. So
watch for quieter signs.
Someone who suddenly does not want to go
out.
Someone spending a long time in the
bathroom,
stained underwear hidden away, or a lot
of toilet paper being used. a loss of
appetite, weight loss, new tiredness, or
new confusion. If you notice these,
gently ask. You might say, "Mom, I have
noticed you have been a bit tired
lately. Is everything all right with
your tummy and your bowels?" A calm,
private question without any judgment
can open the door. And if they agree to
see a doctor, offer to go with them or
to help them write down the changes
first.
That support can make all the
difference.
And one more thing about screening. If
you are between 50 and 75 and you have
no symptoms at all, bowel screening is
one of the best things you can do for
your health. In many countries, a simple
home stool test is posted to you every
one or two years. Please do not leave it
in the drawer. Many people put the kit
aside because it feels unpleasant.
It takes a few minutes. If you are older
than 75, talk to your doctor about
whether screening still makes sense for
you because the answer depends on your
health. But remember what I said
earlier.
Screening is for people without
symptoms.
If you have symptoms, skip the quue and
see your doctor. So, let me recap. 10
bowel changes after 60 that mean you
should see a doctor. Number one, a
change in your pattern that lasts more
than three or four weeks.
Two, blood in or on your stool. Never
assume it is just piles.
Three, black terry stools.
Four, weight loss you cannot explain.
Five, watery diarrhea for weeks at night
or after antibiotics.
Six, pale, greasy, floating stools,
especially with new diabetes or yellow
skin. Seven, sudden tummy pain followed
by bloody diarrhea.
Eight, a feeling of not emptying or a
lump. Nine, new leakage or urgency.
And 10, constipation with watery
leaking, plus the hidden sign, tiredness
from low iron. An honest note before I
go. I do not want this video to frighten
you. The great majority of people with
these changes do not have cancer. They
have piles, a tummy infection, a side
effect from a medicine, or a treatable
inflammation.
But here is why I still want you to go.
When bowel cancer is found early while
it is still inside the bowel, about nine
out of 10 people are alive 5 years
later. According to American Cancer
Society figures, when it is found late
after it has spread to distant parts of
the body, that falls to about 1 or two
in 10. The disease is the same. The
difference is the timing.
That is the whole reason this video
exists.
Please remember this video is general
education.
It is not a diagnosis and not a
treatment plan for you. If something in
this video sounded like you, please book
an appointment this week. And if this
was helpful, please share it with
someone over 60 who might be keeping
quiet about a change. It could make a
real difference.
If you take several tablets every day
and your bowels have slowed down, watch
my video on the medicines that cause
constipation.
You will find it on the screen now. I am
Dr. Nimra.
Thank you for watching and look after
yourself.

records.channelDescription:
Welcome to Dr Nimra | Health After 60 🩺

I'm Dr Nimra, this channel exists for one reason: to explain, in plain and simple language, what your 15-minute doctor's visit doesn't have time to explain.

Every week I break down what really happens inside your body after 60, and what you can do about it:
💊 Medicines: what your pills really do, side effects, and dangerous combinations
🥗 Food & diet: what to eat, what to limit, and why
🚶 Exercise & mobility: simple movement that keeps you strong and independent
😴 Sleep, bathroom and daily habits: the small things that add up
❤️ Heart, blood pressure, blood sugar, kidneys, bones, brain and eyes

⚠️ Disclaimer
The content on this channel is for general education and information only. It is not personal medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Never start, stop or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have a medical emergency, call your local emergency number.

records.text:
Stool stuck in the rectum and no strength to push? After 60 this is very common, and nothing to be embarrassed about. In this video, Dr Nimra explains what is really happening, the 5 gentle steps that help, the one mistake that can make it much worse, and when to see a doctor straight away.

The 5 steps:
1. Stop pushing (why straining is risky after 60)
2. Get into the right position (footstool, lean forward, breathe)
3. Soften it from below (glycerin suppository, safe enemas, and one type to be careful with)
4. Soften it from above (macrogol / lactulose, and why NOT to add bran right now)
5. Know when to get help (and what the doctor actually does)

Plus: the "diarrhoea" that is really a blockage, 5 habits so it never happens again (water, prunes and kiwi, a morning routine, movement, a medicine check), and tips for people caring for an older parent.

💬 Tell me in the comments: which habit will you start this week?

👍 If this helped, please like and share it with someone who may be quietly struggling. Subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: Over 70? This Little Seed Helps the Blood Flow in Your Legs

CHAPTERS
0:00 Stool stuck and nothing moves
0:43 1. Stop pushing (why straining is risky after 60)
2:26 What is actually happening in the bowel
3:19 Why it happens more after 60
4:05 Signs it is stuck, not just constipation
4:31 The "diarrhoea" that is really a blockage
5:45 2. Get into the right position
7:04 3. Soften it from below (and one enema to avoid)
9:12 4. Soften it from above
10:55 5. Know when to get help
11:41 What the doctor actually does
13:15 The 5 steps together
13:29 5 habits so it never happens again
18:36 Tips for carers
19:17 When a bowel change should be checked
20:31 Which habit will you start?

Sources:
Gallagher P, O'Mahony D. Constipation in old age. Best Pract Res Clin Gastroenterol 2009
Serrano Falcón B et al. Fecal impaction: a systematic review of its medical complications. BMC Geriatrics 2016
US FDA Drug Safety Communication (2014): over-the-counter sodium phosphate products and kidney/heart risks
Attaluri A et al. Randomised clinical trial: dried plums (prunes) vs psyllium for constipation. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2011
Chey SW et al. Exploratory comparative effectiveness trial of green kiwifruit, psyllium or prunes in constipation. Am J Gastroenterol 2021
Modi RM et al. Implementation of a defecation posture modification device. Dig Dis Sci 2019
American Gastroenterological Association / ACG guideline on chronic idiopathic constipation, 2023

Important: this video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. Never stop, start or change any medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. Severe tummy pain, a swollen hard tummy, vomiting, being unable to pass wind or urine, fever, bleeding or new confusion need urgent medical help.

#constipation #seniorhealth #healthafter60 #fecalimpaction #bowelhealth

subtitles.plaintext:
You sit down on the toilet.
You feel the pressure.
You know something is there.
But nothing moves.
You wait, you push, and it still will
not come.
If this has happened to you, please do
not be embarrassed.
After 60, it is very common.
When stool gets stuck in the last part
of the bowel, we call it a fecal
impaction.
And the good news is there is a calm,
safe way through it.
Today, I will give you five gentle
steps, the one mistake that can make it
much worse, and how to stop it happening
again.
Quick note, this is general education,
not personal medical advice.
Step number one, stop pushing.
I know.
Every part of you wants to push harder.
But a stuck stool is usually hard and
dry, almost like clay.
Pushing does not move it.
It only presses harder against something
that cannot go anywhere yet.
And straining hard has real costs after
60
When you hold your breath and bear down,
the pressure in your chest rises
sharply, and your blood pressure jumps.
Then, when you let go, it can drop
suddenly.
This is why some older people feel dizzy
or even faint on the toilet.
For people with heart disease, that
strain is something to avoid.
Straining also causes piles and small
painful tears around the back passage,
which make the next visit to the toilet
even harder.
So, the first step is simple.
Stop.
Breathe.
Get up if you need to.
We are going to do this a better way.
Before we go on, I would love to know
something.
Has this ever happened to you or or
someone you care for?
You can simply write yes in the
comments.
You are not alone and your comment helps
other people find this video when they
need it.
And if we have not met before, I am Dr.
Nimra.
On this channel I talk about health
after 60 in plain, calm language. The
kind of conversation a short appointment
does not always have time for.
If that sounds useful, you are very
welcome to subscribe and stay.
Now, before step two, let me explain
what is actually happening because once
you understand it, everything else makes
sense.
Your large bowel is about 5 ft long.
It has two jobs.
It moves waste along towards the exit
and it takes water back out of that
waste as it travels.
It moves things along with gentle waves
of muscle, a little like squeezing
toothpaste along a tube.
When those waves are slow, the stool
sits in the bowel for longer.
And the longer it sits, the more water
the bowel pulls out of it.
Soft stool becomes firm.
Firm stool becomes hard.
And after several days, the stool at the
very end can become a dry, heavy mass
that the body simply cannot push out on
its own.
That is a fecal impaction.
Why does this happen more after 60?
Several small changes add up.
The bowel's muscle waves become slower
and weaker with age.
We feel less thirsty, so we drink less.
Many of us move less than we used to.
Many common medicines slow the bowel and
I will list them later.
And some conditions make it more likely,
too, like Parkinson's disease, diabetes,
an underactive thyroid, memory problems,
or spending a lot of time in a bed or a
chair.
A stay in hospital or an operation is
another common time for the bowel to get
stuck because of the painkillers, the
bed rest, and the change in routine.
So, how do you know it is stuck and not
just ordinary constipation?
Here are the signs doctors look for.
You feel pressure or fullness low down
in the back passage.
You feel the urge, but nothing comes or
only small, hard pieces.
Your tummy feels bloated and
uncomfortable.
You may lose your appetite or feel a
little sick.
And here is the strange one, and it is
very important.
Sometimes, watery stool starts to leak
out, and it looks just like diarrhea.
But, it is not diarrhea.
The liquid from higher up is seeping
around the hard plug and escaping.
Doctors call this overflow.
This is the mistake I promised to warn
you about.
If you have not passed a proper stool
for several days, and then watery stool
starts leaking, please do not take a
diarrhea medicine like loperamide.
Those medicines slow the bowel down even
more, and they can turn a blockage that
could be fixed at home into a hospital
problem.
Speak to a doctor or pharmacist first.
Two more signs that surprise people.
A full, stretched bowel can press on the
bladder, so some people suddenly find it
hard to pass urine or feel they need to
go all the time.
And in older people, especially those
with memory problems, a stuck bowel can
cause new confusion or restlessness.
If an older relative is suddenly not
themselves, constipation is one of the
first things a good doctor checks.
Step number two, get into the right
position.
The way we sit on a modern toilet is not
ideal.
When you sit upright with your feet flat
on the floor, there is a natural bend at
the end of the bowel that stays partly
closed.
So, put a small footstool under your
feet so your knees are higher than your
hips.
Lean forward a little and rest your
elbows on your knees.
This straightens that bend and opens the
way.
Many people are amazed at how much
easier it becomes.
If you do not have a footstool, a small
pile of thick books or an upturned
plastic box works just as well.
Keep it beside the toilet so it is
always there.
Then, relax your tummy and breathe
slowly low down into your belly.
Let your belly soften when you breathe
in.
Do not hold your breath.
A warm drink before you go, like tea or
warm water, can also gently wake up the
bowel.
And give it time, but not too much time.
5 to 10 minutes is enough.
If nothing happens, get up, walk around
the house for a little while, and try
again later.
Sitting for half an hour only adds to
the strain.
Step number three, soften it from below.
When the hard part is right at the end,
the gentlest help comes from below.
A glycerin suppository is a small,
smooth bullet that you place in the back
passage.
You can buy it at any pharmacy without a
prescription.
It draws a little water into the stool
and makes the passage slippery.
Here is how to use it well.
Wash your hands.
Lie on your left side with your knees
bent towards your chest because the
bowel curves that way, and this helps.
Put Put water or water-based gel on the
suppository and gently push it in just
past the muscle ring.
Then stay lying down and wait.
Follow the time on the packet, usually
15 to 30 minutes.
Rushing to the toilet too early means it
comes straight back out.
If a suppository does not work, a
pharmacist can suggest a small, gentle
enema.
Some are just warm water and some have a
little mineral oil to soften and
lubricate the stool.
But please be careful with one type.
Sodium phosphate enemas, sold under
brand names like Fleet, can be dangerous
for older people, especially if you have
kidney problems, heart failure, or take
water pills.
Using more than one dose or holding it
in for too long has put people in
hospital with dangerous salt levels.
So after 70 or with any kidney or heart
problem, please ask your doctor or
pharmacist which enema is safe for you
and never use more than the packet says.
And one more thing I have to say, kindly
but clearly,
please do not try to dig the stool out
with your fingers at home.
It can tear the delicate skin, cause
bleeding, and in some people it can
trigger a sudden drop in heart rate and
fainting.
If it truly needs removing, that is a
job for a doctor or nurse and I will
tell you more about that in a moment.
Step number four, soften it from above.
At the same time, you want the stool
behind the blockage to stay soft and
keep moving.
The medicine doctors most often use for
this is called macrogol or polyethylene
glycol.
You may know it by names like Movicol or
MiraLAX.
It is a powder you mix into a glass of
water.
It works by holding water in the bowel,
so the stool becomes soft.
It is gentle. It does not cause cramps
for most people, and it is safe for
older adults.
For a stuck bowel, doctors sometimes use
a larger dose for a day or two.
But please ask your doctor or pharmacist
how much is right for you.
And drink plenty with it, unless your
doctor has told you to limit fluids.
Another gentle option is lactulose, a
sweet syrup that also draws water into
the bowel.
It can take a day or two to work, and it
can cause some wind, but many older
people use it safely for years.
Now, here is something surprising.
When you are already blocked, this is
not the time to suddenly eat a big bowl
of bran.
A lot of rough fiber on top of a
blockage can make the plug even bigger.
Fiber is wonderful for prevention, and I
will come back to it, but first, clear
the way.
Stimulant laxatives, like senna or
bisacodyl, make the bowel muscles
squeeze harder.
Used for a short time, with your
doctor's agreement, they can help.
But they can cause cramps, and they are
not the right choice if you have strong
tummy pain or vomiting.
Step number five, know when to get help.
If you have tried these steps and
nothing has moved in about a day, please
call your doctor.
Do not wait several more days hoping it
will pass.
The longer it sits, the harder it gets.
And please get urgent help straight away
if you have any of these.
Severe or worsening tummy pain.
A swollen, hard tummy.
Vomiting.
You cannot pass any wind at all.
You cannot pass urine.
A fever.
Bleeding from the back passage.
Or new confusion or dizziness.
These can be signs of a complete
blockage and they need a doctor today.
Now, I know many people are afraid of
what happens at the doctor.
So, let me take that fear away.
The doctor or nurse will gently examine
your tummy and usually check the back
passage with a gloved finger.
Often, a stronger enema given properly
does the job.
Sometimes, if the stool is very hard,
they will gently break it up and remove
it by hand.
I know that sounds uncomfortable.
But, it is a safe, routine thing that
doctors and nurses do often with care
and privacy, sometimes with medicine to
help you relax.
And almost everyone says the same thing
afterwards.
The relief is enormous.
After it is cleared, the area may feel
sore for a day or two.
A warm, shallow bath, just plain warm
water for 10 to 15 minutes, two or three
times a day, can soothe it beautifully.
Eat soft, gentle foods for a few days,
like porridge, ripe bananas, soups, and
cooked vegetables.
And a good doctor will not stop at
clearing it.
They will ask why it happened.
They may check a simple blood test for
things like your thyroid, your calcium
level, and your blood sugar because all
of these can slow the bowel.
They will look at your list of
medicines.
And if this keeps happening, they may
suggest a closer look at the bowel
itself.
The aim is not just to fix today, but to
make sure you do not end up here again.
So, those are the five steps.
Stop pushing.
Get into the right position.
Soften from below.
Soften from above.
And know when to get help.
But the best thing of all is making sure
this never happens again.
So let me share five simple habits that
keep the bowel moving after 60.
The first habit is water on a schedule.
As we get older, the thirst signal
becomes weaker.
You can be a little dry and not feel
thirsty at all.
And the bowel takes its water from what
you drink.
So do not wait for thirst.
Have a glass of water or a cup of tea at
set times. For example, when you wake
up, mid-morning, lunch, mid-afternoon,
and supper.
Soup, milk, and juicy fruits count, too.
If your doctor
The second habit is fiber, added slowly.
Oats, beans, lentils, vegetables, and
fruit with the skin.
Two foods have real studies behind them.
Prunes, about five or six a day, worked
better than a common fiber powder in one
study.
And two green kiwi fruits a day helped
people with constipation in a large
international study with very few side
effects.
Add fiber slowly over two or three weeks
and drink more water with it, or it can
cause wind and bloating.
Here is an easy way to start.
Soak five or six prunes in a little
water overnight and eat them with
breakfast with the soaking water, too.
Or eat two kiwi fruits as a snack in the
afternoon.
And a tablespoon of ground flaxseed
stirred into porridge or yogurt with a
glass of water adds gentle fiber, as
well.
The third habit is a morning toilet
routine.
About 15 to 30 minutes after breakfast,
the bowel naturally wakes up and becomes
more active.
Doctors call this the gastrocolic
reflex.
So, use it.
Every morning after breakfast and a warm
drink, sit on the toilet for 5 to 10
minutes with your feet on the footstool,
even if you do not feel a strong urge.
Over a few weeks, many people find their
body learns the rhythm again.
Here is what a good morning might look
like.
Wake up and drink a glass of warm water.
Have breakfast, maybe porridge with
soaked prunes.
Enjoy a cup of tea.
Then, about 20 minutes later, go and sit
on the toilet, feet on the stool,
leaning forward, breathing slowly.
No rush, no pushing.
Just giving your body the chance.
And alongside this, please never ignore
the urge.
Many of us grew up being polite about
these things, waiting until we got home
or until the bathroom was free.
But every time the urge is ignored, the
stool sits longer and gets drier, and
over the years, the signal gets weaker.
When your body says it is time, go.
It also helps to know what you are
aiming for.
Doctors use a simple chart of stool
shapes.
Hard, separate lumps like nuts, mean the
stool has been in the bowel too long and
needs more water and fiber.
A smooth, soft sausage shape is ideal.
You do not need to go every day.
Anywhere from three times a day to three
times a week can be normal.
What matters is that it is soft and it
comes out without straining.
The fourth habit is daily movement.
Walking gently massages the bowel from
the outside.
Even 20 minutes a day helps.
And if walking is hard, marching on the
spot while holding a chair, or simple
leg lifts while sitting, or still wake
up the bowel.
You can also try a gentle tummy massage.
Lie on your back with your knees bent.
With a flat, warm hand, make slow
circles on your tummy, starting low on
the right side, going up, across under
the ribs, and down the left side.
This follows the path of the large
bowel.
5 to 10 minutes a day before getting up
in the morning is a lovely, calming
habit, and some small studies suggest it
can help.
The fifth habit is a medicine check.
Many common medicines cause
constipation.
Strong painkillers, especially codeine
and morphine-type medicines,
iron tablets,
calcium tablets,
some blood pressure tablets, like
amlodipine and verapamil,
some medicines for bladder control,
allergies, nausea, and depression,
and some stomach antacids.
If you take several of these, the effect
adds up.
Please ask your doctor or pharmacist to
look at your whole list.
Often, a small change makes a big
difference.
But never stop a medicine on your own.
Now, a few words for anyone caring for
an older parent or partner.
People who are frail or have memory
problems often cannot tell you they are
constipated.
So, keep a simple bowel diary.
Just a tick on the calendar on the days
they open their bowels.
If 3 days pass without a tick, start the
gentle steps early and call the doctor
or nurse if there is no result.
And watch for the quiet signs. Going off
their food, being restless or more
confused than usual, holding their
tummy, or leaking watery stool.
Catching it early saves a lot of
distress.
And one last important doctor's note.
If your bowel habit changes and stays
changed for more than a few weeks,
especially with blood in the stool,
weight loss without trying, or
tiredness, please see your doctor.
Most of the time it is something simple.
But after 50, a lasting change in the
bowel should always be checked because
finding a problem early makes it much
easier to treat.
Let me finish with this.
Bowel problems are not something to be
ashamed of.
Every single person has a bowel and
every doctor has helped many people with
exactly this.
If you are struggling, or if you are
caring for an older parent who is,
please speak up.
A short, honest conversation can save a
lot of discomfort.
One last reminder.
This video is for general education and
is not personal medical advice.
Please never stop, start, or change any
medicine without speaking to your own
doctor or pharmacist.
And if you have severe tummy pain,
vomiting, a swollen tummy, or cannot
pass wind or urine, please get medical
help straight away.
Now tell me in the comments, which of
the five habits will you start this
week?
I will be reading.
And here is something nice.
One of the seeds in my last video,
ground flaxseed, is also wonderful for
keeping the bowel regular.
You can watch that video right here on
your screen.
Thank you for watching and please share
this with someone who might be quietly
struggling.
Take good care of yourself.
