records.text:
Hard, dry stools and straining after 60? In this video, Dr Nimra compares the two fruits that have actually been tested for constipation in real studies: green kiwi and prunes. You will learn which one works more strongly, which one is gentler on the tummy, how many to eat, and the one mistake that stops both from working.

The 5 steps:
1. Two green kiwis a day (what the studies found)
2. Prunes, if you need a stronger effect (and how to make them easier to eat)
3. The water rule (the mistake most people make)
4. Start small and give it 4 weeks (timing, recipes, the toilet routine)
5. Who should be careful, and when fruit is not enough

Plus: 3 more foods from the new UK guidelines, 5 myths about constipation, tips for carers, and a simple 7-day plan.

💬 Tell me in the comments: will you try kiwi or prunes first?

👍 If this helped, please like and share it with someone who may be quietly struggling. Subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: Stool Stuck in the Rectum After 60? 5 Gentle Steps a Doctor Recommends

CHAPTERS
0:00 Hard stools after 60
0:56 1. Two green kiwis a day
1:58 Kiwi or prunes? Tell me
2:35 The studies in older people
4:27 What a "normal" stool looks like
5:13 2. Prunes for a stronger effect
6:58 Which one should you choose?
7:54 3. The water rule (the mistake)
9:21 Coffee and mineral water
10:08 4. Start small and give it 4 weeks
12:00 Easy ways to eat them
13:17 3 more foods from the new guidelines
15:18 5 constipation myths
17:10 5. Who should be careful
19:18 When fruit is not enough
20:07 Tips for carers
20:43 Your questions
21:38 Your 7-day plan
22:55 The 5 steps together

Sources:
Chey SW et al. Exploratory comparative effectiveness trial of green kiwifruit, psyllium, or prunes in US patients with chronic constipation. Am J Gastroenterol 2021
Gearry R et al. Consumption of 2 green kiwifruits daily improves constipation and abdominal comfort. Am J Gastroenterol 2023
Rush EC et al. Kiwifruit promotes laxation in the elderly. Asia Pac J Clin Nutr 2002
Attaluri A et al. Randomised clinical trial: dried plums (prunes) vs psyllium for constipation. Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2011
Brown SR et al. Effect of coffee on distal colon function. Gut 1990
Dimidi E et al. British Dietetic Association guidelines for the dietary management of chronic constipation in adults. J Hum Nutr Diet 2025

Some of these studies were partly funded by fruit producers.

Important: this video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. Never stop, start or change any medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have kidney disease, a kiwi or latex allergy, or take warfarin, ask your doctor first. Blood in the stool, black stools, weight loss, ongoing tummy pain, or a bowel change lasting more than a few weeks need a doctor's check.

subtitles.plaintext:
You sit on the toilet and you already
know how it will go.
The stool is hard and dry.
You strain, it hurts, and you come away
feeling you have not finished.
After 60, this is one of the most common
problems doctors see.
Today, I will show you two fruits that
have actually been tested against this
problem in real studies.
Green kiwi and prunes.
One of them pushed things along more
strongly.
The other was much gentler on the tummy
and people liked it more.
I will tell you which is which, how many
to eat, and the one mistake that stops
both of them from working.
I will also bust five common myths about
constipation. And at the end, I will
give you a simple 7-day plan you can
start tomorrow morning.
Quick note, this is general education,
not personal medical advice.
Step number one, two green kiwis a day.
Yes, the simple kiwi.
Brown and fuzzy on the outside, bright
green inside.
It does not look like a medicine, but it
has been studied like one.
In 2021,
doctors in the United States gave 79
adults with long-term constipation one
of three things for 4 weeks.
Two green kiwis a day.
Or about 10 prunes a day.
Or a fiber powder called psyllium.
All three helped.
The number of bowel movements went up in
every group.
But here is what caught my attention.
In the kiwi group, only about one person
in 10 felt bloated.
In the prune group, it was more than one
in three.
Nobody in the kiwi group reported gas or
tummy pain.
And when they asked people how happy
they were with the treatment, the kiwi
group was the most satisfied of all.
Before we go on, I would love to know
something.
Have you ever tried kiwi or prunes for
this?
You can simply write kiwi or prunes in
the comments or neither if you have not
tried them yet.
Your answer helps other people find this
video when they need it.
And if we have not met before, I am Dr.
Nimra.
On this channel, I talk about health
after 60 in plain calm language. The
kind of conversation a short appointment
does not always have time for.
If that sounds useful, you are very
welcome to subscribe and stay.
Now, there is more evidence and some of
it was done only in older people.
In one small study, 38 healthy adults
over 60 with an average age in the early
70s ate green kiwis every day for 3
weeks.
The oldest person in that study was 93.
Their stools became softer, bigger, and
more frequent.
The amount was one kiwi for every 30
kilos of body weight.
For most people, that is about two
kiwis.
In another study from New Zealand,
Italy, and Japan, two green kiwis a day
were compared with the fiber powder in
184 people.
Kiwi gave more complete bowel movements
each week and people had less tummy
discomfort.
Most of those people were younger, so I
give that study less weight for you.
But it points in the same direction.
And in 2025,
the British Dietetic Association, the
group that writes diet advice for
dieticians and doctors in the United
Kingdom, published new guidelines for
constipation.
Kiwi was one of the few foods they
recommended by name.
Two to three kiwis a day.
Why does it work?
Inside a kiwi is a special kind of fiber
that holds onto water like a little
sponge.
When you eat it, that fiber swells and
becomes soft, almost like a gel.
So, instead of a dry, hard stool, you
get a softer stool that keeps its water.
That is the whole secret.
Not a push.
A softer stool.
And please remember that sponge, because
it is the key to the mistake I promised
to tell you about.
Doctors use a simple picture chart to
describe stools called the Bristol stool
chart.
Types 1 and 2 are hard lumps like nuts
or pebbles.
That is constipation.
Types 3 and 4 are smooth like a sausage
and easy to pass.
That is what we want.
Kiwi does not give you diarrhea.
It gently moves you from the hard lumps
towards the smooth, easy shape.
What about golden kiwi, the yellow one?
It is sweeter and one golden variety has
been tested, too, with encouraging
results.
But green kiwi has by far the most
research behind it.
So, if you can find green, choose green.
Step number two, if you need a stronger
effect, choose prunes.
Prunes are simply dried plums.
And they have something kiwi does not
have much of.
A natural sugar called sorbitol.
Our body does not absorb sorbitol well,
so it travels down to the bowel and
pulls water into it.
Add the fiber in prunes and you get a
stronger effect.
In the American study I mentioned,
prunes actually helped the most people,
although the difference between the
three was small.
In another study from 2011,
40 adults with constipation ate six
prunes twice a day for 3 weeks.
That is 12 prunes a day.
Their complete bowel movements went from
fewer than two a week to three and a
half a week.
That was better than the fiber powder.
So, prunes work.
But, the same sorbitol that pulls in
water is also food for the bacteria in
your bowel. And when they eat it, they
make gas.
That is why some people get bloating,
wind, and cramps with prunes.
And for an older person who cannot rush
to the bathroom, a sudden urgent feeling
is not a small thing.
There are some simple ways to make
prunes easier to eat.
If your teeth or your dentures make
chewy food hard, soak the prunes in a
little warm water overnight.
By the morning, they are plump and soft.
You can also cook them gently with a
little water to make stewed prunes and
eat them with porridge or yogurt.
And always buy pitted prunes, the ones
with the stone already taken out.
A hidden stone can crack a tooth.
So, which one should you choose?
Here is a simple way to decide.
If your tummy is sensitive, if you bloat
easily, or if you have irritable bowel,
start with kiwi.
If you have diabetes, kiwi is also the
lighter choice.
Two kiwis have less than half the sugar
of a portion of prunes.
If you do eat prunes, count them as part
of your fruit for the day and eat them
with a meal, not alone.
And if you have tried kiwi for 4 weeks
and it was not quite enough, or you need
a stronger effect, try prunes.
The British guidelines suggest about
eight to 10 prunes a day.
Some people even do both.
One kiwi and a few prunes.
That is fine, too, as long as you build
up slowly.
I will explain how in step four.
Step number three, the water rule.
This is the mistake I promised.
Remember the sponge.
Kiwi fiber and prune fiber both work by
holding water inside the stool.
But a sponge with no water in it is just
a dry sponge.
If you eat more fiber and do not drink
enough, the stool can actually become
harder, and some people feel more
blocked than before.
And after 60, this mistake is very
common because our sense of thirst
becomes weaker with age.
Many older people are a little
dehydrated every single day without
knowing it.
Here is an easy way to check.
Look at the color of your urine.
Pale straw yellow is good.
Dark yellow, like apple juice, usually
means you need to drink more.
Some vitamin tablets and medicines can
change the color, so this is a guide,
not a rule.
So, with your fruit, drink a full glass
of water.
And across the day, aim for about six to
eight cups of fluid.
Tea, milk, soup, and water all count.
There is one exception, and it is
important.
If your doctor has told you to limit
your fluids, for example, because of
heart failure or kidney disease, please
follow your doctor's advice
and do not drink more than they have
told you.
What about your morning cup of coffee?
For some people, coffee wakes up the
bowel within minutes.
In one study,
about one person in three said coffee
gave them the urge to go.
So, if coffee it you, a cup with
breakfast is fine.
But it does not count as a treatment,
and if it makes your heart race or keeps
you awake, you do not need it.
The British guidelines also mention
something interesting.
Mineral water that is naturally rich in
minerals such as magnesium helps some
people.
At about half a liter to 1 and a half
liters a day.
If you see a bottled water with a high
magnesium number on the label, it is a
reasonable thing to try.
But if you have kidney disease, ask your
doctor first.
Step number four, start small and give
it 4 weeks.
Many people try something for 1 day,
nothing happens, and they give up.
Others eat a whole bag of prunes at once
and spend the next day with cramps.
Both are mistakes.
So here is the gentle plan.
For kiwi, start with one a day for the
first few days, then go up to two.
For prunes, start with three or four a
day, and add one or two more every few
days until you reach about eight to 10.
Some people notice softer stools within
a few days.
But in the studies, people were followed
for three to four weeks.
So give it a fair chance.
Four weeks every day before you decide
whether it works for you.
What about the timing?
You may have heard that you must eat
kiwi at night.
Honestly, the studies did not test the
time of day.
What mattered was eating them every day.
So choose a time you will remember.
Many people like their kiwi after dinner
or their prunes with breakfast.
How should you eat them?
A kiwi is easiest if you cut it in half
and scoop it out with a teaspoon like a
little egg.
The skin has extra fiber and you can eat
it if you wash it well, but you do not
have to.
The studies mostly used peeled kiwis.
Choose kiwis that give a little when you
press them like a ripe peach.
If they are hard, leave them in a fruit
bowl next to a banana or an apple for a
day or two and they will soften.
A hard, sour kiwi is unpleasant and if
you do not enjoy it, you will not keep
it up.
Here are a few easy ideas.
Sliced kiwi on plain yogurt.
Chopped prunes stirred into warm
porridge.
A kiwi as your pudding after dinner.
Or a small bowl of soaked prunes with a
spoon of yogurt in the evening.
Simple, cheap and nothing to cook.
For prunes, whole prunes are best
because they have the fiber.
Prune juice has the sorbitol but little
fiber.
It can still help some people but a
small glass is enough and it does it
sugar.
And one more thing that makes the fruit
work better.
Your bowel is most awake in the hour
after breakfast.
So sit on the toilet after breakfast
every day without rushing.
Put a small footstool under your feet so
your knees are higher than your hips and
lean forward a little.
In my video on stool stuck in the
rectum, I explained why this simple
position makes such a big difference.
Movement helps, too.
A gentle 10-minute walk after a meal,
even just around the house or the
garden, helps the bowel wake up.
If walking is difficult, sitting in a
chair and lifting your knees one at a
time, like marching, also helps.
Now, before step five, I promised you
three more things from the new British
guidelines.
These are useful if fruit is not quite
enough, or if you simply do not like
kiwis or prunes.
The first is rye bread.
In studies, swapping white bread for rye
bread helped people go more easily.
The amount used was quite large, about
six to eight slices a day, so not
everyone will manage it.
But even replacing some of your usual
bread with rye is a sensible step.
The second is the fiber powder,
psyllium.
You may know it by brand names like
Fibergrel or Metamucil, or as ispaghula
husk.
It works, but it needs a higher dose
than many people take, at least 10 g a
day, built up slowly, and always with a
big glass of water.
Without the water, it can make things
worse, just like the sponge.
And if you have trouble swallowing, ask
your doctor before using it, because it
thickens quickly.
The third is magnesium oxide, a simple
mineral tablet that draws water into the
bowel.
The guidelines found it helpful.
But please do not start it on your own
after 60.
Too much magnesium can build up in
people whose kidneys are weaker, and
many of us have weaker kidneys without
knowing it.
It can also interfere with some
antibiotics and other medicines.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist first.
And here is something the guidelines did
not recommend.
Senna, a common herbal laxative, did not
show benefit in the studies they looked
at.
And most probiotics did not help either.
Only a few specific strains showed any
effect.
So before you spend money on expensive
capsules, try the simple foods first.
Now, let me clear up five myths I hear
all the time.
Myth number one, you must open your
bowels every day.
Not true.
Anywhere from three times a day to three
times a week can be normal.
What matters is that it is comfortable
and that it has not changed suddenly for
you.
Myth number two, just eat more fiber and
everything will be fine.
For some people, yes.
But the British guidelines found
surprisingly weak evidence for simply
telling everyone to eat a high-fiber
diet for constipation.
And if your bowel is very slow, piling
on bran can make the bloating worse.
That is why specific foods like kiwi and
prunes are now recommended instead.
Fiber is still good for your heart and
your general health, so do not cut it
out.
Myth number three, laxatives will make
your bowel lazy.
This worries many people.
But gentle laxatives that your doctor
prescribes, like macrogol, are
considered safe to use for a long time
when they are needed.
Good studies have not shown that
stimulant laxatives damage the bowel
either, although they can cause cramps.
So if you need a laxative, do not feel
guilty.
Just take it as your doctor advises.
Myth number four, prune juice is the
same as prunes.
As we said, the juice loses most of the
fiber.
It can help, but whole prunes do more.
Myth number five, constipation is just
part of getting old.
It is common, yes.
But it is not something you simply have
to put up with.
Most people can feel much better with a
few small changes and a doctor can help
with the rest.
Step number five, know who should be
careful and when fruit is not enough.
Kiwi and prunes are foods, but even
foods are not right for everyone.
If you have kidney disease and you have
been told to limit potassium, be
careful.
Both kiwis and prunes contain potassium,
and prunes contain quite a lot.
Please ask your kidney doctor how much
is safe for you.
The same care applies to some heart and
blood pressure tablets that keep
potassium in the body.
For example, ramipril, lisinopril,
losartan, and the water tablet
spironolactone.
Most people on these tablets can still
enjoy two kiwis a day.
But if you have been told your potassium
is high, or you take several of these
medicines together, check with your
doctor before eating large amounts of
prunes every day.
If you have ever had an itchy mouth,
swelling of the lips or throat, or a
rash after eating kiwi, do not eat it.
And people with a latex allergy are more
likely to react to kiwi, too, so ask
your doctor first.
If you take warfarin, you do not need to
avoid these fruits.
But keep the amount steady from week to
week, and tell your doctor about the
change, because big changes in diet can
affect your blood tests.
If you take a laxative that your doctor
prescribed, do not stop it on your own.
Add the fruit and talk to your doctor
after a few weeks about whether the
laxative can be reduced.
And here is a quiet cause many people
miss.
Many common medicines slow down the
bowel.
Strong painkillers, iron tablets,
calcium tablets, some blood pressure
tablets, and some medicines for the
bladder and for mood.
If your constipation started after a new
medicine, mention it to your doctor or
pharmacist.
Often a small change helps more than any
fruit.
If you would like a whole video about
these medicines, write medicines in the
comments.
Now, the most important part of this
whole video.
Fruit is for ordinary, everyday
constipation.
It is not a treatment for a serious
bowel problem.
Please see your doctor if you have blood
in your stool, black stools, weight loss
without trying, tummy pain that will not
go away,
or a change in your bowel habit that
lasts more than a few weeks.
After 50, a lasting change in the bowel
should always be checked because finding
a problem early makes it much easier to
treat.
And if you feel that the stool is stuck
at the very end with pressure, straining
and nothing coming out, that is a
different problem and fruit alone will
be too slow.
I explained the gentle steps for that in
my video on stool stuck in the rectum.
A few words for anyone caring for an
older parent or partner.
Kiwi is a wonderful choice for someone
with few teeth because a ripe kiwi is
soft and can be eaten with a spoon.
Prunes can be soaked, chopped, or
blended into a smooth puree and stirred
into porridge.
If the person has trouble swallowing,
check with their doctor or speech
therapist about the right texture and
never give whole, chewy prunes to
someone who coughs or chokes when
eating.
And keep a simple tick on the calendar
on the days they open their bowels so
you notice early if things are slowing
down.
Before the plan, let me answer three
questions people often ask me.
Can I eat dried figs or dried apricots
instead?
You can and they do contain fiber.
Figs have a few small studies behind
them with encouraging results.
But kiwi and prunes have the most
research so start with those if you can.
Should I eat the kiwi on an empty
stomach?
There is no good evidence that this
matters.
Eat it whenever suits you.
If it upsets your stomach, have it after
a meal.
How long can I keep eating them?
For as long as you like.
These are ordinary foods.
Many people keep eating two kiwis or a
few prunes every day for years, simply
because it keeps them regular.
And now, as I promised, your simple
7-day plan.
Day one.
In the morning, drink a glass of water
before breakfast.
After breakfast, sit on the toilet for 5
minutes with your feet on a footstool
and do not strain.
After lunch, eat one ripe green kiwi.
Days two and three.
Keep the same routine.
Add a 10-minute walk after one meal.
Check the color of your urine and drink
a little more if it is dark.
Days four and five.
Go up to two kiwis a day.
One after lunch and one after dinner.
Each one with a glass of water, unless
your doctor limits your fluids.
Days six and seven.
Notice what has changed.
Are your stools a little softer?
Is it a little easier?
If yes, keep going for the full 4 weeks.
If you have had no change at all, you
can add three or four soaked prunes with
breakfast and build up slowly from
there.
If you prefer prunes, follow the same
plan with prunes instead.
Start with three or four a day and add
one or two more every few days.
Let me bring it all together.
Step one, two green kiwis a day.
Gentle, well tolerated, and people liked
it most.
Step two, if you need a stronger effect,
eight to 10 prunes a day.
They work well, but they can cause more
gas.
Step three, the water rule.
Fiber needs water, so drink a glass with
your fruit, unless your doctor limits
your fluids.
Step four, start small, build up slowly,
and give it 4 weeks.
Step five, be careful with kidney
disease or kiwi allergy, check your
medicines, and see your doctor for any
warning signs.
One honest note before I go.
Some of these studies were partly paid
for by the fruit companies, and they
were small.
But the results agree with each other.
These are simple foods, and the risk is
low for most people.
That is why I am comfortable
recommending them.
One last reminder.
This video is for general education, and
is not personal medical advice.
Please never stop, start, or change any
medicine without speaking to your own
doctor or pharmacist.
Now tell me in the comments, will you
try kiwi or prunes first?
I will be reading.
And if you have ever had the feeling
that the stool is stuck and will not
come out, please watch my video about
that next.
It is right here on your screen.
Thank you for watching, and please share
this with someone who might be quietly
struggling.
Take good care of yourself.

After 60, it can feel like every year brings a new pill. But more pills are rarely the answer to feeling old. In this video, Dr Nimra shares 5 simple things that keep people strong, steady and happy after 60, and most of them cost nothing.

The 5 things:
1. A daily walk (and why 6,000 to 8,000 steps is enough)
2. Strong legs (a 10-minute chair routine to prevent falls)
3. Deep, steady sleep (without relying on sleeping pills)
4. Morning sunlight and enough water
5. A reason to get up in the morning, and someone to share it with

Plus: the once-a-year medicine review every person over 60 should ask their doctor for.

💬 Tell me in the comments: how many days a week do you walk right now?

👍 If this helped, please like the video and subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: Is 150 Normal After 65? The REAL Blood Pressure Target

subtitles.plaintext:
After 60, it can feel like every year
brings a new pill. One for blood
pressure, one for cholesterol, one for
sleep, and one for the stomach to
protect it from the others. Your
medicines matter, and you should never
stop one on your own. But more pills are
rarely the answer to feeling old. The
things that keep people strong and happy
after 60 are much simpler, and most of
them cost nothing.
Today I will share five of them. Quick
note, this is general education, not
personal medical advice.
The first thing you need after 60 is a
daily walk, not a marathon,
not a gym membership,
not 10,000 steps because a watch told
you so. Just a walk most days of the
week at a pace that feels comfortable
but awake. Here is why I put this first.
In 2022, researchers pulled together
data from 15 large studies that followed
tens of thousands of adults for years.
They counted how many steps people took
each day, and then they looked at who
was still alive at the end. For people
over 60, the result was very
encouraging.
The more people walked, the lower their
risk of dying early, and the benefit
leveled off somewhere between 6,000 and
8,000 steps a day.
You do not need the famous 10,000.
Even moving from 3,000 steps to 5,000
made a real difference.
Walking does quiet work all over the
body. It helps the heart pump more
efficiently.
It helps blood pressure and blood sugar
come down a little. It keeps the joints
moving so the knees and hips stay
lubricated instead of stiff. It helps
the bowels move and it lifts the mood
which is something no tablet does quite
as gently. There is another reason I
love walking. Doctors have noticed that
walking speed in older people is one of
the best signs of how well the whole
body is doing. People who keep a steady
confident pace tend to stay independent
longer. So every walk is not just
exercise.
It is practice for staying free. If you
have not walked much for a while, start
small. 10 minutes after breakfast,
10 minutes after lunch.
Walking after a meal is especially
helpful because it helps the body use
the sugar from that meal. Then every
week or two, add a few more minutes.
Wear shoes with a good grip. Walk where
the ground is even and well lit.
If your balance is not what it used to
be, there is no shame in a walking stick
or walking beside someone. And if you
get chest pain, unusual breathlessness,
or dizziness when you walk, stop and
tell your doctor because that is
something to look into. But for most
people, the daily walk is the closest
thing we have to a medicine with no side
effects.
That is the first thing. Before we go on
to number two, I would love to know
something. Tell me in the comments, how
many days a week do you walk right now?
One, three, every single day. There is
no wrong answer. I read the comments and
I am curious where everyone is starting
from. And if we have not met before, I
am Dr. Nimra. On this channel, I talk
about health after 60 in plain calm
language. The kind of conversation a
short appointment does not always have
time for. If that sounds useful to you,
you are very welcome to subscribe and
stay. Now, the second thing you need
after 60 is strong legs.
This one surprises people because when
we think about health, we think about
the heart, the blood pressure, the
sugar. We do not often think about the
thighs, but I would argue that strong
legs are one of the most important
things you can have in later life. Here
is what happens.
From around middle age, we slowly lose
muscle. Doctors call it sarcopenia.
It happens to everyone, but it happens
faster if we sit a lot. Many people lose
around 1% of their leg muscle every year
and sometimes more.
You do not notice it from one year to
the next. Then one day, getting up from
a low sofa takes two tries.
Climbing the stairs needs the handrail.
Carrying the shopping feels heavier than
it should. And here is why it matters so
much. About one in four people over 65
has a fall each year. Falls are one of
the main reasons older people lose their
independence.
And the most important thing that
protects you from falling is not a pill.
It is strong legs and good balance.
A large review of more than a 100
studies found that exercise programs
that train balance and strength reduce
falls by around a quarter. That is a big
effect, bigger than many medicines we
prescribe.
The good news is that muscle responds to
training at any age.
Studies have shown people in their 80s
and 90s getting stronger when they
practice simple exercises.
It is never too late. So, what should
you do? Here is a simple routine that
needs nothing but a sturdy chair. First,
sit to stand. Sit on a firm chair, feet
flat, arms crossed or resting on your
thighs.
Stand up slowly.
Sit down slowly.
That is one. Try to do it five times,
then rest, then do it again. If you need
your hands to push up at first, that is
fine. Over the weeks, try to use them
less. Second, heel raises.
Stand behind the chair, holding the back
of it. Rise up onto your toes, then
lower down slowly 10 times.
This strengthens the calves which help
you push off when you walk. Third, a
balance practice.
Holding the chair, stand with one foot
just in front of the other like you are
standing on a line. Hold for 10 seconds.
Then swap. As you get steadier, try
holding the chair with just one hand and
later with only your fingertips.
Do these on two or three days a week.
They take about 10 minutes.
Many people put the chair next to the
television and do them during the news.
The World Health Organization advises
that people over 65 do some muscle
strengthening on at least 2 days a week
and balance training on at least three.
This little routine covers both. If you
have had a recent operation, a joint
replacement, or a lot of pain in your
knees or hips, ask your doctor or a
physiotherapist to show you a version
that suits you. But please do not let
fear of falling make you stop moving.
Sitting still is what makes falls more
likely, not less.
Strong legs mean you can get up from a
chair, go to the toilet on your own,
walk to the shop, and visit a friend.
That is what independence really looks
like. That is the second thing. The
third thing you need after 60 is deep,
steady sleep. So many older people tell
their doctors the same thing. I fall
asleep fine, but I wake at 2 or 3:00 in
the morning and cannot get back to
sleep. Or I lie awake for an hour before
I drift off. And very often the next
step is a sleeping pill. I want to be
gentle but honest here. For most people
over 60, sleeping pills are not the best
answer. The common ones can make you
drowsy the next morning, unsteady on
your feet, and a little confused.
In older people, they are linked with
more falls and hip fractures.
That is why doctor's guidelines around
the world warn against using them
routinely in this age group. If you
already take one, please do not stop
suddenly because that can cause problems
of its own. Talk to your doctor about
whether it is still right for you. So,
what works instead? It helps first to
know what is normal. As we age, sleep
naturally becomes a little lighter and
we tend to feel sleepy earlier in the
evening and wake earlier in the morning.
That is not a disease.
Most older adults still need around 7 to
8 hours, but the shape of the night
changes.
Here are some habits that really help.
Get up at the same time every day, even
after a bad night. This is the most
powerful one. A steady wake up time sets
your body clock, and the clock decides
when you feel sleepy the next night. Use
the bed only for sleep. If you have been
lying awake for what feels like 20
minutes or so, get up, go to another
room, and do something calm in soft
light. Read something gentle.
Listen to quiet music. Go back to bed
only when you feel sleepy. It sounds
strange, but it teaches the brain that
bed means sleep, not worry. Be careful
with naps. A short nap of 20 or 30
minutes in the early afternoon is fine
for many people. A long nap late in the
day steals sleep from the night. Watch
the tea and coffee. Caffeine stays in
the body for many hours, so try to have
your last cup before lunchtime or early
afternoon at the latest. Keep the
bedroom cool, dark, and quiet. And if
you wake at night to pass urine, try to
drink most of your fluids earlier in the
day and less in the last 2 hours before
bed. There is also a treatment called
cognitive behavioral therapy for
insomnia.
It is a set of simple sleep lessons,
usually over a few weeks, sometimes done
online or with a booklet.
Medical guidelines recommend it as the
first treatment for long-term insomnia
before any pill and it works well in
older people. One more important point,
if you snore loudly, if someone has seen
you stop breathing or gasp in your
sleep, or if you feel very sleepy in the
daytime, no matter how long you sleep,
please mention it to your doctor. That
can be a sign of sleep apneoa which is
common after 60 strains the heart and
can be treated. Good sleep is when the
body repairs itself when memories are
stored and when the heart and blood
pressure get a rest. That is the third
thing. The fourth thing you need after
60 is morning sunlight and enough water.
These two sound almost too simple to
mention, but they are two of the things
older people most often go without and
both quietly affect how you feel every
single day. Let's start with the light.
Inside your brain, there is a small
master clock. It controls when you feel
alert, when you feel sleepy, and even
when certain hormones rise and fall.
That clock is set mainly by light,
especially bright light in the morning.
The trouble is that indoor light is much
dimmer than daylight.
Even on a cloudy day, the light outside
is many times brighter than a well-lit
living room. So, someone who stays
indoors most of the day can end up with
a weak, confused body clock. They feel
drowsy in the daytime and wakeful at
night.
The simple fix is to get outside in the
morning. 15 to 30 minutes of daylight,
ideally within an hour or two of waking.
Have your tea by an open window or on
the doorstep. Take your morning walk.
Sit on a bench in the park. You do not
need to look at the sun. Just be out in
the daylight.
Sunlight on the skin also helps the body
make vitamin D, which matters for bones
and muscles. As we age, the skin becomes
less efficient at making it. So, older
people are more likely to run low,
especially in winter or if they rarely
go out. A little sun on the face and
arms helps, but be sensible. Avoid
burning. And if your doctor has advised
a vitamin D supplement, keep taking it.
Now, water. Here is something many
people do not know. As we get older, the
feeling of thirst becomes weaker. Your
body may be running low on fluid, but
your brain does not send the signal as
strongly as it did when you were young.
So many older people are mildly
dehydrated without realizing it. And
mild dehydration can cause a surprising
number of problems. Dizziness when you
stand up, tiredness,
headaches,
constipation,
confusion. Sometimes
it makes falls more likely and it can
make the kidneys work harder.
So after 60, do not wait to feel
thirsty.
Drink small amounts regularly through
the day. A glass of water when you wake.
A drink with every meal. A glass in the
middle of the morning and the middle of
the afternoon.
Soups, fruit, milk, and tea all count. A
simple guide is the color of your urine.
Pale straw yellow is good. Dark yellow
usually means you need more. There is
one important exception.
If you have heart failure or kidney
disease, your doctor may have told you
to limit how much you drink.
In that case, please follow their
advice, not mine. Light in the morning
and water through the day. Simple
things, but they help your sleep, your
mood, your energy, and your balance.
That is the fourth thing. And now the
fifth thing, which I think may be the
most important of all. After 60, you
need a reason to get up in the morning.
When we are younger, life gives us
reasons whether we like it or not.
work, children,
bills,
somewhere to be at 8:00.
Then retirement comes, the children grow
up and move away, and suddenly the days
are wide open. At first, that feels like
freedom. But for many people, after a
while, it starts to feel empty. This is
not just a feeling. It shows up in
health. Researchers in Chicago followed
hundreds of older people for several
years. They asked them how much purpose
and meaning they felt in their lives.
The people with a strong sense of
purpose were much less likely to develop
Alzheimer's disease over the following
years and they kept their memory and
thinking better. Other large studies
have found that people with a stronger
sense of purpose tend to live longer and
have fewer heart attacks and strokes.
And connection matters just as much. A
big review of studies involving hundreds
of thousands of people found that those
with strong social relationships had a
much better chance of survival over the
study period than those who were
isolated.
Loneliness has been linked with a higher
risk of heart disease and stroke.
Some researchers say its effect on
health is in the same range as
well-known risks like smoking.
So, a reason to get up and someone to
share it with is not a luxury. It is
part of your health. But your reason
does not have to be big. You do not need
a new career or a grand mission. Look
for small things that pull you gently
into the day. It might be a plant that
needs watering or a small garden.
A dog that needs walking. A grandchild
you call every Sunday. A neighbor you
check on. A class at the community
center.
Volunteering for an hour a week.
Learning something new like a language,
a recipe, or a craft. Your place of
worship. A friend you meet for tea every
Thursday.
The key is that it is yours and that
something is waiting for you.
And on connection, quality matters more
than quantity. You do not need a crowded
house.
One or two people you can talk to
honestly who notice if you have not been
out can make an enormous difference. If
those people are fewer than they used to
be, it is worth making a small effort to
find new ones.
Say yes to the invitation.
Make the phone call. Sit on the bench
where the same people walk past every
morning and say hello. If you notice
that you have stopped enjoying things
you used to love, that you feel low most
days, or that you do not want to see
anyone, please tell your doctor.
Depression is common in later life. It
is not just part of getting older, and
it can be treated. A reason to get up
and someone to share it with. That is
the fifth thing. So, let's put it all
together.
After 60, you do not need more pills to
feel better. You need a daily walk,
strong legs,
deep steady sleep, morning light, and
enough water, and a reason to get up
with someone to share it. None of these
things is dramatic.
You will not feel a miracle tomorrow.
But these are the habits that quietly
year after year decide whether you stay
independent, steady on your feet, and
happy in your own life. Now, I promised
you this was not a video against
medicines. And I meant it. The tablets
your doctor prescribes for your blood
pressure, your heart, or your sugar can
protect you from strokes and heart
attacks.
Please keep taking them as prescribed.
But here is one thing I would encourage
every person over 60 to do once a year.
Put all your medicines in a bag. Every
tablet, every inhaler, every vitamin and
supplement, every cream, and every eye
drop. Take that bag to your doctor or
pharmacist and ask a simple question. Do
I still need each of these? And is the
dose still right for me? Doctors call
this a medication review?
Sometimes a pill that made sense 10
years ago is no longer needed. Sometimes
two medicines are doing the same job.
Sometimes a dose needs to be lowered
because the kidneys have changed with
age. Many people come out of that review
taking fewer tablets and feeling better.
And all of this should only be done with
your doctor, never on your own. So start
small. Pick one of the five things
today.
Maybe it is a 10-minute walk after
lunch.
Maybe it is a glass of water by your bed
and a cup of tea in the morning
sunshine.
Maybe it is a phone call to an old
friend.
Then next week add another. You do not
have to change your whole life at once.
You only have to make tomorrow a little
stronger than today. If you want to
understand your blood pressure numbers
better, I have made a video called is
150 normal after 65.
It is on the screen now and I think you
will find it reassuring.
Thank you for spending this time with
me. Please remember everything in this
video is for general education and is
not a replacement for advice from your
own doctor who knows your history and
your medicines.
Before you start a new exercise, change
how much you drink or make any change to
your tablets. Please speak to them
first. Take care of your legs, protect
your sleep, and go and find a little
sunshine. I will see you in the next
video.

subtitles.plaintext:
After 60, you can be low on water and
feel completely fine.
No dry mouth, no thirst, nothing.
That quiet is exactly the problem.
And the famous rule of eight glasses a
day,
it is not quite right for you, either,
though not in the way you might expect.
Today, I will show you six things about
water after 60, including your real
daily number. And at the end, a simple
water clock that keeps you topped up
without more trips to the bathroom at
night.
Quick note, this is general education,
not personal medical advice.
Number one, your first alarm gets
quieter after 60.
Thirst does not start in your mouth.
It starts in your brain.
Deep inside the brain, there are tiny
sensors that measure how concentrated
your blood is.
When you lose water, your blood becomes
a little thicker, a little saltier.
Those sensors notice, and they do two
things.
They release a water-saving hormone that
tells your kidneys to hold on to water.
And they make you feel thirsty, so you
go and drink.
When we are young, this alarm is loud
and quick.
A warm afternoon, and you are reaching
for a glass within minutes.
After 60, the alarm is still there, but
it is softer.
There is a classic study on this,
published in the New England Journal of
Medicine in 1984.
Researchers took a small group of
healthy, active men aged 67 to 75, and a
group of young men in their 20s.
Both groups went 24 hours without
drinking.
Both lost about the same amount of
water.
But here is what they found.
The older men's blood became more
concentrated than the young men's.
By every measurement, they were drier.
Yet, they said they felt less thirsty.
And when water was put in front of them,
they drank less and did not fully catch
up.
So, on the inside, the older body was
more dry.
On the outside, the person felt less of
it.
That is the heart of the problem.
And there are two more changes.
The older kidney is not as good at
saving water. So, it letting water go
even when the body is running low.
And muscle, which is mostly water,
shrinks with age.

proved that everyone needs exactly that.

and Metabolism, which wrote a guideline
just people over 65.

So, for women, the floor is a little
lower than eight glasses.
For men, it is about the same.

real danger is not missing the exact
number.
It is drifting below it day after day
without noticing.

If your doctor has given you a fluid
limit because of heart failure or kidney
disease, then that limit is your number.
Please follow your own doctor's advice,
not a general guideline.
In those conditions, too much fluid can
be harmful.
Number four, tea, coffee, milk, and soup
all count.
This is good news because it makes your
number much easier to reach.
Many people over 60 were told that tea
and coffee dry you out.
So, they leave them out of the count or
they drink extra water to cancel them.
But, this belief is mostly a myth for
people who drink them every day.
In a study from 2014,
a group of regular coffee drinkers spent
3 days drinking four cups of coffee a
day
and 3 days drinking the same amount of
water instead.
The researchers measured the water in
their bodies very carefully.
There was no meaningful difference.
In people who are used to it, a moderate
amount of coffee hydrates about as well
as water.
The study was done in men and with
moderate amounts, but tea behaves in a
similar way.
So, your morning tea counts.
Your coffee counts.
Milk counts.
Lassi, buttermilk, and soup count.
Broth and lentil soup count.
Even watery foods help. Cucumber,
watermelon, oranges, tomatoes, yogurt.
A few things to keep in mind.
Very strong coffee or many cups late in
the day can disturb your sleep, so keep
coffee to the morning.
Sugary drinks and juices add a lot of
sugar, especially if you have diabetes.
So, keep them small.
And alcohol does not count.
It makes you lose water.
So, what is the best mix?
Plain water is the simplest, with no
sugar and no caffeine. So, let it be the
base of your day.
Milk and lassi are a lovely second
choice after 60 because along with water
they bring protein and calcium for your
muscles and bones.
Soup and dal are excellent in the
evening because they fill you up gently.
And if plain water feels boring, add a
slice of lemon, a few mint leaves, or a
piece of cucumber.
A drink you enjoy is a drink you will
actually finish.
And if you fast, for example, during
Ramadan, spread your drinks between the
evening meal and the pre-dawn meal,
rather than drinking a lot at once.
And if you are older or unwell, please
speak to your doctor about whether
fasting is safe for you.
Number five, the usual checks miss it.
You have probably seen urine color
charts.
Pale yellow means you are fine. Dark
yellow means drink more.
You may have heard that a dry mouth is
the warning sign or that if you pinch
the skin on the back of your hand and it
stays up, you are low on water.
In 2015, the Cochrane Group, an
international team that weighs medical
evidence very carefully, reviewed these
simple tests in people over 65.
They compared them against a proper
blood test.
The result was humbling.
Dry mouth, feeling thirsty, heart rate,
urine color, and the skin pinch test all
missed many older people who were
dehydrated.
And they wrongly worried about others
who were fine.
A later study looked at urine tests on
their own, color included, and found
none of them accurate enough to rely on
in older people.
Why?
Because, as we said, the older kidney
does not concentrate urine as strongly.
So, your urine can look fairly pale
while your blood is already too
concentrated.
And older skin is less elastic anyway,
so the pinch test is not reliable.
This does not mean urine color is
useless.
Very dark urine, or passing very little
urine in a day, is still a warning sign,
and you should drink more and get
checked if it continues.
But, pale urine does not prove you are
fine.
The only reliable measure is a blood
test, which shows how concentrated your
blood is.
Your doctor may look at your sodium
level, or something called serum
osmolality.
If you are ever unwell, confused, or
have a fall, and you are seen in a
clinic or hospital, it is a fair
question to ask, "Could I be dehydrated,
and was it checked?"
So, you cannot feel your way to safety
here.
You plan your way there.
Number six, some days and some medicines
need extra care.
There are days when the body loses water
much faster than usual.
Hot weather,
sweating while working, gardening, or
traveling,
a fever,
vomiting or diarrhea.

doctor in advance.

medicines may need to be paused for a

kidneys when you are dry.

tablets, water tablets, metformin, some
newer diabetes tablets, and
anti-inflammatory painkillers.

Instead, ask your doctor or pharmacist
now, while you are well, what should I
do with my medicines if I get a stomach

More is not always better.

water, far beyond what you need, can

people it can cause confusion,

tablets and some antidepressants.

through the day, not forcing down liters
at once.

bathroom, because this is the main

and often not the right one.

come from an enlarged prostate in men,

your legs raised for an hour in the
afternoon can help that fluid leave

twice a night, please mention it to your
doctor.

then you can drink properly again.

If you feel very dizzy or faint, become
confused, have not passed urine for most
of the day,

vomiting, please see a doctor the same
day.
These are not things to manage alone at
home.
Now, as I promised, here is the water
clock.
I call it a clock because it runs on the
time of day, not on thirst.
Step one, know your number.
Women, at least about six and a half
glasses of drinks a day.
Men, at least about eight.

unwell.
And if you have a fluid limit from your
doctor, use that instead.
Step two, make it visible.

most of your day, and fill it every
morning.
Mark it with three strips of tape where
the level should be by lunch, by
mid-afternoon, and by early evening.

tea, coffee, and milk, too.
Step three, attach drinks to things you
already do.
One glass when you wake up.
One glass with each meal.
A full glass, not a sip, with every set
of tablets.
One mid-morning and one mid-afternoon.
Add those up and you have almost reached
your number without ever waiting for
thirst.
Here is what a day might look like for a
woman.
A glass of water when she wakes up.
A cup of tea with breakfast.
A glass of water with her morning
tablets,
a glass mid-morning,
a glass of lassi or water with lunch,
a cup of tea in the afternoon.

by mid-afternoon, and anything with the
evening meal, a bowl of soup or lentils,
is extra.
For a man, add one or two more glasses
before the afternoon is over.
Step four, front-load.

drinks finished by mid-afternoon.

two hours before bed.

are not paying for it at 3:00 in the
morning.

habit of stopping all drinks after
lunch.

days.
Heat, hard work, fever, vomiting, or
diarrhea.
Add a glass or two and follow your sick
day rules.
Step six, keep a drink within reach.
A glass on the table next to your chair,
a bottle in your bag or car.

drink you can see is a drink you finish.

parent, offer drinks often in small cups
at set times.

Warm tea, a little juice with water,
soup.

sleepy, think of water early.

In the first few days, you will visit
the bathroom more during the day.
That is normal.
Your bladder is getting used to a steady
flow instead of a flood in the morning
and nothing later.

natural.

their nighttime trips do not increase,
and some find they improve.

fog lifting and constipation easing.

One, your thirst alarm gets quieter
after 60, so do not wait to feel
thirsty.
Two, hidden dehydration is common, and
it often looks like confusion,
dizziness, a fall, or constipation, not
thirst.

about 6 and 1/2 glasses for women and
eight for men, more in heat or illness,
unless your doctor has set a limit.
Four, tea, coffee, milk, lassi, and soup
all count.
Alcohol does not.
Five, dry mouth and urine color can miss
it.
The reliable check is a blood test.

medicines need extra care.

and do not overdo plain water, either.

today, let it be this. After 60, drink
by the clock, not by thirst.
One last reminder.
This video is for general education and
is not personal medical advice.
Please never stop, start, or change any
medicine without speaking to your own
doctor or pharmacist.
If you have heart failure or kidney
disease, follow your own doctor's fluid
advice.
And if you become confused, very dizzy,
or cannot keep fluids down, please see a
doctor the same day.
Now tell me in the comments, what is
your favorite drink that helps you reach
your number?
Tea, lassi, soup, or plain water?
I will be reading.

come from too little water or from the
way you nap, watch this next video where
I explain what your daytime naps are
telling you after 60 and how long a
healthy nap really is.
It is right here on your screen.
Thank you for watching. Please share
this with someone you love who never
feels thirsty and take good care of
yourself.

What really happens when you eat peanut butter every day after 60? In this video, Dr Nimra explains, in plain words, what a daily spoonful does for your muscles and legs, your heart, your blood sugar, your brain and your bones. She also covers what peanut butter cannot do, who should be careful (kidney disease, swallowing problems, peanut allergy, weight, salty jars), and exactly how to choose the right jar and how much to eat.

In a 2026 Australian study, adults aged 66 to 89 who ate about one heaped tablespoon of natural peanut butter a day for 6 months stood up from a chair faster and with more power, and did not gain weight.

💬 Tell me in the comments: your age, and will you try a spoonful of natural peanut butter tomorrow? Yes or no.

👍 If this helped, please share it with a parent, friend or neighbour over 60, and subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The jar in your cupboard
2:10 Why it matters more after 60
3:47 1. Your muscles and legs
7:24 2. Your heart
9:42 3. Your blood sugar
11:42 4. Your brain
13:24 5. Your bones and night cramps
14:40 What peanut butter can't do
15:48 Who should be careful
17:56 How to eat it the right way (5 rules)
20:25 Recap

Sources:
Tan SY et al. (Deakin University, COINS trial). Peanut butter and muscle power in older adults at risk of falls. Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, 2026 (funded by The Peanut Institute)
Guasch-Ferré M et al. Nut consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease. J Am Coll Cardiol 2017
Jiang R et al. Nut and peanut butter consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes in women. JAMA 2002
Morris MC et al. Dietary niacin and the risk of incident Alzheimer's disease and of cognitive decline. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2004
USDA FoodData Central: peanut butter, smooth, natural

Important: this video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. If you have kidney disease, swallowing problems, a peanut allergy or take regular medicines, check with your own doctor or dietitian before changing your diet. Never stop a medicine on your own.

records.channelDescription:
Welcome to Dr Nimra | Health After 60 🩺

I'm Dr Nimra, this channel exists for one reason: to explain, in plain and simple language, what your 15-minute doctor's visit doesn't have time to explain.

Every week I break down what really happens inside your body after 60, and what you can do about it:
💊 Medicines: what your pills really do, side effects, and dangerous combinations
🥗 Food & diet: what to eat, what to limit, and why
🚶 Exercise & mobility: simple movement that keeps you strong and independent
😴 Sleep, bathroom and daily habits: the small things that add up
❤️ Heart, blood pressure, blood sugar, kidneys, bones, brain and eyes

⚠️ Disclaimer
The content on this channel is for general education and information only. It is not personal medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Never start, stop or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have a medical emergency, call your local emergency number.

records.text:
After 70, most falls start with something tiny: a foot that does not lift high enough, a step that is a little too short, or eyes looking at the wrong place. In this video, Dr Nimra shows the one simple change to how you walk that helps protect you from falls, then 5 easy exercises to make it automatic, 3 quick tests you can do at home, and the 5 everyday mistakes that undo it (shoes, glasses, walking stick, standing up too fast, and medicines).

The one change: lift your foot, reach a little further, and land on your heel.

💬 Tell me in the comments: your age, and one word for how your walking feels right now (steady, slow, heavy or careful).

👍 If this helped, please share it with a parent, friend or neighbour, and subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: How Often Should You Shower After 60? (dizziness after a warm shower)

CHAPTERS
0:00 Your independence after 70
2:03 Why falls matter so much
4:41 The careful walk that causes trips
6:12 The one simple change
8:45 Exercise 1: the slow heel walk
9:58 Exercise 2: the hip opener
11:29 Exercise 3: the heel raise
12:33 Exercise 4: the eyes-forward walk
14:10 Exercise 5: the doorway step-over
15:25 Who should check with a doctor first
16:05 3 quick tests you can do at home
18:08 Mistake 1: the wrong shoes
19:19 Mistake 2: varifocal glasses outside
20:25 Mistake 3: the walking stick
21:14 Mistake 4: standing up too fast
22:06 Mistake 5: medicines that affect balance
23:11 What to expect week by week
24:22 Your 10-minute daily plan
25:22 For carers
26:04 Walking changes that need a doctor
26:45 Last words

Sources:
Studenski S et al. Gait speed and survival in older adults. JAMA 2011
CDC STEADI: Older adult fall prevention (1 in 4 adults 65+ fall each year)
Berg WP et al. Circumstances and consequences of falls in independent community-dwelling older adults. Age Ageing 1997
Chapman GJ, Hollands MA. Evidence for a link between changes to gaze behaviour and risk of falling in older adults during adaptive locomotion. Gait Posture 2006
Robertson MC et al. Preventing injuries in older people by preventing falls: a meta-analysis of individual-level data (Otago programme). J Am Geriatr Soc 2002
Sherrington C et al. Exercise for preventing falls in older people living in the community. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019
Araújo CG et al. Successful 10-second one-legged stance performance predicts survival in middle-aged and older individuals. Br J Sports Med 2022
Koepsell TD et al. Footwear style and risk of falls in older adults. J Am Geriatr Soc 2004
Lord SR et al. Multifocal glasses impair edge-contrast sensitivity and depth perception and increase the risk of falls in older people. J Am Geriatr Soc 2002
Rikli RE, Jones CJ. Senior Fitness Test (30-second chair stand)

Important: this video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. Check with your own doctor or physiotherapist before starting new exercises, especially after a fall, a joint replacement, or with a heart or balance problem. Never stop a medicine on your own. Sudden weakness, a drooping face or trouble speaking: call an ambulance.

If you are over 70 and you can still
walk to your own kitchen, make your own
cup of tea, and step out into your
garden, you have something precious.
Your independence.
And I want to help you keep it for many,
many more years.
Because here is something most people
are never told.
You may have heard that you should walk
more.
But there is one small change in how you
walk that matters even more than how far
you walk.
It takes no money, no gym, and no
equipment.
You can start it in your own hallway
today, in your slippers. Well, actually,
not in your slippers. And I will tell
you why in a few minutes.
I am Dr. Nimra.
And studies show that people in their
70s, 80s, and even 90s can walk taller,
steadier, and more confidently after
just a few weeks of simple practice.
Your body is still able to learn.
At 70, at 80, and beyond.
Think about the last time you nearly
tripped.
Maybe it was the edge of a rug, a door
strip, or a step that was a little
higher than you thought.
You caught yourself, your heart jumped,
and you said, "That was close."
Most falls after 70 do not start with a
big mistake.
They start with something tiny.
A foot that does not lift quite high
enough.
A step that is a little too short.
Eyes looking at the wrong place.
So today, I will show you the one simple
change that helps protect you from
falls.
Then five easy exercises to make it
automatic, three quick tests to see how
steady you really are, the shoe mistake
almost everyone makes, and the glasses
mistake that surprises people the most.
So make yourself comfortable, and let us
walk through this together.
Quick note, this is general education,
not personal medical advice.
Let me start with why this matters so
much.
About one in four adults over 65 has a
fall every year.
After 75, it becomes even more common.
And a fall at this age is not just a
bruise.
It can mean a broken hip, a broken
wrist, a head injury, and weeks in
hospital.
Many people never fully get back the
confidence they had before.
But there is something even more
important than the falls themselves.
It is the fear of falling.
After one fall, or even one near miss,
many people start to walk differently.
They take smaller steps.
They slide their feet.
They bend forward and look down at the
floor.
It feels careful.
It feels safe.
And this is the surprising part.
That careful walk can actually make a
fall more likely.
I will explain exactly why in a moment.
There is also a reason doctors care so
much about how you walk.
In a large study published in the
Journal of the American Medical
Association, researchers looked at more
than 34,000 people aged 65 and over.
They found that walking speed was one of
the strongest signs of how well a person
would do in the years ahead.
People who walked a little faster, on
average, lived longer.
Walking speed is not magic.
It is a mirror.
It shows the strength of your legs, the
health of your heart and lungs, your
balance, and your brain all at once.
And the good news is that the things
that improve your walk also improve many
of those things together.
Before we go on, I would love to know
something.
What has happened to you this year?
Write fall if you have had a fall.
Write near if you nearly fell but caught
yourself.
Write scared if you have not fallen but
you worry about it.
Or write steady if you feel safe on your
feet.
And add your age if you like.
It takes 2 seconds and it helps me make
the right videos for you.
And if we have not met before, I am Dr.
Nimra.
On this channel I talk about health
after 60 in plain calm language. The
kind of conversation a short appointment
does not always have time for.
If that sounds useful, you are very
welcome to subscribe and stay.
Now, let me describe a walk and I want
you to think honestly about your own
steps or the steps of someone you love.
The steps have become shorter.
Not suddenly.
Slowly over years.
The feet do not lift cleanly anymore.
They stay close to the floor and slide
forward almost like shuffling.
The body leans a little forward from the
hips.
And the eyes are fixed on the floor just
in front of the feet.
Doctors sometimes call this a cautious
walk.
And it makes sense why it happens.
When your balance feels less sure, your
body tries to keep your feet close to
the ground and your eyes on the danger.
But look at what it does.
When your foot only clears the floor by
a few millimeters, there is no room for
error.
The edge of a bath mat, a door strip, a
crack in the pavement, a fold in the
carpet, any of these can catch your toe.
In studies of older people who fell,
tripping is one of the most common
causes, often around one in three falls.
And because your body is leaning
forward, your weight is already ahead of
your feet.
So, when your toe catches, your body has
no time to recover.
You go down before you can even put your
hands out.
So, the careful walk protects you from
one danger and quietly opens the door to
another.
So, here it is.
The one simple change.
Lift your foot, reach a little further,
and land on your heel.
That is it.
Let me explain each part slowly.
Lift your foot.
Do not slide it along the floor.
Pick it up as if you are stepping over a
thin stick.
Reach a little further.
Not a giant step.
Just a few centimeters.
About two fingers width longer than you
normally step.
And land on your heel.
Let your heel touch the ground first.
Then let your weight roll forward
through the middle of your foot onto the
ball of your foot and push off gently
with your toes into the next step.
Think of how a young child runs across
the garden.
The foot comes up, swings forward, and
lands heel first.
Nobody taught them.
It is how the body is built to walk.
Why does landing on your heel help so
much?
Because it sets off a chain reaction
through your whole body.
To land on your heel, your foot has to
lift higher, so it clears the floor.
Your step becomes naturally a little
longer.
Your body comes back upright instead of
leaning forward.
And the big muscles in your hips and
bottom switch on, and those are the
muscles that keep you steady.
When people lose the heel landing and
start to land flat-footed, that whole
chain switches off.
Small studies in people with walking
problems have shown that simply thinking
about landing on the heel, just paying
attention to it, can make the steps
longer and lift the foot higher off the
floor.
One thought and the whole walk changes.
But here is the problem.
You cannot think about your heel every
second of the day.
You need your body to do it on its own,
even when you are carrying a cup of tea
or talking to your grandchild.
And that is what the exercises are for.
Before we start, one important safety
rule.
Always do these exercises next to
something solid.
A kitchen counter, a wall, or the back
of a heavy chair that will not slide.
Wear shoes with a good grip or do them
barefoot on a carpet.
And if anything causes sharp pain,
dizziness, or chest discomfort, stop and
sit down.
Exercise number one, the slow heel walk.
Find a clear hallway or a stretch of
floor along a kitchen counter.
Walk at half your normal speed.
With every single step, think about only
one thing.
Heel first.
Feel the heel touch.
Feel the weight roll forward through
your foot.
Feel the toes push off.
Then the next step.
Take 10 steps.
Turn around carefully.
10 steps back.
Do this three times with a short rest
between.
Why so slow?
Because you are not training your
muscles here.
You are retraining a message from your
brain to your feet.
That message has gone quiet over the
years.
Slow, careful repetition is how the
brain relearns it.
Think of it as tuning a radio back to
the right station.
When it feels easy, try it on a
different surface.
Carpet, then tile, then the garden path.
This teaches your brain to do it
everywhere, not just in one hallway.
Exercise number two, the hip opener.
Many people who walk bent forward have
tight muscles at the front of the hip
from years of sitting and sleepy muscles
at the back of the hip.
That pulls the body forward like a
fishing rod bending.
Stand behind a sturdy chair and hold the
back of it.
Step your right foot back about the
length of your forearm.
Keep both feet flat on the floor and
your front knee slightly bent.
Now gently push your right hip forward
and squeeze your right buttock.
You should feel a stretch at the front
of the right hip.
Hold it for five slow breaths.
Then change sides.
Do four on each side.
This one exercise does two jobs.
It opens what has become tight and it
wakes up what has gone quiet.
Many people notice they stand taller
after just a week.
Let me pause here for a moment.
Of the things I have described so far,
the short steps, the shuffling feet, or
the forward lean, which one do you
notice most in yourself or in someone
you love?
Write short four short steps.
Write shuffle if your feet slide along
the floor.
Write lean if you bend forward.
Or write none if your walk still feels
normal.
I read every comment and it helps me
know what to cover next.
Exercise number three, the heel raise.
The push from your toes at the end of
each step gives your walk its power.
The calf muscles do most of that work.
When they get weak, your steps become
short and flat, and walking feels
tiring.
Stand at the kitchen counter with both
hands resting on it.
Slowly rise up onto your toes, as high
as is comfortable.
Hold for 2 seconds at the top.
Then come down slowly, counting to
three.
Not a drop.
A slow, controlled lowering.
Do 10 to 15 of these.
Rest.
Then do another set.
If you can, build up to three sets.
When this becomes easy, try it on one
foot at a time, still holding the
counter.
You may notice one side is weaker than
the other.
That is very common, and it is worth
working on because a weaker side is
often the side you trip on.
Exercise number four, the eyes forward
walk.
This is the one that surprises people.
Research on how older people look while
they walk has found something important.
People who are more likely to fall tend
to look away from where they are about
to step too early, or they stare at
their feet.
And when you stare at your feet, your
brain can only react to what is right
under you.
When your eyes are looking a few steps
ahead, your brain can plan.
And planning is always faster and safer
than reacting.
So, here is the exercise.
Stand at one end of your hallway.
Before you take a step, choose a point
at the far end.
A light switch, a door handle, a picture
on the wall.
Now walk towards it, heel first, with
your eyes on that point the whole way.
Do not look at your feet.
When you reach it, turn carefully,
choose a new point, and walk back.
Do four lengths.
Notice what happens to your body when
your eyes look ahead.
Your head comes up.
Your chest opens.
Your back straightens.
You did not have to think about your
posture at all.
Your body follows your eyes.
A small tip, when you are out walking,
glance down every few steps to check the
ground ahead, then bring your eyes back
up.
Look ahead, glance down, look ahead.
That is the safe rhythm.
Exercise number five, the doorway step
over.
Real life is not a smooth hallway.
It is a rug, a door strip, a garden
step, the lip of a shower.
So, the last exercise practices exactly
those moments.
Choose two or three places in your home
that you cross every day, like a doorway
strip or the edge of a rug.
Walk towards one at a normal pace.
About two steps before you reach it,
slow down slightly.
Lift your front foot a little higher
than you need to, step over it with
confidence, and land on your heel on the
other side.
Keep walking a few steps.
Then turn and come back.
Do this five times at each place.
The aim is to teach your brain to notice
the obstacle early, lift the foot in
good time, and step over it calmly, not
at the last second in a panic.
When this feels easy, try it while
holding something light in one hand,
like a folded towel.
Because in real life, that is when most
trips happen.
When your hands are full and your mind
is somewhere else.
Now, before you start, please read this
carefully.
If you have had a hip or knee
replacement in the last 6 months, check
with your surgeon or physiotherapist
first.
If you have severe numbness in your
feet,
a problem with your inner ear,
Parkinson's disease, or you have fallen
more than once this year, please ask
your doctor to refer you to a
physiotherapist or a falls clinic.

and that is one of the most useful
referrals you can ask for.
And do not practice when you are tired,
just after waking up, or soon after a
medicine that makes you drowsy.
Now, let me share three quick tests you
can do at home.

doctors use to check fall risk.
Do them with someone nearby and next to
a counter.
Test number one, the chair stand.
Sit in a firm chair without arms, with
your arms crossed over your chest.

fully and sit back down in 30 seconds.

strength needs work, and that is exactly
what the exercises in this video help
with.
Test number two, the line stand.
Stand with one foot directly in front of
the other, heel touching toe, like
standing on a tightrope.

If not, your balance needs some
practice.
Test number three, the one leg stand.
Hold the counter, lift one foot off the
floor, then let go.

It is a sign of the strength and balance
underneath.
And it can be trained.
Write your scores down today.

Many people are surprised by how much
they improve.
And tell me in the comments which test
was the hardest for you.
Write chair for the chair stand.
Write line for the heel-to-toe stand.
Write one leg for the one leg stand.
Or write all easy if you passed all
three.
I would love to see how everyone does.
Now, the mistakes that undo all this
good work.
Let me start with the one in almost
every home.
Mistake number one, the wrong shoes.
Many people over 70 spend the whole day
at home in soft, backless slippers, or
in socks, or barefoot on hard floors.
Studies of falls at home have found that
walking in socks or in slippers without
a back is linked to a higher risk of
falling.
And that well-fitting shoes with a firm
sole are linked to the lowest risk.
So, here is what a safe shoe looks like.
It has a back that holds your heel.
It has a sole that is thin and firm, not
thick and squishy, so you can feel the
floor.
It has a low, wide heel.
It has a grip on the bottom.
And it fastens with laces or a strap, so
your foot does not slide around inside
it.
If you love your slippers, choose ones
with a closed back and a non-slip sole.
And please, throw away the old ones with
the worn, shiny bottom.
They are like walking on ice.
Mistake number two, walking outside in
reading glasses or varifocals.
This is the one that surprises people
the most.
Bifocal and varifocal glasses have a
reading part at the bottom of the lens.
And when you look down at a curb or a
step through that part, the edge looks
blurry and you can misjudge where it is.
A study found that older people who wore
these glasses had more falls outside the
home, especially on steps and curbs.
The answer is simple.
If you are active and walk outside a
lot, ask your optician about a pair of
single vision distance glasses just for
walking.
And at home, be extra careful on stairs
when you are wearing your varifocals.
Lower your chin a little so you are
looking through the top of the lens, not
the bottom.
And while we are talking about eyes, if
you have not had an eye test in the last
year, book one.
Cataracts come on so slowly that many
people do not realize how much they
cannot see.
Mistake number three, the walking stick
at the wrong height in the wrong hand.
A stick that is too tall or too short
can make your walk worse, not better.
Here is how to check.
Stand up straight in your normal shoes
with your arms hanging down by your
sides.
The top of the stick should come to the
crease of your wrist.
And hold it in the hand on the opposite
side to your weaker leg.
So, if your right knee is bad, hold the
stick in your left hand.
The stick and the weak leg move forward
together.
Many people do this the other way around
and it throws their balance off.
If you are not sure, a physiotherapist
can check your stick in 5 minutes.
It is one of the best 5 minutes you can
spend.
Mistake number four, standing up and
walking straight away.
After 65, many people get a drop in
blood pressure when they stand up,
especially in the morning, after a meal,
or after a warm shower.
For a few seconds, the brain does not
get quite enough blood.
You feel a little light-headed, and that
is when many falls happen.
So, before you walk anywhere, sit on the
edge of the bed or the chair for a
moment.
Move your ankles up and down 10 times.
Stand up slowly.
Then stand still and count to 10 before
you take your first step.
10 seconds that can save you a broken
hip.
I talked about this more in my video on
what to do after a warm shower, and I
will link it at the end.
Mistake number five, not knowing which
medicines affect your balance.
Some common medicines can make you
dizzy, drowsy, or unsteady.
Sleeping tablets,
some medicines for anxiety, depression,
and nerve pain,
some blood pressure tablets and water
tablets,
some allergy tablets, especially the
older ones that make you sleepy.
And the risk adds up when you take
several together.
If you take five or more medicines,
please ask your doctor or pharmacist for
a medicine review, and ask them one
simple question, could any of these be
affecting my balance?
But please, never stop a medicine on
your own.
Some of them are dangerous to stop
suddenly.
Be honest with me now.
Which of these mistakes were you making
before today?
Right, slippers, glasses, stick, or
standing up.
Or write none if you were already doing
everything right.
Many people will be making the same one
as you.
Now, let me tell you what to expect if
you start today.
In the first 1 to 2 weeks, the heel
landing will feel strange and a little
clumsy.
That is normal.
Your brain is learning something it has
forgotten.
After about 2 to 4 weeks of practice
most days, many people notice their
steps feel longer and lighter, and their
feet feel less heavy.
After 6 to 8 weeks, the strength in the
legs and hips is building.
Studies of home exercise programs for
older people, like the well-known Otago
program from New Zealand, have found
that regular balance and strength
exercises reduced falls by around a
third.
And a large review of more than 100
studies found that exercise programs
reduced falls in older people by about a
quarter.
That is real, proven protection from
something you can do in your own
kitchen.
And after about 3 months, the new walk
starts to become automatic.
Your brain no longer has to remind your
feet.
The safe walk becomes your normal walk.
Let me give you a very simple plan, so
you do not have to remember everything.
Every morning, after you have been up
for at least half an hour, do the slow
heel walk. 10 steps there, 10 steps
back, three times.
Then the heel raises at the kitchen
counter.
Every afternoon, do the hip opener and
the eyes forward walk.
Two or three times a week, do the
doorway step over at your two or three
trickiest places at home.
That is about 10 minutes a day.
No gym.
No equipment.
No cost.
And once a week, check your home.
Is there a loose rug that needs to go or
be taped down?
Is there a light you need at night
between the bed and the bathroom?
Is there a rail by the stairs and by the
toilet?
These small changes protect you even on
the days you are tired.
Now, a few words for anyone caring for
an older parent or partner.
Watch how they walk.
If you see shorter steps, shuffling,
holding onto furniture as they move
around the room, or they are going out
less than before, please do not ignore
it.
It is not just getting old.
It is a sign that their walk needs some
help.
Gently suggest these exercises, do them
together, and speak to their doctor
about a physiotherapy or falls clinic
referral.
And if they have had a fall, even one
where they were not hurt, please tell
the doctor.
One fall is the strongest warning sign
of another.
And one important doctor's note.
Some changes in walking need a doctor
quickly, not exercises.
If walking changes suddenly over a few
days or weeks.
If one leg suddenly becomes weak or
drags.
If you have new shuffling with a tremor.
If you have new numbness in your feet,
new problems with your bladder, or new
confusion.
If you feel dizzy or faint when you
walk, or get chest pain or
breathlessness.
Please see your doctor.
And if weakness, a drooping face, or
difficulty speaking comes on suddenly,
call an ambulance straight away because
that can be a stroke.
Let me finish with this.
The fear of falling quietly makes life
smaller.
People stop going to the shops, stop
visiting friends, stop walking in the
park because the ground does not feel
safe anymore.
And the less you walk, the weaker your
legs become, and the more the fear
grows.
But you can break that circle.
Your body is still able to learn at 70,
at 80, and beyond.
The muscles and the signals that keep
you steady are not gone.
They are just waiting to be used again.
So tomorrow morning, start with just 10
steps.
Lift your foot.
Reach a little further.
Land on your heel.
Eyes ahead.
And then do it again the morning after.
One last reminder.
This video is for general education and
is not personal medical advice.
Please check with your own doctor or
physiotherapist before starting a new
exercise, especially if you have had a
fall, a joint replacement,
or a heart or balance problem.
Now, before you go, I would love to hear
from you.
Type your age and one word for how your
walking feels right now.
Write steady, slow, heavy, or careful,
whichever fits you best.
Your answer may be exactly what someone
else needs to read today.
And please share this video with one
person who needs it.
A parent, a friend, a neighbor.
It could genuinely save them from a
fall.
If you have ever felt dizzy after a warm
shower or when you stand up, my video on
what to do after a shower is right here
on your screen.
Thank you for watching and take good
care of yourself.
