Welcome to Dr Nimra | Health After 60 🩺

I'm Dr Nimra, this channel exists for one reason: to explain, in plain and simple language, what your 15-minute doctor's visit doesn't have time to explain.

Every week I break down what really happens inside your body after 60, and what you can do about it:
💊 Medicines: what your pills really do, side effects, and dangerous combinations
🥗 Food & diet: what to eat, what to limit, and why
🚶 Exercise & mobility: simple movement that keeps you strong and independent
😴 Sleep, bathroom and daily habits: the small things that add up
❤️ Heart, blood pressure, blood sugar, kidneys, bones, brain and eyes

⚠️ Disclaimer
The content on this channel is for general education and information only. It is not personal medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Never start, stop or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have a medical emergency, call your local emergency number.

records.text:
Heavy, cold or tired legs after a short walk? In this video, Dr Nimra counts down 5 seeds that can genuinely help the blood flow in your legs after 70, and tells you honestly what each study really found.

The 5 seeds:
5. Pumpkin seeds (magnesium for relaxed arteries)
4. Sesame seeds (protecting the artery lining)
3. Chia seeds (blood sugar and inflammation, and how to eat them safely)
2. Black seed / kalonji (blood pressure, with important safety warnings)
1. Ground flaxseed (the Canadian study in people with narrowed leg arteries)

Plus: the preparation mistake that wastes most of your flaxseed, why to take your tablets apart from it, the walking method doctors use for narrowed leg arteries, and the warning signs that need a doctor straight away.

💬 Tell me in the comments: how old are you, and what would you love to do if your legs felt stronger?

👍 If this helped, please like the video and subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: After 60, You Don't Need More Pills. You Need These 5 Things

CHAPTERS
0:00 Heavy, tired legs? Some hopeful news
0:52 5. Pumpkin seeds (magnesium)
4:20 4. Sesame seeds (the artery lining)
7:00 3. Chia seeds (and how to eat them safely)
9:13 2. Black seed / kalonji (with safety warnings)
11:29 1. Flaxseed and the Canadian study
13:05 The flaxseed preparation secret
14:42 2 doctor tips: medicines and safety
15:14 A simple morning bowl
15:36 The 5 seeds together
15:58 If walking is hard: a chair exercise
16:38 Not every heavy leg is the same
17:20 Warning signs you should never ignore
17:51 Start with one seed: a simple week
18:52 The most important thing is not a seed
20:16 Your plan for this week

Sources:
Rodriguez-Leyva D et al. Potent antihypertensive action of dietary flaxseed in hypertensive patients. Hypertension 2013 (FlaxPAD trial)
Zhang X et al. Effects of magnesium supplementation on blood pressure: a meta-analysis. Hypertension 2016
Wichitsranoi J et al. Antihypertensive and antioxidant effects of dietary black sesame meal in pre-hypertensive humans. Nutrition Journal 2011
Vuksan V et al. Supplementation of conventional therapy with the novel grain Salba (chia). Diabetes Care 2007
Sahebkar A et al. Nigella sativa and blood pressure: a meta-analysis. Journal of Hypertension 2016
Garrison SR et al. Magnesium for skeletal muscle cramps. Cochrane Review 2020

Important: this video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. Never stop, start or change any medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you take blood thinners, blood pressure or diabetes medicines, or have kidney disease, check with your doctor before adding seeds or supplements. A suddenly cold, pale, painful or numb leg is an emergency.

#healthafter60 #seniorhealth #legcirculation #flaxseed #healthyaging

subtitles.plaintext:
If your legs feel heavy, cold, or tired
after a short walk, here is some hopeful
news.
One of the best foods for your legs may
already be in your kitchen, and it costs
only pennies a day.
In Canada, 110 people with narrowed leg
arteries ate a little ground flaxseed
every day for 6 months.
Their blood pressure came down by about
10 points.
No new drug.
Just a seed.
Flaxseed is my number one today.
But most people prepare it the wrong
way, and I will show you the right way
near the end.
No seed opens your veins a million
times, but five seeds can genuinely
help, and I will tell you what each
study really found.
Quick note. This is general education,
not personal medical advice.
Number five, pumpkin seeds.
Picture a small green seed packed with a
mineral your blood vessels love.
That mineral is magnesium.
One small handful of pumpkin seeds,
about 2 Tbsp, gives you around 150 mg of
it.
That is more than a third of what most
older adults need in a whole day.
You can get magnesium from other
everyday foods, too. Spinach, beans,
lentils, almonds, whole grains, and even
a little dark chocolate.
But pumpkin seeds are one of the richest
and easiest.
A small handful, and you are a good way
there.
Why does magnesium matter for your legs?
Your arteries are not just pipes.
Their walls have a thin layer of muscle.
Magnesium helps that muscle relax, so
the artery can open a little wider, and
blood can travel more easily down to
your calves and feet.
In 2016, researchers combined 34 trials
with more than 2,000 adults.
People who took about 368
mg of magnesium a day for 3 months saw
their blood pressure come down a little,
by about two points.
That is modest.
But it is real, and it is food, not a
pill.
Here is the part one want older viewers
to hear.
After 60, the body holds onto magnesium
less well.
The gut absorbs less.
And some very common medicines, like
water pills and acid-reducing stomach
tablets, can lower it further.
So many people over 70 are a little low
without knowing.
Now, many videos say magnesium will stop
your night cramps.
I want to be honest with you.
When researchers tested magnesium for
ordinary night cramps in older adults,
it mostly did not help.
If cramps wake you at night, what helps
more is a gentle calf stretch before
bed. Stand facing a wall, one foot back,
heel down, and hold for 30 seconds on
each side.
And ask your doctor to check your
medicines, because some of them cause
cramps.
How to eat pumpkin seeds.
About 2 Tbsp a day, raw or lightly
roasted and unsalted, because extra salt
pushes blood pressure up.
They make a lovely afternoon snack, or a
topping on soup or salad.
One caution, if you have kidney disease,
ask your doctor first, because your
kidneys decide how much magnesium stays
in your body.
Before we go on to number four, I would
love to know something.
Tell me in the comments, how old are
you? And what would you love to do more
of if your legs felt stronger?
Walking to the park,
gardening,
playing with your grandchildren.
I read the comments, and your answers
help me choose what to talk about next.
And if we have not met before, I am Dr.
Nimra.
On this channel, I talk about health
after 60 in plain, calm language, the
kind of conversation a short appointment
does not always have time for.
If that sounds useful, you are very
welcome to subscribe and stay.
Number four, sesame seeds.
These tiny seeds have been used in
kitchens for thousands of years, and
science is slowly catching up.
Sesame carries two special natural
compounds called sesamin and sesamolin.
You can think of them as little
bodyguards for the inner lining of your
arteries.
Why does that lining matter?
The inside of every artery is coated
with a very thin layer of cells.
When it is healthy, it releases a gas
called nitric oxide, which tells the
artery to relax and open.
With age, that signal gets weaker, and
the arteries become stiffer.
Anything that protects the lining helps
keep that signal alive.
In 2011, a small study in Thailand gave
adults with slightly high blood pressure
about half a teaspoon of black sesame
powder every day for 4 weeks.
Their top blood pressure number came
down by several points, and the
antioxidant protection in their blood
went up.
It was a small study, so I do not want
to promise too much.
But the risk is low, and sesame tastes
wonderful.
Here is the secret with sesame.
The seeds are so small that they often
pass straight through the body whole.
So lightly toast a few tablespoons in a
dry pan for 2 minutes, let them cool,
and grind them.
Keep the powder in a jar in the fridge
and use about 1 Tbsp a day on yogurt,
rice, or vegetables.
If chewing is difficult, tahini, which
is simply sesame paste, works just as
well.
A spoonful stirred into soup or spread
on toast is easy and gentle.
One caution, sesame is a common allergy.
If you have ever reacted to it, please
skip it.
And a tip for all five seeds today.
Seed oils go stale with heat, light, and
air.
Store them in closed jars, ideally in
the fridge.
If a seed smells bitter or sharp, like
old paint, throw it away.
Fresh seeds are cheap, so there is no
need to take chances.
Here is an easy way to use sesame
without any cooking.
Keep a small jar of toasted ground
sesame next to the salt.
Sprinkle a spoonful over your rice, your
salad, your boiled vegetables, or your
eggs.
In many kitchens around the world,
people have done this every day for
generations without ever calling it
medicine.
Number three, chia seeds.
Chia seeds are like tiny sponges.
When they touch water, they swell into a
soft gel.
That gel slows down how fast sugar
enters your blood and it carries plant
omega-3 fats and plenty of fiber.
In 2007,
a team in Toronto gave adults with type
2 diabetes about 3 Tbsp of chia a day
for 12 weeks.
Their top blood pressure number fell by
about six points.
A marker of inflammation in their blood
fell by about 40%.
And a marker of how sticky and stressed
their blood vessel walls were fell by
about 20%.
This was a small study of only 20
people, but the direction was
encouraging.
Why does this matter for your legs?
High blood sugar is rough on small blood
vessels, especially in the feet.
Anything that smooths out sugar spikes
is quietly protecting your circulation.
And chia also brings a little protein,
calcium, and magnesium, which your
muscles need as you age.
Chia also helps the bowels.
That soft gel holds water and keeps
stool soft, which many people over 60
will be glad to hear.
Just remember, like all fiber, it needs
water to do its job.
So, when you add chia, add an extra
glass of water to your day, as well.
Now, one very important safety point.
Never eat dry chia seeds and then drink
water.
They can swell in the throat and cause a
real blockage.
This has sent people to hospital.
Always soak them first.
Here is how. Stir one or two tablespoons
into a cup of milk, water, or yogurt,
and leave it for at least 15 minutes, or
overnight in the fridge.
It becomes a soft pudding.
Add some berries and a pinch of
cinnamon, and breakfast is ready when
you wake up.
If you take a blood thinner, mention
chia to your doctor, because omega-3
fats can slightly affect clotting.
Number two, black seed.
Black seed, also called nigella or
kalonji, has been used in the Middle
East and South Asia for more than 2,000
years.
Some old sayings even call it a cure for
everything except death.
That is an exaggeration, of course.
But modern science has found something
real.
Its main natural compound, called
thymoquinone, calms inflammation inside
the blood vessels.
In 2016, researchers combined the
results of several small trials.
Black seed lowered blood pressure by
about three points on the top number and
about three on the bottom.
Some later reviews also found small
improvements in cholesterol.
These results are modest and the trials
were small, so I will not pretend it is
a miracle.
But it earns its place at number two.
And here is why it is number two and not
number one.
Black seed is stronger than it looks.
It can lower blood pressure and blood
sugar, and it may interact with blood
thinners, blood pressure pills, and
diabetes medicines.
There are also reports of kidney and
liver problems in people taking large
amounts, usually as capsules or oil.
So please speak to your doctor before
you start. Avoid it before surgery and
stay with small food amounts.
If your doctor agrees, start with a
quarter of a teaspoon of the seeds,
crushed and mixed into honey, yogurt, or
food, and do not go above half a
teaspoon a day.
The taste is peppery and a little
bitter, so it goes nicely in bread,
rice, or vegetables.
With seeds, small and steady always wins
over big and sudden.
Many families already cook with black
seed without knowing it.
It is the little black seed sprinkled on
naan bread and on some pickles.
Using it in food like this is the
gentlest way.
The concentrated oils and capsules sold
online are much stronger, and they are
where most of the problems happen.
So food first and capsules only if your
doctor says yes.
And now, number one, flaxseed.
Flaxseed is the seed from that Canadian
study at the beginning.
Think of it as a small brown or golden
seed carrying three gifts at once. Plant
omega-3 fat, lots of fiber, and special
plant compounds called lignans.
Flaxseed has far more lignans than
almost any other food.
Let me tell you more about the study
because I think you deserve the details.
It was called the flax pad trial.
Everyone in it had peripheral artery
disease, which simply means the arteries
that feed the legs have become narrowed.
Half of them ate foods baked with 30 g
of ground flaxseed every day.
The other half ate the same foods
without it.
Nobody knew which group they were in.
After 6 months, the flaxseed group had a
top blood pressure about 10 points lower
and a bottom number about 7 points
lower.
That is similar to what some blood
pressure tablets do.
Their blood levels of plant omega-3 went
up, and the healthy compounds that gut
bacteria make from flax lignans went up
many times over.
Now, I promised to be honest.
That study measured blood pressure.
It did not prove that flaxseed by itself
lets you walk further or clears a
blocked artery.
But lower blood pressure takes years of
strain off every artery in your body,
including the ones in your legs.
That is why it is number one.
Here is the preparation secret I
promised.
Whole flaxseeds have a hard shell like
tiny pebbles.
If you swallow them whole, most of them
pass straight through you, and you get
almost nothing.
You must grind them.
Buy whole flaxseed.
Once a week, grind a small amount in a
coffee grinder or spice grinder.
Keep the powder in a closed jar in the
fridge because the oil spoil quickly
once the seed is broken.
You can also buy it already ground
called milled flaxseed, but keep that in
the fridge, too.
People often ask me, is golden flaxseed
better than brown?
They are almost the same, so choose
whichever you like.
And what about flaxseed oil?
The oil has the omega-3 fat, but it has
lost the fiber and most of the lignans.
In the study, people ate the whole
ground seed.
So, I prefer the ground seed over the
oil.
How much?
The study used 30 g, which is about
three to four level tablespoons.
But please do not start there.
Start with 1 Tbsp a day for the first
week.
Then, if your stomach is happy, go to
two.
Many people stay at two, and that is
fine.
Going too fast can cause bloating and
wind.
And because flax is full of fiber, drink
a glass of water with it.
Fiber without water can make
constipation worse instead of better.
Two more doctor tips that most videos
never mention.
First, flaxseed fiber can slow down how
some tablets are absorbed.
So, take your medicines at least one or
two hours apart from your flaxseed.
Second, if you take a blood thinner,
blood pressure pills, or diabetes
medicines, tell your doctor you are
starting flaxseed, so they can keep an
eye on your numbers.
And if you have trouble swallowing or
have ever had a bowel blockage, ask
first.
Here is a simple morning bowl that many
people love.
Plain yogurt,
2 Tbsp of freshly ground flaxseed,
a small handful of blueberries,
and a pinch of cinnamon.
It takes 2 minutes, it tastes lovely,
and it gives you fiber, omega-3, and
antioxidants in one bowl.
So, let us put the five together.
Pumpkin seeds for magnesium,
sesame for the lining of your arteries,
chia for blood sugar and inflammation,
black seed for blood pressure, but only
with your doctor's blessing,
and flaxseed, the strongest of them all,
ground fresh.
And if walking far is hard for you right
now, start with your chair.
Stand behind a sturdy kitchen chair,
hold the back, and slowly rise up onto
your toes, then lower down.
10 times, three times a day.
It is a small exercise, but it wakes up
that calf pump.
Ask your doctor or physiotherapist about
a proper walking program, too.
In many places, they are free.
So, the seeds help clear the road,
but your legs still have to walk it.
Seeds and walking together are much
stronger than either one alone.
I also want to help you understand your
own legs a little better, because not
every heavy leg is the same.
If your calves ache or cramp when you
walk, and the pain eases a minute or two
after you stop, that often points to
narrowed arteries.
That is the kind of problem today's
seeds and walking can support.
But if your ankles are swollen and puffy
by the evening, and your legs feel heavy
rather than painful, that is more often
the veins, the heart, or sometimes a
medicine.
One common blood pressure tablet, called
amlodipine, is well known for causing
swollen ankles.
Seeds will not fix that, but a
conversation with your doctor might.
And please know the warning signs.
Go to your doctor soon if you have leg
pain even while resting, especially at
night. A sore on your foot or toe that
will not heal, or one foot that is
colder or paler than the other.
And if one leg suddenly becomes cold,
pale, painful, or numb, that is an
emergency.
Call for help straight away.
Seeds are for slow, everyday support.
They are never a reason to wait.
You do not need all five.
In fact, please do not start all five on
the same day.
Pick one, probably flaxseed, and give it
at least 8 to 12 weeks.
Blood vessels change slowly.
Then, if you like, add one more.
If you want a simple week to start with,
here is one idea.
Ground flaxseed in your breakfast every
morning.
Sesame sprinkled on lunch.
And a small handful of pumpkin seeds in
the afternoon instead of biscuits.
Chia pudding a few times a week if you
enjoy it.
And black seed only after you have
spoken with your doctor.
Think of these seeds as small daily
deposits in a savings account for your
blood vessels.
One day makes no difference you can
feel.
But 3 months, 6 months, a year of small
deposits together with walking can add
up to something real.
But now I want to tell you the most
important thing in this whole video.
It is not a seed.
For people with narrowed leg arteries,
the treatment with the strongest
evidence is walking.
Doctors call it supervised exercise
therapy, and in study after study, it
helps people walk further, often much
further, within 3 months.
Here is how it works.
Walk at a comfortable pace until your
calves start to ache, to about a three
or four out of 10.
Then stop, stand and rest until the ache
goes away.
Then walk again.
Keep doing this for about 30 minutes
three times a week.
Over time, the body grows new little
side roads around the narrowed arteries.
Your legs are building their own bypass
slowly, step by step.
You may have heard doctors call the calf
muscle your second heart.
Every time you take a step, the calf
squeezes and pushes blood back up
towards your chest.
When you walk less, that pump gets
weaker, the legs get weaker, and
circulation gets worse.
Walking breaks that circle.
If you smoke, stopping is the single
best gift you can give your leg
arteries.
It is never too late, and your doctor
can help you with it.
Here is your plan for this week.
Tomorrow morning, start with 1 Tbsp of
ground flaxseed in yogurt or porridge
with a glass of water.
Keep your medicines an hour or two apart
from it.
And after one meal each day, take a
short, slow walk, even 10 minutes.
Keep a little notebook by the kitchen
table.
Every 2 weeks, write down how far you
can walk before your legs start to
complain.
Let your own numbers show you what is
working.
Many people are surprised by how much
changes in 3 months.
Your legs are not just muscles and blood
vessels.
They carry you to your garden, to your
friends, to your grandchildren, and out
of your own front door.
They are your freedom.
And it is never too late to look after
them.
I have seen people in their 80s walk
further than they had in years.
One last reminder.
This video is for general education and
is not personal medical advice.
Please never stop, start, or change any
medicine without speaking to your own
doctor or pharmacist.
And if you take blood thinners, blood
pressure, or diabetes medicines,
or have kidney disease, check with your
doctor before adding new seeds to your
daily routine.
Now tell me in the comments, which seed
will you try first?
I will be reading.
And if you would like more simple things
that keep you strong after 60, watch
this next video.
After 60, you do not need more pills.
You need these five things.
It is right here on your screen.
Thank you for watching and take good
care of those precious legs.

records.text:
Once you turn 80, a few things in the body change, whether you like it or not. In this video, Dr Nimra explains the 5 most common changes after 80, why they happen, the gentle things that make each one easier, and the one sign every family should know, because it can save a life.

The 5 changes:
1. You feel the cold more (and how to stay safely warm)
2. Your sleep becomes lighter and earlier (naps, morning light, sleeping pills)
3. Your quick muscles fade, so falls happen differently (3 simple exercises, home safety, what to do if you fall)
4. Your memory becomes slower (normal ageing vs warning signs, and why to check your hearing)
5. Illness looks different (sudden confusion, no fever, and why to call the doctor the same day)

Plus: the good change after 80 that research has found.

💬 Tell me in the comments: which of these changes have you noticed most, in yourself or in someone you love?

👍 If this helped, please share it with someone caring for a parent in their eighties, and subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: Over 70? This Little Seed Helps the Blood Flow in Your Legs

CHAPTERS
0:00 Once you turn 80, things change
0:41 1. You feel the cold more
2:01 How to stay warm safely
3:04 When feeling cold needs a check
4:13 2. Sleep becomes lighter and earlier
5:28 Naps, morning light and regular times
6:19 Sleep problems that are not normal
7:13 3. Quick muscles fade, so falls change
8:51 3 simple balance exercises
9:29 A safer home
9:57 What to do if you fall
11:10 4. Memory: normal or worth checking?
13:08 Why to check your hearing
14:29 5. Illness looks different
15:23 Sudden confusion (delirium)
16:13 Thirst gets weaker after 80
16:59 When to call the doctor the same day
17:30 A yearly medicine review
18:12 The 5 changes together
18:43 The good news about life after 80
20:03 A final reminder

Sources:
Sherrington C et al. Exercise for preventing falls in older people living in the community. Cochrane Review 2019
Lin FR et al. Hearing intervention versus health education control to reduce cognitive decline in older adults with hearing loss (ACHIEVE). Lancet 2023
Inouye SK et al. Delirium in elderly people. Lancet 2014
Ohayon MM et al. Meta-analysis of quantitative sleep parameters from childhood to old age. Sleep 2004
Carstensen LL et al. Emotional experience improves with age. Psychology and Aging 2011
American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria, 2023 update
WHO Housing and Health Guidelines, 2018 (indoor cold)

Important: this video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. Never stop, start or change any medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If someone over 80 suddenly becomes confused, unusually sleepy or unable to walk as before, seek medical help the same day.

#healthafter80 #seniorhealth #healthyaging #elderlycare #healthafter60

subtitles.plaintext:
There is a birthday that quietly changes
things.
Not 60,
not 70, 80. Once you turn 80, a few
things in the body change whether you
like it or not. But here is what I want
you to know from the very start. Every
one of these changes is normal. Every
one of them can be made easier. And the
last one on my list, number five, is the
one every family should know because it
can save a life. Quick note, this is
general education, not personal medical
advice.
Let us begin with number one. Number
one, you feel the cold more. Many people
over 80 tell me the same thing. Everyone
else in the room is comfortable and they
are reaching for a cardigan. Their hands
and feet feel cold even in summer. Their
family says, "But it is warm in here.
This is real and it has simple reasons.
As we get older, we carry a little less
muscle and muscle is the body's heater.
The layer of fat under the skin becomes
thinner, so we lose heat more easily.
And the small blood vessels in the skin
are slower to tighten up when it is
cold, so warmth escapes faster.
There is one more change that surprises
people. After 80, the body is also
slower to notice that it is cold. So,
you can get chilly without really
feeling it until your hands are like
ice.
Now, here is why this matters. Being too
cold for a long time is not just
uncomfortable.
It makes the heart work harder. It
raises blood pressure. And in very cold
homes, it can be dangerous.
Doctors call a dangerous drop in body
temperature hypothermia and older people
can slip into it quietly indoors in
their own homes.
So here is the gentle thing to do. Dress
in layers because several thin layers
keep heat in better than one thick
jumper. Wear warm socks and soft
slippers with a good grip. Keep a light
blanket by your chair. Have warm drinks
and at least one hot meal a day. And try
to keep the room you sit in comfortably
warm, around 18 to 21° C, which is about
64 to 70° F.
Keep the bedroom warm at night, too,
because the early morning hours are when
many older people get coldest. If you
like a hot water bottle or a heating
pad, please be careful. After 80, the
skin is thinner and feels heat less
sharply, so it can burn without warning.
Wrap the bottle in a cover. Never use
boiling water. And do not fall asleep
with a heating pad switched on against
your skin. An electric blanket that
warms the bed before you get in and is
then switched off is a safer choice. And
one doctor's tip. If you suddenly feel
much colder than you used to, along with
tiredness, weight changes, or dry skin,
ask your doctor to check your thyroid
and your blood count. A slow thyroid or
low iron can make you feel cold and both
are easy to treat. So that is the first
change.
You feel the cold more and that is okay.
You simply dress for it. Before we go on
to number two, I would love to know
something. Tell me in the comments how
old is the oldest person you love? your
mother, your father, a grandparent, or
maybe it is you. I read the comments and
I love hearing about the people you care
for. And if we have not met before, I am
Dr. Nimra. On this channel, I talk about
health after 60 in plain calm language,
the kind of conversation a short
appointment does not always have time
for. If that sounds useful, you are very
welcome to subscribe and stay.
Number two, your sleep becomes lighter
and earlier. Many people over 80 say, "I
do not sleep like I used to." They fall
asleep earlier in the evening. They wake
up very early in the morning. They wake
two or three times in the night and then
in the afternoon they doze off in the
chair. Families sometimes worry that
something is wrong. But most of this is
a normal change in how the aging brain
sleeps.
Let me explain.
Sleep has stages.
There is light sleep and there is deep
sleep. The slow heavy sleep that makes
you feel truly rested. As we get older,
we spend much less time in that deep
sleep. Sleep becomes lighter. So small
noises, a full bladder or an aching
joint wake us more easily. At the same
time, the body clock moves earlier. The
brain releases its sleepy signal sooner
in the evening. So you feel sleepy at 8
or 9:00 and you wake at 4 or 5. That is
not a disease. It is your clock
shifting.
So here is the gentle thing to do.
First, do not fight a short nap. A nap
of 20 to 30 minutes before about 3:00 in
the afternoon can leave you refreshed. A
long nap late in the day, though, steals
sleep from the night. Second, get
morning daylight.
Sit by a bright window or step outside
for a little while after breakfast.
Morning light is the strongest signal
for setting your body clock, and it
helps you sleep better at night.
Third, keep regular times.
Go to bed and get up at roughly the same
time each day. And if you wake at night
and cannot sleep, do not lie there
worrying. Get up, sit somewhere calm
with a dim light, and go back to bed
when you feel sleepy.
Now, two things that are not normal and
should be checked. If you snore loudly
and someone notices you stop breathing
or gasp in your sleep, that can be sleep
apnnea. And treating it can help the
heart and the memory. And if you feel
very sleepy all day, every day, even
after a good night, please tell your
doctor because some medicines and some
illnesses can cause that. And please be
careful with sleeping pills after 80.
Many of them make people unsteady at
night which leads to falls and they can
cause confusion the next day. Never stop
one suddenly on your own but do ask your
doctor whether you still need it. So
that is the second change.
Your sleep becomes lighter and earlier
and that is okay. You simply work with
your new rhythm instead of against it.
Number three, your quick muscles fade,
so falls happen differently. Everyone
knows that we lose some muscle as we get
older. But here is something most people
are never told. We have two kinds of
muscle fibers.
Slow fibers for steady things like
walking and standing, and fast fibers
for quick movements like catching
yourself when you trip. After 80, we
lose the fast fibers faster than the
slow ones. That is why many people over
80 can still walk to the shops or work
in the garden for an hour, but then they
fall from something very small, catching
a toe on the edge of a rug, turning
around quickly when someone calls their
name, stepping off a curb, their
strength for steady work is still there.
It is the quick catching reflex that has
faded. There is a second reason for
falls after 80. When you stand up
quickly, the blood pressure can drop for
a moment, especially if you take blood
pressure pills or water pills or have
not had enough to drink. You feel laded
and down you go. Now, here is the
hopeful part. This is one of the changes
we can do the most about. When
researchers combined many studies,
exercise programs that train balance and
strength reduced falls in older people
by about a quarter. And it is never too
late. People in their 80s and 90s get
stronger when they train. So here is the
gentle thing to do. Practice standing up
from a firm chair without using your
hands slowly 5 to 10 times a few times a
day. Hold the kitchen counter and rise
up onto your toes. Then lower down. Hold
the counter and stand with one foot in
front of the other like on a tight trope
for 10 seconds.
These simple exercises train the very
reflexes that catch you. If you can, ask
your doctor about a physiootherapist or
a falls prevention class. In many
places, these are free and they are
excellent. Then make your home kinder to
your feet. Remove loose rugs or tape
them down. Keep the floors clear of
wires and clutter. Put a night light
between the bed and the bathroom.
Wear shoes or slippers that fit well and
have a good grip, not loose backless
slippers. And when you get out of bed,
sit on the edge for a moment first. Move
your feet and then stand up slowly. And
one more thing that very few people
practice. What to do if you do fall?
First, stay still for a moment and take
a few slow breaths.
Check whether anything hurts badly. If
you are hurt or you cannot get up, do
not struggle. Call for help and try to
keep warm with anything nearby, a
cushion or a blanket while you wait. If
you are not hurt, roll onto your side,
then onto your hands and knees. Crawl to
a sturdy chair. Put your hands on the
seat. Bring one foot forward and push up
slowly. Then turn and sit down. If you
live alone, please think about a
personal alarm, a pendant, or a watch
you press to call for help. Or simply
keep a mobile phone in your pocket at
all times, not on the table across the
room.
Lying on the floor for hours after a
fall is one of the most dangerous things
that can happen after 80. A small button
can prevent it. So that is the third
change.
Your quick muscles fade and that is
okay. You can train them and make your
home safer starting today. Number four,
your memory changes and not every change
is a warning sign. Many people over 80
notice this. You can remember your
wedding day, your first house, and your
old school friends in perfect detail.
But the name of the new neighbor or why
you walked into the kitchen slips away.
This worries families a great deal. They
wonder, "Is this dementia?"
So, let me explain what is normal and
what is worth checking. With age, the
brain becomes slower at storing new
information and slower at finding names
and words. That is normal. Old memories
that have been told and retold over many
years are stored very deeply, so they
stay clear. Newer, less important things
are stored more lightly.
So, these things are usually normal
aging.
Taking longer to remember a name, but
getting there in the end. Walking into a
room and forgetting why. Needing lists
and notes to remember appointments.
Occasionally misplacing your glasses.
But these things are worth talking to a
doctor about. Getting lost in a place
you know well. Struggling with things
you used to manage easily, like paying
bills, cooking a familiar meal, or using
the phone. Repeating the same question
many times in a short while.
big changes in personality like becoming
suspicious, withdrawn or unusually angry
or poor judgment that is not like the
person at all. The key difference is
this. Normal aging makes memory slower.
Dementia starts to take away the ability
to manage everyday life. If you are not
sure, a doctor can do a simple memory
check and there is no shame in asking.
And here is one of the most important
things I can tell you about memory after
80. Check your hearing. When hearing is
poor, the brain works so hard to catch
the words that it has less energy left
to remember them. People also stop
joining in conversations and loneliness
is hard on the brain. A large study
found that for older people at higher
risk, getting hearing aids was linked
with slower decline in thinking over 3
years. So, if you are saying pardon a
lot or turning the television up loud,
please get your hearing tested. The
gentle things that help memory are
simple. Stay connected with people,
talk, laugh, and visit. Keep learning
whether it is a new recipe, a puzzle, a
hobby, or a few words of a new language.
Keep moving because walking helps the
brain as much as the heart. Sleep well
and use notes, calendars, and a fixed
place for keys and glasses without any
embarrassment.
These are not signs of weakness.
They are smart tools.
So that is the fourth change.
your memory becomes slower and that is
okay.
Slower is not the same as lost.
And now number five, the one I said can
save a life. Illness starts to look
different. When a younger person has an
infection, the signs are usually
obvious.
A high fever, pain, coughing.
They feel ill and they know it. After
80, illness often does not follow the
textbook.
The immune system reacts more quietly.
Someone over 80 can have a chest
infection or a bladder infection with no
fever at all and no clear pain. Instead,
the only sign may be that the person
suddenly is not themselves.
They become confused or sleepy or
restless.
They stop eating. They have a fall or
suddenly cannot walk as well as
yesterday.
They become incontinent when they were
not before. Doctors have a name for
sudden confusion like this. It is called
delirium.
And here is the most important sentence
in this whole video. Sudden confusion in
an older person is a medical problem
until proven otherwise.
It is not just old age and it is not
dementia arriving overnight.
The most common causes are things that
can be treated. A urinary infection,
a chest infection,
not drinking enough, constipation,
pain, a new medicine, or a change in
dose, low blood sugar, or low salt
levels in the blood. Once the cause is
found and treated, the confusion very
often clears.
Let me say a word about not drinking
enough because it is so common after 80.
The feeling of thirst becomes weaker
with age. Many older people are a little
dry without ever feeling thirsty.
Some also drink less on purpose so they
do not have to get up to the toilet at
night. But a body that is short of water
becomes dizzy, constipated, and confused
much more easily. So do not wait for
thirst. Keep a glass or a bottle where
you can see it. Take small sips through
the day and drink more of it in the
morning and early afternoon so the
nights stay quieter. And if your doctor
has limited your fluids because of your
heart or your kidneys, follow their
advice.
So here is the gentle but very important
thing to do if someone over 80 suddenly
changes over hours or a few days
becoming confused, unusually sleepy,
agitated or unable to walk as well.
Please call the doctor that same day. Do
not wait to see if it passes
and tell the doctor clearly this is not
normal for her or this is not normal for
him. You know the person best and
doctors need to hear that. And there is
one more part to this change.
After 80, the kidneys and the liver
clear medicines more slowly. So a dose
that was perfect at 70 can be too strong
at 85.
That is why a yearly medicine review is
so important.
Bring every tablet, cream, drop, and
supplement to your doctor or pharmacist
and ask, "Do I still need all of these?
And are the doses still right for me?"
Never stop anything on your own, but do
ask. So that is the fifth change.
Illness looks different and that is okay
as long as you know what to look for. So
let us put the five together. After 80,
you feel the cold more, so you dress in
layers and keep warm. Your sleep becomes
lighter and earlier, so you take short
naps and get morning light. Your quick
muscles fade, so you train your balance
and make your home safer. Your memory
becomes slower, so you check your
hearing and stay connected. An illness
looks different, so a sudden change
means a call to the doctor that same
day. But before I finish, I want to tell
you about one more change after 80. And
this one is good news.
Researchers who study aging have found
something lovely. On average, many
people become emotionally happier and
calmer as they get older. Older people
tend to focus more on what matters,
worry less about small things, and
remember the good moments more than the
bad ones.
Many people in their 80s say they feel
more content than they did in their busy
40s. This does not happen to everyone
and loneliness and loss are real. But it
tells us something important.
Turning 80 is not only about what we
lose. It can also be a time of
gratitude, of deep friendships, of time
with grandchildren, of sharing what you
know, and of finally doing things at
your own pace.
So, here is my wish for you or for the
person you love who is 80 or older. Keep
warm, rest well, keep moving,
stay connected, and know the signs that
mean it is time to call the doctor. Do
those five things and the 80s can be
some of the most peaceful, meaningful
years of all.
One last reminder,
this video is for general education and
is not personal medical advice.
Please never stop, start or change any
medicine without speaking to your own
doctor or pharmacist.
And if someone over 80 suddenly becomes
confused or unwell, please seek medical
help the same day.
Now tell me in the comments which of
these five changes have you noticed most
in yourself or in someone you love. I
will be reading. And if you would like
to keep your legs strong and steady
after 70, watch this next video about
the little seed that helps the blood
flow in your legs. It is right here on
your screen. Thank you for watching and
please share this with someone who is
caring for a parent in their 80s. Take
good care of yourself.

subtitles.plaintext:
If you are between 60 and 80, and you
sleep during the day, here is the first
thing to know.
The nap itself is almost never the
problem.
What matters is how long you sleep,
when, and why your body is asking for
it.
Today, I will show you six things your
daytime sleep can tell you, and at the
end, a simple recipe for the perfect
nap.
Quick note, this is general education,
not personal medical advice.
Number one, a short early nap is good
for you.
A daytime nap can be one of the kindest
things you do for your brain.
For many years, people felt guilty about
napping.
A nap was seen as lazy, or as a sign
that you were getting old.
But, the research tells a kinder story.
When you are awake, a natural chemical
called adenosine slowly builds up in
your brain.
You can think of it as sleep pressure.
The longer you are awake, the heavier it
gets.
A short nap lowers that pressure, a
little like letting some steam out of a
pressure cooker.
You wake up lighter.
There is also a natural dip in alertness
in the early afternoon, usually
somewhere between 1:00 and 3:00.
This is not just because of lunch.
Your body clock is built that way.
That is why so many cultures around the
world have a rest after the midday meal.
What happens in your brain during a
short nap?
A NASA study on airline pilots found
that a nap of about 26 minutes improved
their performance by about a third, and
their alertness by about half.
Those were younger adults, but the same
principle holds for us.
In older adults, a study from China
followed more than 2,000 people over 60.
Those who took a regular afternoon nap
did better on tests of memory,
orientation, and word finding than those
who did not nap.
And a large study from the UK Biobank,
which used genetic data to look at this
question, found that people who were
naturally inclined to nap had slightly
larger total brain volume.
The difference was small, and that study
cannot prove a nap protects your brain.
But it is reassuring.
A habit of napping does not seem to harm
the brain.
So, what is a good nap after 60?
Short, about 20 to 30 minutes.
Early, finished before about 3:00 in the
afternoon.
And regular, at roughly the same time
each day.
Why short?
Because after about 30 minutes, the
brain starts to slide into deep sleep.
If you wake up from deep sleep, you feel
heavy, confused, and grumpy, sometimes
for half an hour.
Doctors call this sleep inertia.
A short nap gives you the benefit
without the fog.
And why early?
Because a late nap uses up the sleep
pressure you need for the night.
A nap at 5:00 in the evening is a little
like eating a big snack just before
dinner.
You will not be hungry when the meal
comes.
Before we go on, tell me in the
comments, do you take a nap during the
day, and how long is it usually?
10 minutes, half an hour, or longer?
I read the comments, and your answers
help me choose what to explain next.
And if we have not met before, I am Dr.
Nimra.
On this channel, I talk about health
after 60 in plain, calm language, the
kind of conversation a short appointment
does not always have time for.
If that sounds useful, you are very
welcome to subscribe.
Number two, a nap that keeps getting
longer is a message.
Here is the other side of the story, and
it is important.
Several large studies have looked at
older people who nap for more than an
hour a day.
In a review that pulled studies from
many countries, naps longer than an hour
were linked with a higher risk of heart
disease and a higher risk of death.
Naps shorter than about 40 minutes were
not linked with any extra risk.
Then there is a study I find very
interesting.
Researchers in Chicago followed more
than 1,400 older adults for up to 14
years.
Instead of asking people how much they
napped, which most of us guess badly,
they gave everyone a small watch-like
device that measured their sleep.
And they did this every year.
Here is what they found.
In people whose memories stayed healthy,
daytime napping slowly increased with
age, by about 11 minutes a year.
That is normal.
But in people who went on to develop
memory problems, napping increased
faster.
After mild memory problems started, it
went up by about 24 minutes a year.
And after a diagnosis of Alzheimer's
disease, by about 68 minutes a year.
People who napped more than an hour a
day had about a 40% higher risk of
developing Alzheimer's disease in later
years than those who napped less than an
hour.
Now, please hear this carefully, because
it is easy to misunderstand.
This does not mean that a long nap
causes dementia.
It is much more likely the other way
around.
The parts of the brain that keep us
awake during the day can be affected
very early in some brain diseases, years
before memory problems are obvious.
So, a nap that keeps growing may be an
early messenger, not the cause.
And brain changes are only one possible
reason.
A long nap is just as often caused by
poor sleep at night, a medicine, low
mood, or a heart, lung, or thyroid
problem.
Many of these are very treatable.
So, the message is not, "Stop napping."
The message is this,
"If your naps have been getting longer
over the last year, or if you sleep more
than an hour or two during the day and
still feel tired, that is worth a
conversation with your doctor."
Not with panic,
with curiosity.
Your body is telling you something, and
the rest of this video will help you
work out what.
Here is a simple way to notice the
change.
For 2 weeks, keep a small nap diary.
A notebook by your chair is enough.
Each day, write down what time you lay
down, roughly how long you slept, and
how you felt when you woke up, fresh or
heavy.
Also, write what time you went to bed
the night before, and how many times you
woke up.
It takes 1 minute a day.
Then, when you see your doctor, you are
not guessing.
You can say, "I nap about an hour and a
half every afternoon, and I still feel
tired."
That one sentence helps your doctor far
more than, "I am always tired."
And if someone lives with you, ask them,
too.
They often notice changes before we do.
Number three, your night sleep changes
after 60, and the day pays for it.
Many people believe that older adults
need less sleep.
That is not quite true.
Most people over 65 still need about 7
to 8 hours.
What changes is how well we sleep.
There are three big changes.
First, deep sleep becomes shorter.
Deep sleep is the most restful part of
the night.
It is when the body repairs itself and
the brain clears out waste.
With age, the amount of deep sleep
falls, so the same 7 hours in bed feel
less refreshing.
Second, sleep becomes lighter and more
broken.
We wake more often during the night,
sometimes without remembering it.
A noise, a pain in the hip, a full
bladder, a hot flash, a partner who
snores.
Each small waking cuts the night into
pieces.
Third, the body clock moves earlier.
Many people over 60 feel sleepy at 9:00
in the evening and wake at 4:00 or 5:00
in the morning.
If you fight that, staying up late out
of habit, but still waking early, you
lose sleep every night without noticing.
Put these three together and it is no
surprise that the body asks for sleep in
the afternoon.
In many people, a growing daytime nap is
simply the body collecting the sleep it
did not get at night.
So, the first question to ask is not,
"Why am I sleepy in the day?"
It is, "How am I really sleeping at
night?"
Here are the gentle things that help
most.
Get up at the same time every morning,
even on weekends.
This is the anchor that sets your body
clock.
Get daylight into your eyes in the
morning, ideally 20 to 30 minutes
outside or by a bright window.
Morning light tells your brain when the
day has started and that helps you feel
sleepy at the right time at night.
Move your body during the day, even a
walk after lunch.
Keep tea, coffee, and cola to the
morning because caffeine can stay in an
older body for 6 hours or more.
And if you wake at night to pass urine,
try having most of your drinks earlier
in the day rather than drinking less
overall.
If you have heart or kidney problems,
follow your own doctor's advice on
fluids.
And one more thing.
If you lie in bed awake for long
periods, it is better to get up, sit in
another room with a dim light, and come
back when you feel sleepy.
The bed should mean sleep to your brain,
not worry.
Number four, snoring, gasping, and
morning headaches can point to sleep
apnea.
This is the cause of daytime sleepiness
that I most want you to know about
because it is very common after 60. It
is easy to miss, and it is very
treatable.
Sleep apnea means that during sleep, the
airway in the throat relaxes and
narrows, so breathing becomes shallow or
stops for a few seconds at a time.
When oxygen drops, the brain wakes you
up just enough to take a breath.
You usually do not remember these
wakings.
But they can happen dozens of times an
hour all night long.
So you may spend 8 hours in bed and
still wake up as if you never slept
properly.
And then, in the afternoon, you fall
asleep in your chair in front of the
television or even while reading.
Studies that tested sleep in older
people at home found that a large share
of people over 60 have some degree of
sleep apnea, in some studies more than a
third.
Most of them did not know.
Here are the signs to look for.
Loud snoring, especially if it stops and
starts.
A partner who notices you stop breathing
or gasp or choke in your sleep.
Waking with a dry mouth or a headache.
Getting up often at night to pass urine.
Falling asleep easily during the day in
quiet moments.
And high blood pressure that is hard to
control.
Why does it matter?
Because untreated sleep apnea strains
the heart.
It is linked with high blood pressure,
an irregular heartbeat called atrial
fibrillation, stroke, and problems with
memory and concentration.
And people with it are more likely to
have accidents, including when driving.
The good news is that the test is
simple.
Often it can be done at home with a
small device you wear for a night.
And the treatments work.
The most common is a machine called
CPAP, which gently blows air through a
mask to keep the airway open.
Many people find their daytime
sleepiness clearly improves after
starting it.
For milder cases, a mouth guard made by
a dentist, losing some weight, or
sleeping on your side can help.
So, if you snore loudly and feel sleepy
in the day, please do not accept it as
old age.
Ask your doctor about a sleep test.
Number five. Some medicines make you
sleepy during the day.
This one is easy to overlook because the
sleepiness creeps in slowly and nobody
connects it to the tablets.
After 60, the liver and kidneys clear
many medicines more slowly.
So, a medicine that was fine at 50 may
linger longer at 70.
And when you take several medicines,
their sleepy effects can add up.
Here are some of the common ones.
Allergy tablets of the older kind, which
make you drowsy, and some cough and cold
medicines.
Many nighttime sleep aids bought at the
pharmacy contain these same drowsy
antihistamines.
Sleeping tablets and anxiety tablets,
especially the older group called
benzodiazepines.
Their effect can carry over into the
next day, and in older people they are
linked with falls and confusion.
Some painkillers, especially the
stronger ones related to codeine and
morphine, and nerve pain medicines such
as gabapentin and pregabalin.
Some antidepressants, some medicines for
an overactive bladder, some muscle
relaxants, and some blood pressure
medicines can also cause tiredness in
some people.
Here is the important part.
Please do not stop any of these on your
own.
Some of them, like sleeping tablets and
nerve pain medicines, must be reduced
slowly and safely.
Instead, bring all your tablets,
including the ones you buy without a
prescription, to your doctor or
pharmacist, and ask one simple question.
Could any of these be making me sleepy
during the day?
Often a dose can be lowered, the timing
can be changed to the evening, or a
gentler medicine can be used.
Number six, when daytime sleepiness is a
sign of something more.
Sometimes sleepiness in the day is a
symptom of a medical problem that has
nothing to do with sleep at all.
Here are some of the common ones a
doctor will think about.
Low thyroid, which can bring tiredness,
feeling cold, weight gain, and
constipation.
Anemia, a low blood count, often from
low iron or low vitamin B12.
It makes you tired and breathless on the
stairs.
Low mood or depression.
In older people, depression often shows
up not as sadness, but as tiredness,
sleeping more, and losing interest in
things you used to enjoy.
Diabetes, when blood sugar runs too
high, or sometimes too low.
Heart failure and lung problems, where
the body is working harder just to get
enough oxygen.
Kidney problems and not drinking enough
water, both of which can make you feel
drained.
Most of these can be found with a simple
examination and a few blood tests.
And most of them can be treated.
So, if you are sleeping much more than
you used to, a checkup is a wise step,
not a fuss.
Now, there is one situation that is
different and I want you to remember it.
If sleepiness comes on suddenly, over
hours or a few days, especially with
confusion, that is not a nap problem.
In older people,
a sudden change like this can be the
first sign of an infection, such as a
urine or chest infection, or of a side
effect from a new medicine.
It needs to be checked by a doctor the
same day.
And if sudden drowsiness comes with
weakness on one side of the body,
a drooping face, slurred speech, or
difficulty finding words, that may be a
stroke.
Call an ambulance straight away.
Do not wait to see if it passes.
Now, as I promised, here is the recipe
for the perfect nap after 60.
Step one, choose your time.
Early afternoon, after lunch, and finish
before about 3:00.
Try to make it roughly the same time
each day.
Step two, keep it short.
20 to 30 minutes.
Set a gentle alarm on your phone or a
kitchen timer, so you do not have to
worry about oversleeping.
Step three, choose your place.
Many people sleep better and wake more
easily in a comfortable armchair or a
recliner than in bed.
Lying fully in bed with the curtains
closed tells your body it is night time
and the nap tends to grow.
Step four, wake up gently.
When the alarm rings, do not jump up.
Sit on the edge of the bed or chair for
a minute first.
Just like after a warm shower, blood
pressure can dip when you stand after
lying down and the first steps after a
nap are when many people feel unsteady.
Then stand slowly and go towards
daylight.
Open the curtains, step outside, or
drink a glass of water.
Step five, if you cannot fall asleep,
that is fine.
Just resting quietly with your eyes
closed for 20 minutes still lowers your
heart rate and gives your mind a break.
And who should be more careful with
naps?
If you have trouble sleeping at night,
insomnia, it is often better to skip the
nap for a few weeks
or keep it very short so that all your
sleep pressure is saved for the night.
Once your nights improve, you can bring
back a short early nap.
Let us put the six things together.
One, a short early nap of 20 to 30
minutes before 3:00 is good for you.
Two, a nap that keeps getting longer or
more than an hour a day is a message
worth taking to your doctor calmly.
Three, your night sleep changes after
60, so protect it with a fixed wake up
time, morning light, daytime movement,
and caffeine only in the morning.
Four, loud snoring and daytime
sleepiness can be sleep apnea, which is
common and very treatable.
Five, some medicines make you sleepy, so
ask your doctor or pharmacist to review
them and never stop them on your own.
Six, sleepiness can be a sign of low
thyroid, anemia, low mood, diabetes,
heart, lung, or kidney problems.
And sudden sleepiness with confusion
needs a doctor the same day.
If you remember just one sentence from
today, let it be this. After 60, a short
nap is a gift, but a nap that keeps
growing is a message.
So, watch your naps the way you watch
your blood pressure.
Not with fear, just with attention.
If you notice a change, tell your
doctor.
That small conversation can find
something treatable early.
One last reminder.
This video is for general education and
is not personal medical advice.
Please never stop, start, or change any
medicine without speaking to your own
doctor or pharmacist.
If sleepiness comes on suddenly with
confusion, see a doctor the same day.
And if it comes with weakness, a
drooping face, or slurred speech, call
an ambulance at once.
Now, tell me in the comments, what time
do you usually take your nap and how
long is it?
I will be reading.
And because the minutes after waking
from a nap and the minutes after a warm
shower are both times when blood
pressure dips and falls happen, watch
this next video where I explain six
small changes after your shower that
protect you from dizziness, dry skin,
and falls.
It is right here on your screen.
Thank you for watching. Please share
this with someone you love who naps
every afternoon and take good care of
yourself.

records.channelDescription:
Welcome to Dr Nimra | Health After 60 🩺

I'm Dr Nimra, this channel exists for one reason: to explain, in plain and simple language, what your 15-minute doctor's visit doesn't have time to explain.

Every week I break down what really happens inside your body after 60, and what you can do about it:
💊 Medicines: what your pills really do, side effects, and dangerous combinations
🥗 Food & diet: what to eat, what to limit, and why
🚶 Exercise & mobility: simple movement that keeps you strong and independent
😴 Sleep, bathroom and daily habits: the small things that add up
❤️ Heart, blood pressure, blood sugar, kidneys, bones, brain and eyes

⚠️ Disclaimer
The content on this channel is for general education and information only. It is not personal medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Never start, stop or change a medicine without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have a medical emergency, call your local emergency number.

records.text:
Constipated after 60, even though you eat well and drink water? The cause may be in your pill box. In this video, Dr Nimra explains 10 common medicines that can slow your bowels, including one blood pressure tablet that surprises most people, hidden codeine, iron, calcium, bladder tablets, night-time sleep aids and more.

You will also learn about the dangerous combination that makes constipation much worse, the one rule you must never break, and 5 simple questions to take to your doctor or pharmacist.

💬 Tell me in the comments: how many tablets do you take every day?

👍 If this helped, please share it with someone who takes a lot of tablets. Subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: Laxatives After 60: Which Are Safe and Which Are Risky? A Doctor Ranks 10

CHAPTERS
0:00 Constipated? Check your pill box
1:22 1. Blood pressure tablets (verapamil and others)
2:33 How many tablets do you take?
3:05 Why older people are hit harder
3:47 2. Opioid painkillers and hidden codeine
5:39 3. Iron tablets (and every-other-day dosing)
6:55 4. Calcium and aluminium antacids
7:36 What "anticholinergic" means
8:18 5. Overactive bladder tablets
8:56 6. Allergy and night-time sleep tablets
9:40 7. Amitriptyline and tricyclics
10:24 The dangerous combination
11:46 The one rule: never stop on your own
12:29 3 myths
14:21 8. Water tablets
14:53 9. Anti-sickness tablets (ondansetron)
15:26 10. Antipsychotics and Parkinson's medicines
16:08 A few others
16:56 3 questions I am often asked
18:22 When to see a doctor urgently
19:05 For carers: the medicine bag review
19:56 What you can do today
20:59 5 questions for your doctor
21:47 Recap
22:38 An honest note

This video is general education, not personal medical advice. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine without talking to your doctor first.

Sources:
Verapamil prescribing information (adverse reactions: constipation 7.3 to 8.8 percent vs 0.9 percent placebo)
Tolkien et al., PLoS One 2015: ferrous sulfate and gastrointestinal side effects (43 trials, 6,831 adults)
Stoffel et al., Lancet Haematology 2017: alternate-day iron dosing and absorption
FDA Drug Safety Communication, 28 January 2020: clozapine and serious bowel complications
Ondansetron prescribing information (constipation 6 to 9 percent vs under 1 percent placebo)
Polypharmacy in US physician offices, 2009 to 2016 (National Ambulatory Medical Care Survey)
American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria (anticholinergic medicines)

subtitles.plaintext:
A man in his 70s once told me, "Doctor,
I have always been regular, every
morning like a clock.
But for weeks now, nothing works.
I eat my fruit. I drink my water. I even
bought a laxative."
So, I asked him one question.
Did anything change in your medicines?
He thought for a moment.
"Only one small thing.
My blood pressure tablet was changed."
And that was the answer.
Many people over 60 think constipation
is just part of getting older.
Sometimes it is.
But very often, the real cause is
sitting in your pill box.
Today, I will walk you through 10 common
medicines that can slow down your
bowels.
Some of them you would never suspect.
I will also tell you about the dangerous
combination that makes constipation much
worse. The one rule you must never break
when you find the cause. And at the end,
five simple questions to take to your
doctor or pharmacist.
Quick note before we start. This is
general education, not personal medical
advice.
Please do not stop any medicine because
of this video.
Let me start with the one that surprises
people the most.
Number one, blood pressure tablets in a
group called calcium channel blockers.
The strongest one for constipation is
verapamil.
In the trials listed on its label, about
7 to 9 in every 100 people taking
verapamil had constipation.
With a dummy pill, it was fewer than one
in a hundred.
Diltiazem, which is in the same family,
can do it, too.
Amlodipine and nifedipine are in a
slightly different branch of the family,
and they cause it less often, but it can
still happen.
How does a blood pressure tablet block
your bowels?
These medicines relax muscle.
That is how they lower blood pressure by
relaxing the muscle in your blood
vessels.
But your bowel is also a tube made of
muscle.
When that muscle relaxes too much, the
squeezing waves that push stool along
become weaker and slower.
So if your constipation started a few
weeks after a new blood pressure tablet
or after a dose went up, tell your
doctor.
There are many other blood pressure
medicines and switching is often simple.
Before we go on, I would love to know
something.
How many tablets do you take every day?
Just write the number in the comments.
1 5 10, it does not matter.
You will see in a minute why that number
is so important.
And if we have not met before, I am Dr.
Nimra.
On this channel I talk about health
after 60 in plain, calm language.
If that is useful to you, you are very
welcome to subscribe.
So why are older people hit harder by
this?
There are three reasons.
First, the bowel naturally slows down a
little with age.
Second, many of us move less and drink
less than we used to.
And third, and this is the big one, we
take more medicines.
A large study of doctor visits in
America found that more than a third of
people over 65 were taking six or more
medicines.
Each one might only slow the bowel a
little.
But add them together and a little
becomes a lot.
Keep that idea in mind because it is the
dangerous combination I promised to
explain.
Number two, strong painkillers called
opioids.
This includes codeine, tramadol,
morphine, or oxycodone, and fentanyl
patches.
Opioids are the most powerful cause of
medicine-related constipation.
Somewhere between about half and nine in
every 10 people who take them regularly
become constipated.
They slow the bowel down, make it absorb
more water from the stool, and tighten
the muscle at the exit.
And here is something very important.
With most opioid side effects, like
sleepiness or feeling sick, your body
gets used to them after a while.
But with constipation, it does not.
It usually stays for as long as you take
the medicine.
That is why many doctors now start a
laxative on the same day as a regular
opioid.
Usually senna or a powder called
polyethylene glycol.
Two things do not help much here.
The stool softener docusate did no
better than a dummy pill in trials for
opioid constipation.
And fiber alone can make things worse if
you are not drinking a lot.
A good target is a soft bowel movement
without straining, at least every other
day.
If you have not been for 2 days while
taking an opioid, tell your doctor or
nurse.
And if ordinary laxatives are not
enough, there are prescription medicines
made specially for this.
They block the effect of the opioid on
the gut without taking away the pain
relief.
Also, watch out for hidden codeine.
It is inside some cough syrups and in
combination painkillers, like
paracetamol with codeine.
Many people take these for weeks without
realizing they are taking an opioid.
Number three, iron tablets.
Many older people are low in iron, so
iron tablets are very common.
But, the most widely used one, ferrous
sulfate, is hard on the gut.
A large review of 43 trials with almost
7,000 adults found that people taking
ferrous sulfate had more than double the
odds of stomach and bowel side effects
compared with a dummy pill.
That includes constipation, dark hard
stools, tummy pain, and feeling sick.
Here is a newer idea worth asking about.
Iron is absorbed best when it is not
taken too often.
When you take iron, your body releases a
hormone that blocks the next dose from
being absorbed well for about a day.
In one study, taking iron every other
day led to about a third more iron being
absorbed from each dose than taking it
every day.
That study was in younger women, not
older people.
But, many doctors now suggest every
other day dosing, which may mean fewer
tablets and less constipation.
Please do not change your dose yourself.
Ask your doctor whether it is right for
you.
Number four, calcium tablets and some
antacids.
Calcium supplements, especially calcium
carbonate, are a well-known cause of
constipation in some people.
Not everyone, but enough that it is
worth checking.
If calcium bothers you, ask your doctor
whether you can take a smaller dose.
Split it across the day, or get more
calcium from food like milk, yogurt, and
cheese.
And some indigestion remedies contain
aluminum.
Aluminum antacids are constipating, too.
Many people take them every day for
heartburn without thinking of them as a
medicine at all.
Now, let me explain a word that connects
the next few medicines.
The word is anticholinergic.
Your body uses a natural messenger
called acetylcholine to tell your bowel
muscles to squeeze.
Anticholinergic medicines block that
messenger.
Think of it as pressing the brake on
your bowel.
They also cause a dry mouth, blurred
vision, trouble passing urine, and in
older people, confusion and falls.
Many of them are on a famous list called
the Beers Criteria.
That is a list from the American
Geriatrics Society of medicines that
older people should usually avoid or use
with great care.
Number five, tablets for an overactive
bladder.
These include oxybutynin, tolterodine,
solifenacin, and fesoterodine.
They work by calming the bladder muscle.
But they calm the bowel muscle at the
same time.
Constipation is one of their most common
side effects, along with a dry mouth.
Oxybutynin, in particular, is one
doctors try to avoid in older people
because it can also affect memory.
If you need help with your bladder, ask
whether a different type of medicine or
bladder training might work for you.
Number six, old-style allergy and sleep
tablets.
These include diphenhydramine,
chlorphenamine, hydroxyzine, and
doxylamine.
And here is the hidden trap.
Many nighttime painkillers and sleep
aids sold in shops contain
diphenhydramine or doxylamine.
The box may say night or PM, and many
people take one every night for years.
They are strongly anticholinergic.
Newer allergy tablets like cetirizine,

I'm Dr Nimra, this channel exists for one reason: to explain, in plain and simple language, what your 15-minute doctor's visit doesn't have time to explain.

records.text:
Do your hands shake when you lift a cup of tea, sign your name or eat soup? After 60, the most common cause is NOT Parkinson's. In this video, Dr Nimra explains essential tremor and how it differs from a Parkinson's tremor, with 3 simple tests you can do at your kitchen table (hands in your lap vs arms out, the spiral and handwriting test, and the cup of water test). You'll also learn the 6 everyday things that make hands shake (caffeine, stress and poor sleep, low blood sugar, an overactive thyroid, alcohol, and common medicines like the blue asthma inhaler and some anti-sickness tablets), the warning signs that mean you should see a doctor soon, the treatments available, and 8 practical tricks for eating, drinking and writing.

💬 Tell me in the comments: your age, and which test you tried today: the lap test, the spiral, or the cup.

👍 If this helped, please share it with someone who has shaky hands, and subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The rattling teacup
2:02 What a tremor is: essential tremor, the most common cause
4:51 How Parkinson's tremor is different
6:22 Test 1: hands in your lap vs arms out
7:06 Test 2: the spiral and your handwriting
8:05 Test 3: the cup of water
9:07 6 everyday causes of shaking
11:18 Medicines that can cause tremor
12:46 Warning signs: when to see a doctor
13:40 What the doctor will check
14:24 Treatments for essential tremor
15:57 8 practical tricks for daily life
17:50 Recap

Sources:
Louis ED, McCreary M. How common is the most common adult movement disorder? Update on the worldwide prevalence of essential tremor. Tremor Other Hyperkinet Mov 2021
Bhatia KP et al. Consensus statement on the classification of tremors (International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society). Mov Disord 2018
Ferreira JJ et al. MDS evidence-based review of treatments for essential tremor. Mov Disord 2019
Morgan JC, Sethi KD. Drug-induced tremors. Lancet Neurol 2005
NICE guideline NG71: Parkinson's disease in adults

Important: this video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. Only a doctor who examines you can diagnose the cause of a tremor. Never stop a medicine on your own. Sudden weakness, a drooping face, slurred speech or sudden confusion: call an ambulance.

are propranolol, which is a beta
blocker, and primidone.
They help many people, but not everyone,
and both need [music] care after 60.
Propranolol can slow the heart and is
not suitable for some people [music]
with asthma.
Primidone can cause drowsiness and
unsteadiness at first, so doctors
[music] start with a very small dose.
Other options include topiramate and
gabapentin. [music]
For a severe tremor that medicines do

deep in the brain without any cut to the

There are also wrist devices [music]
that send gentle electrical pulses
through the nerves.
These are worth asking a neurologist
about.
And now, as promised, eight practical
[music] tricks that help today, with or
without medicine.
One,
use weight.

Weighted cutlery, a heavier mug, a

[music] can make a real difference.
Many are sold as aids for tremor.

When you eat or drink, rest your elbow
on the table and keep your arm close to

An electric toothbrush, an electric

Telling people, "I have a tremor. It is

So, let us recap.

Essential tremor shows up when you use

Three home tests can help you describe
it.
>> [music]
>> Hands in your lap versus arms out, the
