records.text:
Stool color after 60: what does each color mean, and when do black or red stools need help today?

Most stool colors are harmless and come from food or tablets. But black and red can be signs of bleeding. In this video we go through every color one by one: brown, green, yellow and greasy, pale or clay-colored, black, and red. You will learn the harmless causes (iron tablets, Pepto-Bismol, beetroot, leafy greens), the warning signs, and exactly when to see your doctor, when to call the same day, and when to call 999 or 911.

There is also a special section for anyone on blood thinners or aspirin, and a simple 2-second "look before you flush" habit.

💬 Which color surprised you most? Tell us in the comments.
👍 Please share this with a friend or family member over 60.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Look before you flush
0:20 Why stool is brown
1:26 Brown: every shade
2:24 Green stool
3:37 Yellow, greasy and hard to flush
4:50 Pale, white or clay-colored stool
6:37 A quick recap
7:17 Black stool: harmless causes
8:45 Black stool: the dangerous cause
10:02 How to tell iron from blood
10:41 Black stool: when to get help today
12:01 Red stool: harmless causes
12:47 Red stool: what it can mean
14:03 Blood from the bottom: when to act
15:18 If you take a blood thinner
16:02 Other bowel cancer symptoms
16:57 Free home bowel screening test
18:05 Your 2-second toilet check
19:12 The stool color chart
20:31 Final words

IMPORTANT: This video is for general education only and is not personal medical advice. Never stop, start or change a medicine, including a blood thinner, without speaking to your own doctor or pharmacist. If you have a lot of blood, red toilet water, clots, or black stool with faintness, dizziness, vomiting blood or severe tummy pain, call 999 (UK), 911 (US) or your local emergency number now.

#stoolcolor #healthafter60 #seniorhealth #bowelhealth #bloodinstool

subtitles.plaintext:
Before you flush today, stop for two
seconds and look. Most
stool colors are harmless.
But two are different. Black
and red can be a sign of bleeding,
and sometimes they mean you should get help
today, not next week.
Let us go through every
color and exactly when to act.
First, a quick picture of
why stool is brown at all.
Your liver makes a fluid called bile. It
helps you digest fat.
Bile starts out green-yellow.
As it travels through your gut,
enzymes change it, and the color slowly
turns from green to brown.
So brown is the color of a gut that is
doing its normal job.
Mayo Clinic, one of the best-known
hospitals in the United States,
puts it simply, "All shades of brown, and
even green, are considered typical.
Only rarely does stool color
point to a serious problem."
That is the calm part.
Keep it in mind as we go,
because most of what you see in the toilet
will fall into the normal group.
What changes the color? Two things, mostly.
What you eat and drink, and
how much bile reaches the stool.
Medicines and
supplements can change it too.
And blood, from anywhere in
the gut, can change it a lot.
That is why we will spend
the most time on black and red.
Let us start with the good news. Light
brown, mid brown, dark brown.
All of these are normal. Your shade can
change from day to day.
A day with more vegetables, a day with more
meat, a cup of strong tea or coffee,
a change in how much water you drink. All
of these can move the
shade a little lighter,
or a little darker. That is not a warning.
What matters more than the exact shade is
change that does not go away.
If your stool has been one way for years,
and now it has looked different for weeks,
with no food or medicine to explain it,
that is worth mentioning to your doctor.
Not an emergency. Just worth a check.
And remember, color is
only one part of the picture.
Changes in how often you go, or in the
shape and softness of
your stool, matter too.
We will come back to those near the end.
Next, green. Green stool often worries
people, but it is usually harmless.
There are three common reasons. The first
is food. Green leafy
vegetables like spinach and kale,
and anything with green food
coloring, can turn stool green.
Think of a green iced cake at a birthday
party, or a very green smoothie.
The second is iron tablets. Iron
supplements can turn stool green,
and often dark green to almost black. We
will talk more about
iron when we reach black,
because it matters there. The third reason
is speed. Remember the
bile that starts out green.
If food moves through the large bowel too
quickly, for example
when you have diarrhea,
the bile does not have time to change to
brown. So the stool comes out green.
So when is green worth a call? If it comes
with diarrhea that does not
settle, if you feel unwell,
or if it keeps going for weeks with no food
or tablet to explain it,
ask your doctor or pharmacist.
On its own, after a big plate of greens,
green stool is usually
nothing to worry about.
Now yellow. And here, the color is only
half the story. What really
matters is what comes with it.
Watch for stool that is yellow or pale,
looks greasy or oily,
smells much worse than usual,
floats, and is hard to flush away.
Sometimes you need to
flush two or three times.
That pattern can mean there
is too much fat in the stool.
In other words, your body is not absorbing
fat properly from your food.
Why might that happen? Mayo Clinic names
"malabsorption", for
example celiac disease,
where gluten damages the lining of the gut.
The NHS lists very smelly
poo that floats and is hard
to flush as one symptom of chronic
pancreatitis, a long-term
inflammation of the pancreas,
the organ that makes the juices that digest
fat. A very fatty meal
can do this once. A rich,
greasy takeaway, for example. That is not a
worry if it settles.
But if greasy, floating,
smelly stool keeps happening, please see
your doctor. And see
them sooner if it comes with
tummy pain or with weight loss you cannot
explain. Now we move to one
of the more important colors.
Pale, white, gray or clay colored stool.
The color of putty or wet clay.
Remember, bile is what makes stool brown.
So when stool turns
very pale, it can mean that
not enough bile is reaching the gut. One
cause, as Mayo Clinic
explains, is a blockage in the bile
duct, the small tube that carries bile from
the liver and gallbladder
into the gut. Gallstones
can do this. So can problems in the liver
or the pancreas. There are
some harmless reasons too.
If you had a barium test, an x-ray where
you drink a white
liquid, your stool can be pale
or white for a day or two. Large doses of
bismuth, the ingredient in Pepto-Bismol,
and some antacids that contain aluminium
can also make stool lighter.
But here is the combination
I want you to remember. Yellow skin or
yellow whites of the
eyes. Darker pee than usual.
Paler poo than usual. Sometimes itchy skin
too. That group of
signs is called jaundice.
The NHS says jaundice can be
a sign of something serious,
such as liver disease, and that you need to
get urgent medical help.
In the UK, that means an
urgent appointment with your GP or calling
NHS 111 the same day. In
other countries, call your
doctor's surgery that day and say the word
"jaundice". If your stool is
pale once, after a barium test,
and then goes back to brown, that is
expected. If it stays pale
for more than a day or two,
and you have not had a barium test, call
your doctor. Let us
take a short breath here,
because this can feel like a lot. So far,
brown is normal. Green is
usually food, iron or speed.
Yellow and greasy needs a check if it keeps
happening. Pale with yellow eyes and dark pee needs help the same day.
Before we get to the two colors that
matter most, I would love to know,
did anything so far surprise you? Write the
color that surprised you in the comments.
It helps other people your age find this
video, and I read them.
Now, the most important part of this video.
Black and red. Black
stool. This one needs care,
because black can be completely harmless,
or it can be a sign of
bleeding high up in the gut.
So let us first clear the harmless causes,
then talk about the dangerous one,
and then exactly how to tell them apart.
The harmless causes first.
Iron tablets. This is the most common
reason older people
see dark or black stool.
The NHS medicine page on ferrous sulfate,
the most common iron
tablet, says darker than usual
poo is common when taking iron, and is
usually nothing to worry
about. Bismuth. That is the
active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol and some
other tummy medicines.
It can turn the stool,
and sometimes even the tongue, black.
Foods. Black licorice, and a lot of dark
foods like blueberries,
can make stool look dark or black. So if
your stool turns dark a
few days after you started iron tablets,
and you feel well, that is usually the
tablet. But, and this
is an important but, even the
NHS iron medicine page says, talk to a
doctor or call 111 straight
away if your poo is black,
tar-like or red, or has blood in or on it,
or if you also feel unwell.
So being on iron does not mean every black
stool is the iron. Which
brings us to the dangerous
cause. Black stool can be a sign of
bleeding in the upper part of the gut,
such as the stomach. When blood travels a
long way through the gut, it gets digested,
and it turns from red to black. So it does
not look like blood at
all. It looks like black tar.
Where does that bleeding come from? A
common cause is a stomach
ulcer, a sore in the lining
of the stomach, or the first part of the
small bowel. The NHS says
the risk of stomach ulcers
increases as you get older. Two of the main
causes are an infection called H. pylori,
and taking anti-inflammatory painkillers
like ibuprofen regularly.
And here is the part that
matters most for people over 60. Many of us
take medicines that
make bleeding more likely.
The NHS names aspirin, anti-inflammatory
painkillers such as ibuprofen, and blood
thinning medicines, called anticoagulants,
such as warfarin and
apixaban. These are important
medicines. They prevent strokes and heart
attacks. But they also mean that if
bleeding does start in
the gut, it can be more serious. So if you
take any of these, black
stool is something to take
seriously, quickly. So how can you tell
iron or food from blood?
The NHS describes the worrying
kind of black stool as black, sticky and
very smelly. Think of
tar on a road on a hot day.
Shiny, sticky, and a strong, unusual smell,
different from your usual. Iron tablets can
turn stool dark green or black too, so the
color alone does not
settle it. But please hear this clearly.
You cannot always tell by looking. Even
doctors cannot be sure without a test.
So if you are unsure, treat it as possible
blood and get it checked.
Here is the action plan for black stool.
Black or very dark red stool with no clear
harmless cause and you feel otherwise well,
the NHS says ask for
an urgent GP appointment
or call NHS 111. That means today. Not next
week, not after the
weekend. In other countries,
call your doctor's surgery or a nurse line
the same day. Now, the emergency signs.
Call 999 in the UK or 911 in the US or your
local emergency number
if you have black stool
and any of these. You are vomiting blood or
your vomit looks like
coffee grounds. You feel faint,
dizzy or confused. Your skin is cold,
clammy and pale, or your breathing is fast.
You have severe tummy pain. These can be
signs of a serious bleed. The
NHS lists them as reasons to
call 999 or go to A&E. And the NHS stomach
ulcer page lists poo that
is black, sticky and very
smelly in its "go now" group too. One more
thing. If you feel faint,
please do not drive yourself to
hospital. Call an ambulance or ask someone
to take you. Now the
last color. Red. Again,
let us clear the harmless causes first
because there are several.
Beetroot is the famous one. A good portion
of beetroot can turn
stool and sometimes urine,
red or pink the next day. It can look
alarming. Tomatoes and tomato soup,
cranberries, red jelly,
red drink mixes and red food coloring can
do the same. So if you ate
beetroot yesterday and the
color is the same pinkish red as the
beetroot and you feel
completely well, food is the likely
reason. If it does not clear by the next
day or so, or you are not
sure, please ask. A pharmacist or
NHS 111 can help you decide. Real blood
that is bright red usually
comes from lower down near the
end of the gut, the large bowel or the back
passage. Blood from high
up turns black, as we said.
Blood from low down stays red. Mayo Clinic
says bright red blood in
the stool often comes from
hemorrhoids, which many people call piles.
Piles are swollen blood
vessels around the back passage.
They are very common and often show up as
bright red blood on the
toilet paper or streaks on the
outside of the stool, especially after
straining. Constipation and
straining can also cause a small
tear, called a fissure,, which can bleed and
sting. But here is why I
never want you to simply assume it
is piles. The NHS says bleeding from the
bottom is sometimes a sign
of bowel cancer. And blood in
your poo, which may look red or black, is
one of the main symptoms of
bowel cancer listed by the
NHS. Blood thinners like warfarin, apixaban
and aspirin can also cause
bleeding. Most of the time
it is piles, but only a check can tell you
that for sure. So even if
you have had piles before,
new bleeding deserves a check. Here is the
NHS plan for blood from
the bottom in three steps.
Step one, a small amount of bright red
blood once on the paper.
The NHS says a small one-off
amount of bleeding is not usually serious,
but a GP can check. See
your GP if you have had blood in your poo
for three weeks, or if your poo has been
softer, thinner or longer
than normal for three weeks.
Also see a GP if you are more tired than
usual, losing weight for no reason,
or have pain or a lump in your tummy. Step
two, your poo is dark red or black,
or you have bloody diarrhea. The NHS says
ask for an urgent GP
appointment or call 111. Today.
Step three, the emergency. You are bleeding
non-stop or there is a
lot of blood. For example,
the toilet water turns red or you see large
blood clots. The NHS
says go to A&E or call 999.
In the US, call 911 or go to the emergency
room. And again, do not drive yourself.
A special word for anyone on a blood
thinner or on aspirin. If you
see black stool or red blood,
please do not stop your blood thinner on
your own. These medicines
protect you from strokes
and clots and stopping them suddenly can be
dangerous too. Instead, call your doctor,
your anticoagulant clinic or NHS 111 the
same day and tell them three
things. Which blood thinner
you take. What you saw, and when. And how you
feel right now. They will
decide what to do with your
medicine. And of course, if you have any of
the emergency signs, call
999 or 911 straight away.
Color is only one clue. The NHS lists the
main symptoms of bowel cancer,
and some of them have nothing to do with
color at all. Blood in your
poo, which may look red or
black. Bleeding from your bottom. Changes
in your poo, such as it
becoming softer or thinner.
Needing to poo more often or less often
than usual. Tummy pain, a
lump in your tummy or bloating.
Losing weight without trying. Feeling very
tired or breathless.
This can happen when slow,
hidden bleeding causes low iron called
anemia. The NHS says see a
GP if you have any of these
symptoms. Most of the time, they turn out
to be something much less
serious. But they deserve a
proper check and bowel cancer is much
easier to treat when it is
found early. There is one more
thing you can do that does not even need a
symptom. In England,
the NHS offers a free home bowel
cancer screening test to everyone aged 50
to 74 every two years.
It is called a FIT test.
You collect a tiny sample of poo at home
and post it back. It checks for tiny
amounts of blood that
you cannot see. If you are 75 or over, you
can still ask for it. The
NHS says you can call the
bowel cancer screening helpline on 0800 707
6060 and ask for the test.
If you live outside England,
ask your own doctor what bowel screening is
offered where you
live. Two important things
about the test. A positive result does not
always mean cancer. It
means blood was found and needs
to be looked into and the cause can be
something like polyps or a
small tear. And a clear result
does not always mean you do not have bowel cancer.
So if you have symptoms,
see your GP even if your last
screening test was clear. So here is a
simple habit for every
day. Look before you flush.
Two seconds, that is all. If the color
seems unusual, ask
yourself three questions. One,
what did I eat or drink
in the last day or two?
Beetroot, greens, licorice, blueberries,
tomato soup, something with food coloring?
Two, have I started a new tablet? Iron,
Pepto-Bismol, an
antacid or a new antibiotic?
Three, how do I feel? Well or faint, dizzy,
in pain or tired in a new way?
If there is a clear food or tablet reason
and you feel well, watch it
for a day or so. If there is
no clear reason, if it keeps happening or
if you feel unwell, ask for
help. And if you are caring
for a parent or partner, it is kind to ask
gently, have you noticed
anything different in the toilet?
Many older people feel embarrassed and will
not mention it unless asked.
Let us put it all together.
Brown, any shade. Normal. Green. Usually
leafy greens, food
coloring, iron, or food moving
through quickly. Ask if it keeps going with
diarrhea or you feel
unwell. Yellow, greasy,
smelly and hard to flush. See your doctor
if it keeps happening,
sooner with weight loss or tummy pain.
Pale, white or clay. If it comes with
yellow eyes or skin and dark
pee, get help the same day.
Black, could be iron, bismuth or licorice.
But black, sticky,
tar-like stool can be bleeding.
Get help today. Call 999 or 911 if you also
feel faint, dizzy, vomit
blood or have severe pain.
Red, could be beetroot or tomatoes. Bright
red blood is often piles,
but always worth a check.
Dark red or bloody diarrhea, get help
today. Lots of blood, red
water or clots, call 999 or 911.
And if you take a blood thinner, never stop
it on your own. Call
for advice the same day.
Your stool will never be the most pleasant
topic at the dinner table.
But two seconds of looking each day can
help you catch a problem
early when it is much easier to
fix. If this was useful, write "checked" in
the comments so I know you
will look before you flush.
And please share this with a friend or
family member over 60.
It might be the video
that helps them speak up.
Take care of yourself
and thank you for watching.

After 60, the riskiest part of a shower is not the water. It is the few minutes after you turn it off. In this video, Dr Nimra explains 6 small, cheap changes that protect you from dizziness, dry itchy skin and bathroom falls, and answers the question: how often should you really shower after 60?

The 6 changes:
1. Finish lukewarm, and sit for a minute before you stand
2. Pat your skin dry, don't rub
3. Put on a cream within 3 minutes
4. Dry between your toes (and keep cream away from there)
5. Get dressed sitting down
6. Calm the night-time itch the right way
Bonus: how often should you shower after 60?

💬 Tell me in the comments: which of these 6 changes will you try first?

👍 If this helped, please share it with someone you love who lives alone, and subscribe for calm, simple health advice for life after 60.

▶ Watch next: After 60, a Handful of This Fruit Helped Protect Hip Bones for a Whole Year
